title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
body_text: HackerTube – karpathy karpathy Home Blog HackerTube 31 Oct, 2026 It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org ! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews , filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
body_text: Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it | What's new What's new Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao Home About Career advice On writing Books Mastodon+ Applets Subscribe to feed Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it 1 November, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: Frank Calegari | by Terence Tao [This is a guest post by Frank Calegari . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Why we should not be sad The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy? Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent. Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament : Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved. I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance. How would I respond to that? The classification of finite simple groups. I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith). The classification of finite simple groups was in many ways a huge success, but it was also a failure in that it — apologies to my group theorist friends and collaborators — cooled a lot of the interest around the subject. The “famous problem” had gone, and mathematicians on the whole turned their attention elsewhere. And yet, there remain very rich questions in finite group theory and even about the classification itself (to name just one: John Conway’s favorite question is why does the Monster group exist? ). Perhaps for some fields, the OpenAI dump feels like how a group theorist may have felt in 1970 if the classification was dumped in their office, not in the form of the actual papers, but printed out on a spirit duplicator, smudged a little, then spread randomly like confetti all over the floor. Right now, we need efforts like that of Gorenstein, Lyons, and Solomon and their work on the revised classification. If this was all we had to do, then it would be a fairly thankless task. But we also have the responsibility not to pronounce the subject “done” but rather — with these new tools available — ripe for further investigation. When mathematicians lament the winding paths missed by the construction of a galactic bypass, they need to realize that those old paths still exist and seek them out. And we need to reward that behavior when it comes to offering people jobs. The promise of AI, and the (dis)-unity of mathematics: Since I was 15, I’ve wanted to know what was. First, there was the childhood fantasy of finding a formula that Euler missed. But soon one learns more: how Grothendieck’s period conjecture, together with a sufficiently fine understanding of the geometry of mixed Tate motives (following work of Don Zagier, Sasha Goncharov, Francis Brown, and others) gives a completely satisfying structural, conjectural explanation of what’s going on. The irrationality of , or even its transcendence, is a mere shadow of the actual interesting underlying problem. Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of has inspired me for over years not because of its conclusion, but for how it reveals the tiniest hints of some still secret story relating algebraic -functions to arithmetic. I hope AI can help mathematicians break out of the straitjacket of being constrained by the first natural conjecture they cannot prove, and work on unraveling the deeper mysteries woven throughout our subject. In the last thirty years, progress in mathematics by humans has been remarkable. But at the same time, I have felt a growing unease; the number of times I have seen mathematicians of all levels being unable to explain to someone even slightly outside their field why what they are doing is interesting has been distressing. The natural grooves of our profession have very much been bent toward more narrow technical expertise than a bigger vision. AI allows us an amazing opportunity to broaden ourselves as mathematicians. I have tried (not always successfully) to be broad as a mathematician. I had some help by the fact that, while I knew since I was 17 that I wanted to work in algebraic number theory and the Langlands program, I grew up in the crucible of Melbourne University, which was a home to many Thurston students and low-dimensional topologists. This meant I was bathed in the sweet liqueur of hyperbolic 3-manifolds. That exposure has helped my career immeasurably. As with any two deep areas of mathematics, hyperbolic three-manifolds and arithmetic are much more closely connected than would first appear. But it’s still hard to be an expert on both, let alone pursue a crazy idea combining them. Let me get technical for a moment. For every imaginary quadratic field , there are many commensurability classes of compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds indexed by non-split quaternion algebras . Manifolds in each of these commensurability classes give rise to elements in via the decomposition of into hyperbolic tetrahedra, and their volumes are always rational multiples of . I have always had this idea that one could conceive of elements in these different commensurability classes as forming some type of geometric Kolyvagin system (“Heegner points”) associated to , which one could yoke together by some unknown integral arithmetic version of the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence. This is not a question I have pursued, for two reasons. First, there were so many underlying conjectures involved that any result I could prove was going to be conditional on many of them, something that’s not always appreciated by the mathematical community. Second, assembling all the technical background to formulate such an idea precisely would have taken a huge amount of background work. Now, with AI, the barriers to trying such a problem are much lower. It’s not trying to prove a theorem. It’s trying to explore some completely new direction that may or may not be nonsense. There are so many problems in mathematics that are still so fresh and vital but were previously untouchable that the opportunity to approach them is massively exciting. We need to be more ambitious, to create bold research plans that weren’t even conceivable a year ago. This is not to say that everyone must (or must not) use AI. But we have to rethink and readjust what’s important. Proofs of major conjectures, using AI or otherwise, are going to remain part of the new mathematics. But working toward broader programs (new and old) and structural understanding is going to play a more fundamental role. Christian Szegedy raised the following point: Mathematics prided itself on being meritocratic, with deep reverence for the explorers: the people who could climb what nobody else could. That specific kind of heroism will matter less, and other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world. I’m ready to board the plane, because I want to see what’s there. At the same time, I would add that people who previously have been walking around on earth with their eyes closed are not going to recognize anything however high they fly; I still believe that many of the skills that mathematicians have now will not only be transferable but vital to the new world order. The difference in reaction between the optimists and the pessimists is that, for the pessimists, the game is over. For the optimists, the game has just changed. I acknowledge that there are aspects of our mathematical culture that we treasure that won’t survive, and it is only human to grieve that loss. But there now exists an amazing new tool to study mathematics. To turn away and say that the community of mathematics as it currently exists is more important than mathematics itself would be a terrible mistake. The ugly truth. For all that everyone has been saying on this blog and elsewhere about how mathematics is about understanding, it takes one look at the arXiv to see many people in our profession rushing out AI-assisted papers in a somewhat unsightly rush to be the “first” to prove things. As many others have noted, there is quickly becoming a gulf between the ability to produce novel proofs and the ability to either demonstrate understanding or push the subject in new and interesting directions. As people crank out more and more results, the Leiden declaration is being honored more in name than in spirit, and it seems like “business as usual” except with a much more compressed time scale and the constant threat of being scooped hanging over people’s heads. To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof. Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs. Our obsession with conjectures tends to greatly undervalue the exploratory work that makes answering (or even asking) these problems possible. We are in danger of making that mistake a hundredfold now by encouraging or rewarding the rush for everyone to press the button to get these new results out as soon as possible. I would encourage all senior mathematicians (with the privilege of tenure) to take up the work of creating future problems and exploring new ideas rather than simply using AI to answer existing questions. If you, as a senior mathematician, are stressed about being scooped by AI, then you are not being ambitious enough. So what are we actually going to do? Think pieces are ultimately pointless unless they propose some mechanism for actually affecting how people act. The tools that are going to be the most effective are going to be economic rather than rhetorical. Mathematicians want recognition, mathematicians want jobs, mathematicians want grants. The tools that we currently have to affect this are hiring and accepting papers at journals. Let me offer some very basic concrete suggestions, followed by a few details. Evaluate all work as if it is AI-assisted. Make hiring much more about personal interactions rather than a paper file. Interview postdocs and graduate students in person. Demand more from journals, and abandon those that do not adapt. Put a greater emphasis on breadth in graduate education, but do not abandon technical skills. Give better seminars. Take more ownership of the results of AI. Evaluations: Nelson Cole famously spent three years of Sundays discovering the prime factorization In , this was a contribution to mathematics. Factoring the same number in by hand would be an equally impressive feat of arithmetic, but its contribution to mathematics (even if it had not previously been known) would be far less, since this can be done on a computer algebra system in far less than a second. It’s obvious that AI is changing the economics of what is “easy” or “hard” — much has already been said about the coming collapse of the theorem economy. In time (perhaps quickly) there will emerge a new sense of what remains a substantial contribution to mathematics, whether it be asking interesting questions, developing new programs, or something completely different. In the future, I see no reason to reward a paper based purely on a result that could be produced by machine, whether it was or not. A new proof can still deserve substantial credit for the ideas it introduces, even when its conclusion is already obtainable by machine. So why not start now? Importantly, I do not think this in any way means that access to AI will be required to make progress in mathematics — as long as we continue to value human understanding. While I feel that this is the most controversial recommendation, I also feel it is the most inevitable. It requires relinquishing an aspect of our reward structure that has been around for a long time, but at the same time a structure that will make no sense in the future. Right now, the use of AI carries a stigma, and the phrasing of many AI disclosures reads more like an attempt to minimize the contribution of the machine. If we evaluate every paper as potentially AI-assisted, then we must insist that its authors explain why the mathematics is interesting, what questions it raises, and how it connects to the broader subject. Don’t we want people to be doing this anyway? Hiring: It’s not going to be possible to get people to change unless we change how we evaluate people at the level of hiring. Lazy committees in the past have sometimes pointed toward a JAMS paper, an Annals paper, or some other collection of publications to justify how a candidate is impressive. I am looking for a narrative of where you want mathematics to go, the technical ability to explain why this may be possible, being able to converse about many areas of mathematics, and a demonstrable record of having done all of this in the past. This is not in any way a radical new idea. The hiring process is going to have to be much more about personal interactions than a paper file. It should become standard practice to interview not only for tenure-track jobs, but also for postdocs and graduate student positions. I’m sure we have all had the experience of admitting a graduate student who was “working on higher homotopy theory” to only find out after they are admitted they can’t compute the homology of the circle. At the same time, I have interviewed candidates at the tenure level whom I was initially ambivalent about, but after a 30 minute conversation in my office I was totally convinced that here was someone who not only had a deep vision of mathematics but who was also able to communicate this to their colleagues. Once we take this approach, we then have the responsibility to train our own graduate students to be better able to communicate mathematics, something that we should take much more seriously. Note there is also a difference between knowing mathematics deeply and explaining it fluently; they are related but different skills. Ideally I want both, but it is the first that I ultimately value more highly. Journals: The journal system was in dire need of reform even before AI. Our current incentives already are to produce more and more incremental mathematics which is only flooding the system. The radical overhaul required is not going to happen through consensus agreements with editorial boards. (Do you know how hard it is to get academics to agree on anything?) Being accepted by a journal has long since ceased to be a guarantee of correctness (if it ever was) and has simply acted as an imprimatur of quality. I explained above the philosophy of how I think we should evaluate manuscripts going forward. On that basis, I would say that a significant proportion of papers posted to the arXiv should not be published anywhere. If journals demand much more from a paper in terms of writing, ideas, and exposition, I think that would make life better for everyone — editors, reviewers, and even ultimately authors. If editorial boards are unable to adjust, then a more radical idea is to (at least temporarily) abandon journals altogether. (I still see a place for journals which emphasize exceptional utility and clarity (consider Essential Number Theory )). I am not advocating that people stop writing papers, but removing the fig leaf of journal publication forces the paper to stand on its own merits. Is the paper telling a compelling story? Is it Lean-verified? We should be producing fewer (and better) papers, not more. Autonomously AI-produced proofs, hopefully Lean-checked, also have their place, and should be recorded as part of our collective body of knowledge. (see hexagonmath .) Graduate students, first-year courses, and seminars. One of the thorniest issues we face is how to train graduate students. The typical thesis has always been to assign a problem in the overhang, an exercise that will teach the student the technical skills to solve a variation on some old problem, with the expectation that, as they continue, they can expand the techniques they’ve learned to new cases and then hopefully branch out to wider problems. In an age where such a thesis can be produced by the press of a button, we need to re-evaluate based on what we hope a good student will be doing in the future. Even with AI resources, no one is going to be able to explore the links between compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds and Kolyvagin systems if they don’t know what either of these terms means. (And even if somehow they could, why would they care?) It has become much more important to give students a broader overview of mathematics as a discipline. What I want a graduate student to achieve at the end of their PhD is a view of mathematics that extends well beyond their discipline, and yet with demonstrable technical skills on at least some class of problems. Often, students graduate with technical skills in a subarea, but their experience with other aspects of their area, let alone other areas of mathematics, consists of technical instruction which they have since forgotten, without any real vision. I advocated above that we need to evaluate work as if AI was involved. But this does not imply that we don’t need to teach students to do deep mathematics without AI just as the existence of computers doesn’t mean we should no longer teach children arithmetic. This has consequences for what we teach, as well as how students learn to talk about it. A graduate course should leave students with some understanding of what the topic makes possible elsewhere in mathematics. We should expect them to retain a sense of the questions and connections, even when they have forgotten some of the technical details. If we are to evaluate people more on how they can demonstrate understanding in person, we clearly need to be far more conscious of training our students to explain mathematics to other people, either in person, or in seminars, and to their peers. We need to work on giving our students opportunities to learn this skill. Remember that the most successful cohorts of students are the ones who learn together and who talk mathematics with each other. We should also not forget that not everyone who completes a PhD in mathematics goes on to academia. We should also ask whether the length and structure of doctoral training serve students who will pursue careers outside academia. Seminars: Seminars are traditionally where someone presents the details of their latest result. Because math is difficult, this almost always consists of explaining some minor tweak to a previous method, often without anywhere near enough broader context to make it interesting. Instead, seminars should rarely be focused entirely on new work. They should be framed around the broader interesting questions, explaining the avenues on which we are stuck, on which we can make progress, on which we are hopeful, and then perhaps at the very end explaining some novelty, if there is any. This is how I have always encouraged my students to give talks! As senior faculty we all need to be vocal in our seminars demanding more from our speakers. Ownership. Mathematicians as a profession would do well to take more ownership of these results. What has come out of the machine has been built on the intellectual foundations of several millennia of human mathematical endeavor. Once you start to take credit on behalf of humanity (rather than attributing these results to either a Silicon Valley tycoon or a mathematical Twitter buffoon), you’ll immediately start to feel much better. The world is looking at us. My dean recently visited New York to meet with donors and other friends of the University of Chicago, and everyone she spoke to, regardless of whether they were a math major or not, wanted to talk to her about mathematics. The world is looking at us. There are many many people who care about mathematics without necessarily having a deep technical background ( 3Blue1Brown has over six million subscribers!). All of my friends in the humanities truly believe that having mathematicians in society both as custodians of one of humanity’s oldest intellectual activities and explorers of the frontiers of knowledge is important. I understand that some part of the culture we so deeply care about will disappear, and as humans, an emotional response to that is very natural. But this is a time to explain to everyone that there are so many great new opportunities, possibilities, and reasons to be optimistic. We are on the verge of a new era of mathematics, and I am excited to see what happens. Notes: For more context on Duminil-Copin’s remarks, see also this numberphile video . His full quote also says “We are a resilient community, and I have no doubt that we will adapt”. Many of the themes mentioned here have been brought up in other posts. To give three examples: The idea that mathematicians should take more ownership of the results produced by AI was also explored in Nestor Guillen’s post . The idea that AI gives us the opportunity to be far more ambitious is raised in Ben Antieau’s post . The idea that we need to revisit our reward structure to create the right incentives was explored in Bryna Kra’s post. title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
body_text: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks | Read the Tea Leaves Skip to content Read the Tea Leaves Software and other dark arts, by Nolan Lawson Search this blog Search home apps code talks about Previous post: « Do web components have a future if nobody is writing them? 28 Oct The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks Posted October 28, 2026 by Nolan Lawson in Web , AI . One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?” Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward: Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised) Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.) Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating) Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.: I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test. To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite. Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs , etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required. One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance. With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results. Results I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.) The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.) Cost Cost per run, in US dollars Framework Cost ($) Hono+htmx $2.67 (2.23–3.19) −0.44 +0.52 Astro $2.76 (2.16–3.63) −0.60 +0.87 Nuxt $2.82 (2.39–4.25) −0.43 +1.43 Vanilla $2.98 (2.24–3.37) −0.74 +0.39 Next.js $3.14 (2.58–4.13) −0.56 +0.99 Qwik $3.27 (2.35–3.80) −0.92 +0.53 TanStack Start $3.54 (3.11–3.96) −0.43 +0.42 SolidStart $3.79 (2.84–4.81) −0.95 +1.02 React Router $3.81 (2.82–3.97) −0.99 +0.16 SvelteKit $4.28 (3.59–4.65) −0.69 +0.37 Gracile+Lit $4.65 (3.92–5.07) −0.73 +0.42 Angular $4.97 (3.19–6.82) −1.78 +1.85 0 2 4 6 8 Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Cost ($), low to high Cost ($), high to low Show as table Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month. Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge. Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules . For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below). I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one: Click to see AI tool usage Framework Installed Used by the agents? Angular Angular MCP and Angular agent skills MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 Astro Astro MCP server MCP in 2/5 runs Gracile+Lit N/A N/A Hono+htmx Hono skills Skill tool in 5/5 runs Next.js next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill Skill files in 1/5 runs, AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs Nuxt Nuxt MCP N/A Qwik N/A N/A React Router React Router skill Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs SolidStart N/A N/A SvelteKit Svelte Claude Code plugin MCP in 5/5 runs TanStack Start N/A Skill files in 2/5 runs Vanilla N/A N/A For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely). Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment. For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure. The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost: Time per run Framework Time (minutes) Astro 8.2 min (6.2–9.7) −2.0 +1.5 Hono+htmx 8.6 min (5.9–9.6) −2.7 +1.0 Nuxt 9.0 min (8.0–17.6) −1.0 +8.6 Vanilla 10.1 min (6.9–18.6) −3.2 +8.5 TanStack Start 10.3 min (8.3–13.9) −2.0 +3.6 Qwik 10.7 min (7.1–12.9) −3.6 +2.2 SvelteKit 10.8 min (8.6–13.8) −2.2 +3.0 Next.js 10.9 min (8.3–11.9) −2.6 +1.0 SolidStart 11.2 min (8.2–15.9) −3.0 +4.7 Gracile+Lit 12.1 min (10.8–12.9) −1.3 +0.8 React Router 12.5 min (8.4–13.6) −4.1 +1.1 Angular 17.2 min (9.8–23.7) −7.4 +6.5 0 5 10 15 20 25 Wall-clock minutes from the agent’s perspective. Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Time (minutes), low to high Time (minutes), high to low Show as table Tokens per run, in millions Framework Tokens (M) Nuxt 3.85 M (3.16–8.18) −0.69 +4.33 Astro 4.13 M (3.03–7.57) −1.10 +3.44 Hono+htmx 4.26 M (3.40–5.61) −0.86 +1.35 Next.js 4.99 M (3.54–8.82) −1.45 +3.83 Vanilla 5.00 M (3.44–6.32) −1.56 +1.32 Qwik 5.64 M (3.41–7.03) −2.23 +1.39 TanStack Start 7.07 M (5.85–7.99) −1.22 +0.92 SolidStart 7.13 M (5.02–10.07) −2.11 +2.94 React Router 7.58 M (4.55–8.18) −3.03 +0.60 SvelteKit 8.53 M (6.79–9.29) −1.74 +0.76 Gracile+Lit 9.04 M (7.36–11.10) −1.68 +2.06 Angular 9.76 M (4.92–14.94) −4.84 +5.18 0 5 10 15 Cache reads, uncached input and output. Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Tokens (M), low to high Tokens (M), high to low Show as table The tokens, by the way, were reported by Claude Code. The duration is just the total wall-clock time. Quality Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly. I should first note two caveats about my benchmark: The Pokémon app is small and doesn’t represent a large, complex real-world application. Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals in general are biased against SPAs, so the MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time (TBT), JavaScript bytes, etc. I considered adding some in-app performance metrics but backed off because it added complexity and variability to the benchmark, and these would be metrics I invented as opposed to industry standards. For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them. In short: the Lighthouse scores for Performance, Accessibility, and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) are nearly saturated and don’t vary much by framework: Framework CLS Performance Accessibility Angular 0.000 98 100 Astro 0.000 100 100 Gracile+Lit 0.000 100 100 Hono+htmx 0.000 100 100 Next.js 0.000 99 100 Nuxt 0.000 100 100 Qwik 0.000 100 100 React Router 0.000 100 100 SolidStart 0.000 100 100 SvelteKit 0.000 100 100 TanStack Start 0.000 99 100 Vanilla 0.111 97 100 So to get some more interesting numbers, we need to look at other metrics. The most reliable one is the JavaScript bytes sent, which largely tracks the client-side framework size: JavaScript bytes transferred Framework JS (KiB) Astro 0 KiB (0–1) −0 +1 Vanilla 7 KiB (6–7) −1 +0 Gracile+Lit 8 KiB (1–13) −7 +5 Hono+htmx 18 KiB (18–18) −0 +0 SvelteKit 36 KiB (35–36) −1 +0 SolidStart 40 KiB (38–40) −2 +0 Qwik 40 KiB (40–41) −0 +1 Nuxt 84 KiB (83–85) −1 +1 Angular 93 KiB (81–102) −12 +9 React Router 115 KiB (115–119) −0 +4 TanStack Start 118 KiB (112–119) −6 +1 Next.js 142 KiB (136–143) −6 +1 0 50 100 150 As reported by Lighthouse. Median of 5 apps (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z JS (KiB), low to high JS (KiB), high to low Show as table The Total Blocking Time (TBT) is interesting in that it’s not purely a function of the JavaScript bytes; some of the apps spend more time on the main thread than others. That said, the numbers are all quite small: Total Blocking Time (TBT) Framework TBT (ms) Astro 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 Gracile+Lit 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 Hono+htmx 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 SvelteKit 0 ms (0–1) −0 +1 Vanilla 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 TanStack Start 1 ms (0–36) −1 +35 Qwik 3 ms (0–30) −3 +27 SolidStart 11 ms (0–12) −11 +1 React Router 17 ms (0–52) −17 +35 Nuxt 40 ms (14–54) −26 +14 Next.js 71 ms (66–121) −5 +50 Angular 103 ms (93–123) −10 +20 0 25 50 75 100 125 As reported by Lighthouse, simulated mobile throttling. Median of 5 Lighthouse runs per app, then median of 5 apps after that (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z TBT (ms), low to high TBT (ms), high to low Show as table Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is highly variable due to the aforementioned issues with the metric itself. As expected, though, it does broadly punish SPAs and reward MPAs: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) Framework LCP (ms) Astro 810 ms (792–1662) −18 +852 Gracile+Lit 956 ms (796–980) −160 +24 Hono+htmx 978 ms (977–1662) −1 +684 Qwik 979 ms (954–1278) −25 +299 SvelteKit 1130 ms (1129–1131) −1 +1 SolidStart 1204 ms (1203–1278) −1 +74 Vanilla 1667 ms (764–1676) −903 +9 Nuxt 1727 ms (1427–1844) −300 +117 React Router 1729 ms (1729–1770) −0 +41 Angular 1954 ms (1351–1955) −603 +1 TanStack Start 2028 ms (1805–2104) −223 +76 Next.js 2090 ms (1028–2187) −1062 +97 0 500 1000 1500 2000 2500 As reported by Lighthouse, simulated mobile throttling. Median of 5 Lighthouse runs per app, then median of 5 apps after that (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z LCP (ms), low to high LCP (ms), high to low Show as table Test environment: 2025 Framework 13 Laptop on Ubuntu 24.04, 4x CPU throttling, and “Slow 4G” network throttling. I only ran Lighthouse’s mobile tests, not its desktop tests. Note that the wild variance in the Next.js numbers can be explained by the fact that one app avoided lazy-loading images and the other four didn’t . Astro and Vanilla have similar swings that appear to be caused by prioritization or LCP quirks. In general though, it’s unsurprising that the metric tends to reward MPAs that paint quickly with HTML rather than SPAs that paint after client-side JavaScript runs (along with possibly multiple throttled round-trips to grab the Pokémon data). Ignoring variance, LCP here is mostly a function of JavaScript bundle size. (Qwik is a notable exception here: technically it’s an SPA that uses client-side routing, but it scores among the MPA frameworks.) Note though that some of the frameworks varied in whether they focused more on the client or the server, or even whether they used a client-side framework. For example, the Gracile agent didn’t even use Lit in two runs . For “Vanilla,” the agent had full latitude (aside from being told to use Vite), but still chose to build an SPA all 5 times. SSR vs CSR is also partly where the trouble with Angular came from: in 2 runs, the agent built an SSR app that rejected non-localhost (even though the instructions explicitly said that the app would be behind a reverse proxy). I considered this a valid failure to adhere to the spec and decided not to re-run the 2 failed iterations. (This only affects the code size and performance measurements; I have reported all 5 Angular iterations for the “cost” section.) Maintainability There are lots of ways to measure maintainability (including fancy things like cyclomatic complexity), but I decided to keep it simple and report something tried-and-true: total lines of code. Lines of code Framework Lines of code Hono+htmx 1370 (1264–1489) −106 +119 Nuxt 1415 (1382–1458) −33 +43 Astro 1461 (1379–1503) −82 +42 Vanilla 1492 (1437–1742) −55 +250 Next.js 1539 (1452–1627) −87 +88 React Router 1564 (1421–1621) −143 +57 SvelteKit 1611 (1503–1816) −108 +205 SolidStart 1630 (1528–1894) −102 +264 TanStack Start 1697 (1506–1771) −191 +74 Gracile+Lit 1717 (1412–1748) −305 +31 Qwik 1744 (1646–1827) −98 +83 Angular 2009 (2003–2051) −6 +42 0 500 1000 1500 2000 2500 Number of non-blank source file lines. Median of 5 apps (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Lines of code, low to high Lines of code, high to low Show as table To me this is one of the more interesting charts. In a sense, the whole point of a framework is to reduce the amount of code you need to maintain. In Rich Harris’s memorable words: “Frameworks are not tools for organizing your code; they are tools for organizing your mind.” – Rich Harris, “Rethinking reactivity” In the agentic era, this hits even harder because the code size ultimately impacts the number of tokens, including in future edits, meaning it affects the literal cost to maintain a codebase over time. This doesn’t mean that succinctness is the only value that matters, but it’s certainly interesting to see that Hono+htmx can do roughly the same thing as Angular with ~70% of the code (and faster, to boot). Conclusion There are many ways you could improve this benchmark. For example, you could mandate that the agent use Service Workers for offline caching, or optimize the Pokémon image files, or use lazy-loading, fetchpriority , the Speculation Rules API, etc. Even though I know a lot of these performance hacks, I deliberately didn’t steer the agents toward any of them, because it’s not what a typical vibe-coder would do. On the other hand, this entire benchmark could be cheated by just pre-generating all the HTML files as static assets (there are only so many Pokémon). I specifically forebade that in the instructions and made it an explicit check in the test harness, because I felt that it wasn’t in the spirit of the benchmark. (My aim is to simulate a large volume of possibly-dynamic data, which is more challenging than a purely static site.) You could also improve the way I ran the benchmark by running more iterations, using different coding agents, trying different effort levels, using different frameworks or different versions of the frameworks, trying with and without MCPs/skills, testing in more browsers than just Chromium, building different types of apps, etc. I didn’t do these things mostly in the interest of time. However, if anybody wants to run the benchmark themselves or fork it, it’s on GitHub , so I encourage you to go nuts. I’ll happily report your results here (along with any mistakes or flaws you may find). My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes. The benchmark itself is largely vibe-coded, although I did review the code, so if there are mistakes then please consider them mine. I’d also be perfectly happy to see competitor frameworks try to improve on what I’ve done here. I’m also not trying to vilify any particular framework. I didn’t know which one would “win” before running the benchmark, although I did suspect that MPAs would outperform SPAs (which I’ve cheerfully admitted throughout this post). You could certainly write a more SPA-favored benchmark by making the app a complex dashboard, a video game, a productivity app, etc. You could also pick different metrics: Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals are pretty tough on SPAs, so you could measure in-app interactivity instead. I’m also sure that the framework authors themselves could improve their frameworks or AI tools and do better on this benchmark. I have a strong suspicion, for example, that the current crop of MCPs and skills may be doing more harm than good. So if this post is the last word on these frameworks’ performance, I’ll be sorely disappointed. I’m sure there are also emerging frameworks that are champing at the bit to do well on benchmarks such as this one. If nothing else, I hope this post inspires you to apply additional scrutiny to your choice of JavaScript framework in this weird new era of vibe coding. Are you really picking your tech stack based on evidence? Or are you just going with what you already know? That’s certainly understandable, especially if you’re still reading, reviewing, and debugging the code yourself. But if you’ve gone largely hands-free, then what attachment do you really have to the choices you made back when you were typing code line-by-line like an animal? If you’re re-evaluating the entire way you build software, maybe it’s worth re-evaluating what you type after npm install ? Just saying. Personally, I don’t have any attachment to the frameworks I’ve evaluated above, except that I believe we should strive to build the best possible experiences for our users. I know and respect many of the authors of the above frameworks, and I know that they are working tirelessly for the same values I champion. My hope is just to push the entire community in a better direction toward better, faster, and more accessible frameworks to power the next generation of web apps. Addendum Framework versions used in the test (note Qwik had a patch release partway through the test): Framework Version Angular @angular/core 22.2.3 Astro astro 7.4.2 Gracile+Lit @gracile/gracile 0.11.0, lit 3.3.3 Hono+htmx hono 4.13.14, htmx.org 2.0.11 Next.js next 16.4.3, react 19.3.1 Nuxt nuxt 4.6.2, vue 3.5.44 Qwik @builder.io/qwik-city 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5), @builder.io/qwik 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5) React Router react-router 8.5.0, react 19.3.1 SolidStart @solidjs/start 2.1.0, solid-js 1.9.17 SvelteKit @sveltejs/kit 3.1.0, svelte 5.57.2 TanStack Start @tanstack/react-start 1.169.4, react 19.3.1 Vanilla vite 8.3.5 Update: an earlier version of this post overstated the Angular agents’ inability to build a working app. I’ve clarified the number of iterations per metric and reworded the post to avoid ambiguity. An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
body_text: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems Lina Zeldovich Photographs by Clara Vannucci November 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books. Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen. Clara Vannucci Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine now for just $19.99 This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine Subscribe For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile. “I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today? Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says. Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.  In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.  In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.  In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.  Grossi holds sheaves of his grain, cultivated on the same farm his great-grandfather tilled starting around 1915.  Clara Vannucci Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo —“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.” Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets. Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table. Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent —the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field. Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano , or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development. In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl , during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain. The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug , focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events. In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting. They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says. One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli , a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special. Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali , then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum —literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains. The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago , an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more. Grossi displays a bag of barley coffee, made with heirloom plants grown on his farm. This  barley is known as “Leonessa,” or “lioness.”  Clara Vannucci For Grossi, Perobelli’s findings offered scientific proof of his grain’s goodness. He persuaded Molino Grassi , a local organic grain company, to offer the flour to artisanal bakers. Over the next few years, Grossi upped production, so Molino Grassi could sell the flour to restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad. By the 2010s, traditional recipes were enjoying a renaissance. So were artisanal bakers and pasta makers, who also became more discerning about which grains they used, says Francesco Sottile , an expert in biodiversity of agrosystems at the University of Palermo. Ancient grains aren’t necessarily perfect. For example, Grossi has found that miracolo’s height can be a liability—which may be why it fell out of favor with Mussolini. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. But Grossi circumvented the problem by planting miracolo with shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support. “I’m quite happy because I developed something that’s like a discovery,” he says. Relying on a limited number of wheat cultivars, Sottile argues, leaves humanity vulnerable to agricultural disasters: prolonged droughts, extreme heat, new diseases or pests that develop resistance to our chemicals. Diversifying grains reduces the risk—even if some varieties succumb to environmental pressures, others will stand. Sottile shared an example. “I’m based in Sicily,” he says, where 2024 saw “one of the worst droughts in the last 35 to 40 years.” It was so bad that many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields in April of that year, realizing they wouldn’t be able to reap the seeds they sowed. Sottile was heartened to see a better fate among smaller-batch farmers who grew heritage grains, more resilient to extreme weather. “Most of the farmers who were adopting ancient grains, they were able to collect, to harvest,” Sottile says. The world needs more crop biodiversity, he adds—including more ancient grains like grano del miracolo. By the same token, we need more people like Grossi, who, much like the ancient grain he sows, have the tenacity to make a miracle happen. Stories of gods and grains “Miracle wheat” is hardly the first divine cereal. Across millennia, gods have taught mortals how to earn their bread By Sonja Anderson Louvre Museum / Public Domain Greece: While Dionysus provided grapes and Athena was responsible for olives, the goddess Demeter brought grain to the Greeks. In myth, the latter goddess taught farming to a man named Triptolemus (pictured at right), then sent him out on a winged chariot to deliver the knowledge to all of Greece—an episode immortalized on ancient vases. Mesopotamia: Ancient Sumerians of the Fertile Crescent attributed farming to Ashnan, the grain goddess, “whose face is honey-covered / The lady, the procreatress, the vigor of the land,” per an ancient Sumerian poem. In myth, Ashnan and her sibling Lahar, deity of livestock, once drunkenly debated whether grains or sheep were more important. Enlil and Enki, the paramount Sumerian gods, declared Ashnan the winner, saying that without grain—often fed to herds—there could be no sheep. Egypt: Osiris ruled over death and the afterlife but was also a god of fertility, and it was said he taught mankind to cultivate wheat. Ancient Egyptians became famously adept at managing this crop: Their growing seasons regularly produced surpluses, thanks to the Nile’s floods. Some priests honored Osiris by planting grain in earthenware shaped like the god. China: Some ancient Chinese myths trace the country’s agriculture back to one emperor of legend: Shennong , born of a princess and a dragon some 4,000 years ago. The ruler supposedly had a bull’s head and a man’s body and is known as the divine farmer, or emperor of five grains (including rice, millets and wheat). He taught his people how to till their land, expanding the ancient Chinese diet—consisting mainly of meat, clams and wild fruits—to include grains and vegetables. Mexico: Quetzalcoatl was a deity of the Aztec civilization who, according to myth, created the humans of our current era—the Fifth Sun—and their world. He taught people how to carve rocks, dye cotton, read the stars and—most important—grow food. One day, Quetzalcoatl observed a black ant carrying a kernel of corn, turned himself into an ant and followed the insect through a crack in a stone mountain, where he found a trove of maize, beans, peppers and sage. He took a corn kernel, brought it to man and taught him how to plant it. title: Running a bootstrapped SaaS for 20 years with my brother
body_text: 20 years. 766 million files. Two Chameleons. - The Zamzar Blog Skip to content Close Menu Search for: Search The Zamzar Blog Free Your Files Menu 20 years. 766 million files. Two Chameleons. by The Zamzar Team October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 In 2006, two brothers launched a website using dial-up modems and a battered book on writing HTML4, named it after a character who woke up as a giant insect , and hoped someone might find it useful. Twenty years and 766,615,348 file conversions later, apparently someone did. Some Ridiculous Numbers Back when we launched Zamzar in 2006 we proudly offered a whopping 150 different conversion types. We now offer almost 15x that 👀, with 2,128 conversions supported in 2026. Over 550 million people have used Zamzar since launch, converting over 766 million files . We now process over 1 million API requests per day. Big numbers are great (they keep our resident stats-man Mike happy) but more important than features and numbers are the people that find and use Zamzar every day. Last year alone, we had: One visitor from the remote pacific island of Tokelau – with a population of 1,499 it is the fourth smallest sovereign state in the world. Three from Svalbard – a remote Norwegian archipelago which bans cats and has more snowmobiles than people. 38 from Antarctica 🥶 – 🙌 to the 1,000 scientists who stay there over Winter (hope the vending machines are well stocked). 41 from the Vatican – h.t. to Leo 🕍 🕊️ 🙏 We have questions … Twenty years of unexpected adventures It turns out that running a file conversion website can lead you to some pretty strange places. We’ve helped the inventor of PowerPoint recover long-lost presentations ( yes, really ), supported internet pioneer Vint Cerf in his efforts to preserve our digital history, and partnered with Xerox to help their printers turn documents into spoken word audio. We’ve been asked to convert sewing machine patterns (we couldn’t), resurrect ancient eFax files ( we could ), and solve more obscure file format mysteries than we ever imagined existed. Along the way, we’ve appeared on the BBC’s Click , received a cease-and-desist letter from Google for letting people download YouTube videos, and somehow ended up sponsoring a team of Scottish curling champions . That last one definitely wasn’t in the original business plan. Still small, still independent Twenty years on, we’re still a small, proudly independent UK company. No venture capital, no unicorn valuations, and no plans to pivot to an AI-powered blockchain for converting your Gran’s Word documents. We’ve watched countless technology trends come and go – social media, Web 2.0, smartphones, blockchain, wearable tech, NFT’s, the metaverse and more recently the arrival of Al Pacino , sorry AI.. Throughout it all people still need to convert their files. Being independent has also given us the freedom to do things our own way. We’ve supported more than 60 charities, schools and good causes, donating a portion of our profits to organisations doing far more important work than converting PDFs. The people behind the files Behind every one of these 766 million files is a real person with a real problem. Like Robin, who thought 36 pages of work had been lost to “gibberish”, until Zamzar brought them back to life. Or Simha, who discovered Zamzar through a friend in Israel more than a decade ago, and still uses us today from Mexico. It’s stories like these that remind us why we started – making someone’s day a little easier, one file at a time. THANKYOU! Mike and I have loved building and running Zamzar for the last 20 years, but we couldn’t have done it without an amazing team along the way – Suz, Nick, Louis, Grace, Mike, Anna, Sarah and Kate thanks for all you have done. And thanks also to our many, many customers who have sent us notes of encouragement over the years – we read them all and we ❤️ you all 🙂 We built Zamzar because we had files we couldn’t open, and didn’t want to download a program, requiring a CS degree to use it. It turns out 550 million other people had much the same problem. Anyway, somewhere out there is a file that won’t open. We’d better get back to work … Happy Converting, Chris & Mike Whyley, Co-Founders @ Zamzar. title: U.S. workers took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947
body_text: U.S workers just took home their smallest share of capital since 1947—and the lowest ever recorded | Fortune Search Subscribe Home Latest Fortune 500 Finance Tech Leadership Lifestyle Rankings Multimedia Trending now 1 If California undid its 'original sin' and matched Texas on taxing property, it would raise more revenue than the billionaire tax, economists say 2 Jeff Bezos once gave Eva Longoria and the admiral behind Osama bin Laden's capture $100 million—but she says you don't need wealth to give back 3 ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem 1 If California undid its 'original sin' and matched Texas on taxing property, it would raise more revenue than the billionaire tax, economists say 2 Jeff Bezos once gave Eva Longoria and the admiral behind Osama bin Laden's capture $100 million—but she says you don't need wealth to give back 3 ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem Economy Labor U.S workers just took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947—and the lowest ever recorded By Sasha Rogelberg Sasha Rogelberg Reporter Down Arrow Button Icon By Sasha Rogelberg Sasha Rogelberg Reporter Down Arrow Button Icon October 31, 2026, 10:38 AM ET U.S. workers are earning the smallest share of U.S. GDP on record. Lea Suzuki/The San Francisco Chronicle—Getty Images Google source logo Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google As corporate earnings soar and U.S. GDP balloons, the American workforce isn’t feeling the same boom. American workers are taking home less of the country’s overall income, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, and employment in the U.S. is set to continue to slow. Recommended Video Labor share, or the portion of the U.S.’s economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, decreased to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, its lowest level since the BLS started recording this data in 1947, according to its labor productivity and costs report . In the previous quarter, labor share was at 53.6%. This decade, the labor share average was about 55.6%. That’s despite corporate earnings skyrocketing, with profits for Fortune 500 companies hitting a record $2.1 trillion in 2025. The U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter last year, exceeding economists’ predictions. That growth has not only come at the expense of how much of the pie of wealth workers are taking home, but also how many Americans are in the workforce, economists warn. “That decline in the share of labor has got to be either falling earnings or falling numbers of people,” Raymond Robertson, a labor economist at Texas A&M’s Bush School of Government, told Fortune. “The falling share of income is having to do with the shift towards capital.” Indeed, there are growing signs that as national income balloons, the U.S. workforce is deflating. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2% in September, and employers added just 584,000 jobs in 2025 compared to 2 million added in 2024. The U.S. added 29,000 jobs in September, about one-third of economists’ projections. The bifurcation of corporate victories and weak labor data raises concerns among economists of jobless growth jeopardizing the U.S. workforce, as well as a K-shaped economy , where the rich get richer while the poor get poorer, becoming more exaggerated. “Data right now is very mixed,” Robertson said. “But I think it also all consistently points to this idea that things are getting worse for workers and much better for billionaires.” What is causing jobless growth? Robertson attributes weakening labor share averages to the rise in automation, which he noted is displacing workers, with productivity—a metric essentially measuring worker output—continuing to rise. Second-quarter GDP data showed nonfarm productivity growth grew 1.4% last quarter , though the rate has slowed from 2.2% in the same quarter a year ago. “All these things, bit by bit, are replacing people, and they’re concentrating income and their share of capital,” he said. Goldman Sachs analysts Joseph Briggs and Sarah Dong estimated in a report, based on Department of Labor job numbers, that AI automation could displace 25% of all work hours . They predicted that over the course of the AI adoption period, a 15% increase in AI-driven productivity would displace 6% to 7% of jobs, and, at its peak, a 1 million increase in unemployed workers, though job displacement as a result of AI has not shown up meaningfully in any economic data. The displacement could be substantial, the analysts said, but said the impacts of automation will be tempered by a wealth of new jobs created as a result of the technological changes. Automation is expected to be a boon to corporate profits and GDP, projected to boost GDP by 1.5% by 2035, according to a Wharton brief published in September 2025. Early signs indicate AI could drive productivity gains, with around 80% of employees reporting AI makes them faster at specific tasks, but only 37% of companies seeing an impact of that productivity on operating profits, according to McKinsey data , and AI operating costs continue to constrain its deployment. Robertson added that growing unemployment, which he expects to see rise over the next few months, keeps wages down, allowing margins and profits to expand. To be sure, the recent productivity surge has been an “ open question ,” Morgan Stanley economists have argued, not unanimously attributed to increased adoption of AI or automation. The analysts suggested this increase would be cyclical, or vestiges of pandemic-era habits of companies making more from less. An Oxford Economists research brief from earlier this year suggested companies are disguising overhiring-related layoffs as a result of AI, but said automation-related workforce reductions have not yet happened en masse. Additionally, while unemployment has been ticking up over the past year, it is still relatively low. Why is an immigration crackdown backfiring on U.S. labor ? Mark Regets, senior fellow at National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), sees a different reason for a slowing workforce. He told Fortune President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown has not done what Trump administration officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, said it would in increasing the number of U.S.-born workers . Instead, according to Regets, Trump’s immigration policies have not only decimated the foreign-born workforce, but has also created fewer opportunities for domestic-born workers to find jobs. NFAP data shows a 1.1 million to 1.4 million-person reduction in the foreign-born workforce since January 2025, consistent with the Congressional Budget Office’s report last year indicating shrinking U.S. population growth as a result of migrants being deported or refusing to come to the U.S. out of fear of hostile polities. “The data is raising huge red flags that we are losing immigrants of all types that we otherwise would be advancing America’s economy,” Regets said. Recent BLS data is counter-evidence to Miller’s argument that harsher immigration policy would grow the U.S. workforce. The labor participation rate for foreign-born workers fell from 66.3% to 66% from September 2025 to September 2026, and labor participation for native-born workers has similarly fallen from 61.6% to 60.9% over the same period. Fewer immigrant workers may actually make it harder for U.S.-born individuals to find work. “A company unable to find the workers it needs for some roles could shut down operations rather than continuing,” Regets said. He noted skillset diversity in a workplace could boost productivity and justify employing more people. Greater immigration can also increase consumer spending and stimulate businesses, as well as encourage businesses to take advantage of ample labor market availability and seek out their labor instead of offshoring jobs. How does the U.S. reverse a shrinking labor force ? While friendlier immigration policies could help reverse an exodus of foreign-born workers, Robertson said addressing the workplace automation push would be key to growing the U.S. workforce. “There are trades that are technology-assisted,” he said. “Those are going to be in higher demand, but you really still have to have a significant investment in skills.” The young generation of workers are already prepared to adapt to a changing labor landscape. Gen Z are flocking to trade schools in hopes of a finding a job as a carpenter or welder not so easily outsourced by AI, and in 2024, enrollment in vocation-based community colleges increased 16% , according to data from the National Student Clearinghouse. Companies have taken it upon themselves to provide reskilling opportunities to employees. A CareerTrainer survey from June found that 72% of hiring managers intended to reskill employees. While the U.S. Department of Labor updated guidelines to encourage states to adapt workplace development systems, Robertson argued the government hasn’t done enough in several decades to imbue the workforce with necessary skillsets for future jobs. “Democrats and Republicans have not significantly invested in training [or] the retraining or active labor market programs that you need to match workers to jobs,” Robertson said. “That’s the obvious solution.” Without changes, economists see the pattern of an employment slowdown continuing, but with greater concern about the ability for the U.S. economy to sustain growth. “We need job growth to have a growing economy, and I think we need job growth to pay our debts,” Regets said. “I don’t know how you have job growth with a shrinking labor force.” A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 13, 2026. More on the American workforce and wages: Goldman says the economy is rewarding capital ownership over labor —and most Americans don’t own enough of it to benefit Trump’s farmworker pay cut moved $2.5 billion a year from workers to growers. A judge says it’s illegal, and back pay could follow The minimum wage is now the lowest it’s been in 70 years—making the federal wage floor ‘ officially a poverty wage, ’ report finds Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here.
