title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4
body_text: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4 JEPSEN Blog Analyses Talks Consistency Services Ethics ParticleDB 1.1.4 Kyle Kingsbury 2026-10-31 ParticleDB is a multi-model database designed for AI workloads. We tested versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 and found that ParticleDBâs claims of âFull ACIDâ were somewhat premature. We present 96 issues in ParticleDB, ranging from the pedestrian (crashes, deadlocks, data loss, etc.) to the piquant (partially-invisible rows which could not be deleted, WHERE 4 = 5 , dropped tables re-emerging in distorted forms, confused columns, strings turning into integers, and so on). Most issues required just a single server, single client, and no faults. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, all but ten of those issues appeared resolved. However, ParticleDB continued to lose committed writes during normal operation with the default occ transaction mode, and allowed internal anomalies and Lost Update with serializable , the strongest setting. Orkes, the makers of ParticleDB, have since released version 1.1.19-rc.13; they claim that it resolves all remaining issues discussed in this report. This research was funded by Orkes, Inc., and conducted in accordance with the Jepsen ethics policy . 1 Background Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem . ParticleDB 1 aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called Particles . 2 To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces , including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics. ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor . Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductorâs queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai . Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4. While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior. 1.1 Safety ParticleDBâs home page advertised that ParticleDB was âformally provenâ with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built. ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The sync mode called fsync on each commit, groupsync batched multiple transactions into a single fsync , and nosync skipped fsync altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described sync as offering âstronger durabilityâ than groupsync . On the other hand, particledb start --help said the groupsync mode ensured that âCOMMIT waits for flushâ, and Orkesâ internal operator guide concurred: groupsync offered the âsame durability as sync â. ParticleDBâs home page proudly claimed âFull ACID. 159K TPS.â However, the text immediately below this said âsnapshot isolationâ, which is not fully isolated . Most SQL databases use the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement to control the concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB ignored or rejected these statements . In some cases it instructed users to choose READ COMMITTED , a relatively weak isolation level. In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary). Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the --txn-mode setting passed at startup. The transaction engine documentation described four modes : Mode Behavior When to use fast No locks; commit-on-write Bulk loads, single-writer benchmarks occ Overlay + commit-time OCC validation (default) General OLTP â safe under concurrency zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC; single-partition txns skip cross-partition coordination High-throughput OLTP on partition-affine workloads (TPC-C, key-value) table-2pl Exclusive table locks at first touch Strictest serialization, simple semantics This table was difficult to interpret. While the best practices documentation warned that users should âpick --txn-mode deliberatelyâ, since âit changes correctness and throughput characteristics more than SQL text doesâ, the documentation did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The fast mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The occ mode was similarly unclear. âCommit-time OCC validationâ could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but âsafe under concurrencyâ suggests it might be Serializable. The zero-copy-occ mode described a performance optimization which could be as safe as occ , but it was not described as âsafe under concurrencyââraising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally, if table-2pl offered the âstrictest serializationâ, was occ some weaker isolation level? The CLI reference page contained another table which described occ and table-2pl as âJepsen-safeâ, whereas fast was not âJepsen-safeâ, but did not explain their safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret these terms. 3 Running particledb start --help provided the following table: Mode Description fast No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe under concurrency) occ Table locks + commit-time validation (safe for most OLTP) row-2pl Alias for occ zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput safe mode) table-2pl Exclusive table locks, full serialization (strictest) serializable Alias for table-2pl serializable-ssi Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding â see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md) The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to avoid taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a row-2pl 4 alias was surprising. Moreover, âsafe for most OLTPâ undermines the claim that occ was âsafe under concurrencyâ; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads which are unsafe! Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong: occ was actually optimistic, and the row-2pl alias was to preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions of the various transaction modes. This document was difficult to interpret , but did specify the following consistency models: Mode Consistency Model fast Unknown occ-v3 (a.k.a. occ , occ-v2 , row-2pl ) Snapshot Isolation zero-copy-occ (a.k.a. zocc ) Snapshot Isolation serializable-ssi (a.k.a. ssi ) Serializable table-2pl (a.k.a. serializable ) Strong Serializable Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes, but in general, occ-v3 and groupsync appeared to be the default. 2 Test Design We wrote a test suite for ParticleDB using the Jepsen testing library . We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of un- fsync ed writes using LazyFS , and truncate or corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and all three WAL sync modes. We first tried ParticleDBâs official Java SDK. While the documentation indicated that the library was available as a Maven dependency, neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later added support for the ParticleDB Java SDK , versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2. 2.1 Workloads We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB. The rw workload performed randomly generated transactions involving reads and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer constraints on the version orders and transaction dependency graphs . Jepsenâs transactional checker, Elle , then searched for cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic phenomena like G1a (Aborted Read) . The append workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a comma-separated text field, and used SQL concat to append to them. Rows could be selected via primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic phenomena. When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single transaction, we designed an internal workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a series of randomly generated transactions involving INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE , and SELECT statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each individual transaction, reads observed prior writes. To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the internal workload, we designed the compare workload. This workload used Clojureâs test.check generative testing library to produce random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDBâs behavior was not equivalent to PostgreSQLâs, the compare workload would search for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simpleâjust a few basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic, transactions, and some simple LIMIT , OFFSET , and ORDER BY clausesâit proved remarkably fruitful. Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid internal-sim workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more complex transactions. This workload generated a random set of tables, then concurrently executed random transactions over them. It then checked each transaction independently to ensure that each of its statements observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a transaction executed DELETE ... WHERE 2 < c , then observed a row with c = 3 , we could prove that transaction was not internally consistent. 3 Results We found 96 issues with ParticleDB, which we present in several categories below. All but three of these issues occurred in healthy, single-node instances of ParticleDB. Busy readers may wish to jump to the Discussion section, which summarizes our findings. Availability and Performance Broken Features Predicates Constraints Joins Zombies State Corruption Transactions and Concurrency With Faults Additional results are presented in Appendix A : Type Safety and Syntax Arithmetic Strings 3.1 Availability and Performance Under normal operation, ParticleDB was slow, deadlocked, and crashed without warning. 3.1.1 Abysmal Performance With table-2pl (#62) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, --txn-mode table-2pl was so slow as to be essentially unusable. While some transactions might complete in a few milliseconds, most took 10, 20, or even 30 seconds, then failed. For example, take this test run with a single node running 1.1.18.4, transaction mode table-2pl , and WAL mode groupsync . With ten concurrent clients, most transactions blocked for tens of seconds before throwing could not serialize access due to concurrent update , or an IO error. High latencies ( #62 ) appeared improved by 1.1.18.6, which could execute transactions with sub-100 millisecond latencies for at least a few seconds. 3.1.2 Mystery Crash (#81) While 1.1.18.6 improved latencies, it also crashed frequently. Crashes occurred spontaneously with various transaction modes, WAL modes, and client interfaces; there was no obvious cause. Nodes would run for a few hundred to a few thousand seconds before exiting. No error messages were printed. These crashes ( #81 ) no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 3.1.3 Deadlock After Two Transactions (#27) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.8, submitting as few as two concurrent transactions to a healthy, single-node deployment could cause it to deadlock. This occurred both using the Postgres and ParticleDB interfaces. The node would log an error message like [DEADLOCK] 1 cycles detected at SystemTime ... , and an empty backtrace. In some cases new clients could attach and perform transactions; in others, new clients would also hang indefinitely. This may reflect multiple deadlock bugs. With the append workload, version 1.1.18.9 generally could not run for more than 45 seconds without locking up. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 could reliably run for two minutes without lockups, and we declared the issue ( #27 ) resolved. 3.1.4 Deadlock With table-2pl (#71) While version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 fixed the most frequent deadlocks, we continued to find deadlocks through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 when running with table-2pl . An otherwise healthy ParticleDB node would execute transactions for about 30 seconds, then get stuck forever. The node would log a similar deadlock error message to #27, and all requests with the ParticleDB client would throw PDB JDBC: null after a 100 second default timeout. These deadlocks ( #71 ) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-7. 3.2 Broken Features Orkesâ public documentation claimed broad support for Postgres features, and the internal operator guide concurred: The engine speaks PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol natively â anything that speaks pgjdbc / libpq / psycopg2 / pq connects unchanged. BEGIN , COMMIT , ROLLBACK , prepared statements, parameterised queries, and extended-query pipelining all work as expected. These claims were somewhat optimistic. ParticleDB was missing support for a wide array of Postgres features, and others were badly broken. 3.2.1 No Aggregates Within CASE (#20) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, aggregate expressions like COUNT(*) were not supported within CASE expressions. SELECT CASE WHEN COUNT ( * ) = 2 THEN 'CASE_COUNT_STAR_OK' ELSE 'CASE_COUNT_STAR_BAD' END FROM t; This threw Error: cannot evaluate wildcard expression . ParticleDB gained support for this feature ( #20 ) by version 1.1.18.6. 3.2.2 Unsupported Exponentiation (#28) ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 did not support the Postgres exponentiation operator: root => SELECT 2 ^ 3 ; ERROR: unsupported binary operator : PGExp Version 1.1.18.9 added support for the ^ operator ( #28 ). 3.2.3 Malformed Responses for Prepared Statements (#2) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, any attempt to execute a prepared statement using the Postgres JDBC driver caused an exception like Execution error (NoSuchElementException) at java.util.ArrayDeque/removeFirst . Since the JDBC driver automatically switches to prepared statements after the first few calls to execute() , this rendered the database essentially unusable. As a workaround, we disabled the clientâs use of prepared statements. Prepared statements are executed using Postgresâ extended query protocol , which takes place in several (potentially reusable) phases: Parse, Bind, Execute, and so on. Orkes believes that ParticleDB likely failed to return a response for one of those phases, or returned an extra message, causing the clientâs queue to underflow. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-1, this issue ( #2 ) appeared fixed. 3.2.4 Most Postgres Queries Fail (#83) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-7 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, many queries using the Postgres interface threw Bad value for type long: some_column . This rendered the database largely unusable. CREATE TABLE ints (a int ); SELECT * FROM ints; -> Bad value for type long : a Orkes believes this issue ( #83 ) was fixed in 1.1.19-rc.12. 3.2.5 Tuples Without Fields (#111) In 1.1.18.11.rc-18 and rc-19, queries with the Postgres interface occasionally threw errors like Received resultset tuples, but no field structure for them . 5 For example, take this test of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, with no faults, a new strict-serializable transaction mode, and WAL mode sync . It executed a transaction like: BEGIN ; SELECT * FROM t_38; INSERT INTO u_38 (d, a, c, b) VALUES ( null , null , false , "oudt1THxi" ); INSERT INTO t_38 (d, b) VALUES ( false , "BCczDbueXLz9zXnpgbdCeFbC5y6XSEys3" ); COMMIT ; This complained of resultset tuples with no field structure, suggesting an error in ParticleDBâs Postgres protocol state machine. While Jepsen has not tested this version, Orkes reports this issue ( #111 ) was fixed in version 1.1.19-rc.13. 3.2.6 Broken Postgres Authentication (#1) The Postgres wire protocol usually authenticates clients using a username and password. ParticleDB had a --pg-password option, but 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 lacked any option to set the username. Some of the documentation indicated the default username was admin , while other pages said it was particledb . Neither appeared to work; the only option was to use --no-auth to disable authentication altogether. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 introduced a --pg-username option ( #1 ). 3.2.7 Java Client Could Not Execute Transactions (#3) Version 1.0.0 of the official ParticleDB Java client refused every attempt to execute a transaction. Any call to begin a JDBC transaction, or to execute a BEGIN statement, would result in an error message: PDB wire error 1064: SQL plan error: transaction/session statements do not produce a query plan . ParticleDB 1.1.4 could execute transactions via its Postgres interface, but using the official Java SDK was essentially impossible. This issue ( #3 ) seems to have been resolved by ParticleDB 1.1.15. 3.3 Predicates ParticleDB struggled to interpret predicates. WHERE clauses failed to match rows they should have, or matched unexpected or nonexistent rows. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults. 3.3.1 SELECT Ignores WHERE Clause (#40) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, SELECT queries without a table accepted a WHERE clause, but ignored it. root => SELECT 5 WHERE FALSE ; 5 --- 5 ( 1 row ) This should have returned zero rows. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved this issue ( #40 ). 3.3.2 WHERE 1 < (a + 2) (#47) Version 1.1.1.18.9 introduced a new problem with predicates: inside a transaction, a WHERE clause which performed sufficiently complex floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a real ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 3 ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE 1 < (a + 2 ); a --- ( 0 rows ) The same problem applied to SELECT , UPDATE , and DELETE : predicates like WHERE (a * 2) IS NOT NULL would silently fail to match. However, simpler predicates like WHERE a IS NOT NULL would match correctly. The effect disappeared if the column was an integer. Moreover, some predicates which would throw errors outside a transaction would silently match zero rows within a transaction, suggesting these predicates were not being evaluated at all: root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE 1 < ( 5.0 % 3 ); ERROR: internal error root => BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE 1 < ( 5.0 % 3 ); a --- ( 0 rows ) This issue ( #47 ) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 3.3.3 WHERE 4 = 5 (#18) ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 aggressively interpreted WHERE something = x as a primary-key lookup of x , regardless of the value of something . root => CREATE TABLE t (a int primary key , b int ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 4 , 5 ), ( 5 , 6 ); root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE b = 4 ; a | b ---+--- 4 | 5 ParticleDB would ignore a row with b = 5 in favor of a = 5 : root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE b = 5 ; a | b ---+--- 5 | 6 ( 1 row ) You could write predicates over non-existent columns: root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE definitely_not_a_column = 4 ; a | b ---+---- 4 | 5 ( 1 row ) Or ask if 4 = 5 : 6 root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE 4 = 5 ; a | b ---+---- 5 | 6 ( 1 row ) By version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB had learned that not every equality comparison involved a primary key ( #18 ). 3.3.4 SELECT in a Transaction Returns Nonsense (#35) The behavior of SELECT within a transaction in ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 was thoroughly confusing. Consider a single client connected to a fresh single-node instance of ParticleDB 1.1.18.8. It creates a simple table of integers with two rows, 1 and 2 , and begins a transaction: root => CREATE TABLE t (a INT UNIQUE ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 1 ), ( 2 ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t; a --- 1 2 ( 2 rows ) So far, so good. But now consider: root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = 1 ; a --- 2 ( 1 row ) root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = 3 ; a --- 2 ( 1 row ) root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE a IN ( 1 , 2 ); a --- 2 ( 1 row ) root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE FALSE ; a --- 2 ( 1 row ) One might conclude that every SELECT with a predicate returned a single row from the requested tableâperhaps the most recently inserted row. But this is not true, because many predicates evaluating to TRUE returned nothing. root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE TRUE ; a --- ( 0 rows ) root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE 3 = 3 ; a --- ( 0 rows ) This behavior ( #35 ) seemed improved by ParticleDB 1.1.18.9. 3.4 Constraints ParticleDB often violated constraints like NOT NULL or UNIQUE , even with a single server, single client, and no faults. 3.4.1 Not-Null Constraints Allow Null (#8) While ParticleDB allowed users to add NOT NULL constraints to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored them, resulting in bizarre states. root => CREATE TABLE t (a BOOLEAN NOT NULL ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( NULL ); INSERT 0 1 While the resulting row existed in some sense, it was partly invisible. root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- ( 0 rows ) root => SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t; COUNT ------- 1 ( 1 row ) root => SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t WHERE a IS NULL ; COUNT ------- 0 ( 1 row ) In version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB started to enforce null constraints ( #8 ). 3.4.2 Unique Constraints Allow Duplicates (#9) Similarly, while ParticleDB allowed users to add unique constraints to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 simply ignored them. root => CREATE TABLE t (a boolean UNIQUE ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( TRUE ); INSERT 0 1 root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( TRUE ); INSERT 0 1 root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- t t ( 2 rows ) In version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB partially enforced unique constraints ( #9 ). 3.4.3 Duplicate Primary Keys (#29) Although 1.1.18.6 made UNIQUE constraints somewhat more robust, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 allowed an UPDATE to produce multiple rows with the same primary key. root => CREATE TABLE t ( id text PRIMARY KEY , desc text); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 'a' , 'a' ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 'b' , 'b' ); root => UPDATE t SET id = 'c' ; UPDATE 2 Selecting a row by primary key returned only one of the two rows, but other predicates could return both: root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 'c' ; id | desc ----+------ c | b ( 1 row ) root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE id LIKE 'c' ; id | desc ----+------ c | a c | b This issue ( #29 ) appears to have been fixed by 1.1.18.9. 3.4.4 Null Primary Keys (#57) Per the SQL standard, primary keys may not be null. This makes intuitive sense, since NULL represents an unknown value. ParticleDB would not allow you to insert null values for primary keys. However, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 were perfectly happy to update the primary key of one (or more!) rows to NULL . root => CREATE TABLE t (a int PRIMARY KEY ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 3 ), ( 4 ); root => UPDATE t SET a = NULL ; root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- ( 2 rows ) ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 rejected attempts to set primary keys to NULL ( #57 ). 3.4.5 Primary Key Conflicts with Deleted Rows (#82) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-11, a transaction which deleted a row, then inserted a new row with the same primary key, would abort due to a primary key constraint violation. For example: CREATE TABLE t (a int PRIMARY KEY ); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 7 ); BEGIN ; DELETE FROM t; INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 7 ); COMMIT ; The second INSERT would throw PDB wire error 1064: SQL execution error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint (key=7) , but only when using the ParticleDB interfaceâthe Postgres interface was unaffected. Orkes partially addressed this issue ( #82 ) in version 1.1.18.11.rc-9, and fixed another case of it in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 3.4.6 Lack of Primary Key Conflicts with Extant Rows (#90) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9, a transaction executing concurrently with other transactions could read a row with a primary key, then successfully insert a row with that same primary key. For example, take this internal-sim test , which created a table with two integer columns: CREATE TABLE u_14 (b int, a int PRIMARY KEY); A transaction ran SELECT * FROM u_14 and observed several rows, including {:b 1020026655, :a -1} . It then ran INSERT INTO u_14 (b, a) VALUES (-27, -1) , which should have conflicted with the extant primary key, but succeeded instead. It went on to SELECT * FROM u_14 again, and observed the newly inserted row, but not the previously existent one. This is a violation of internal consistency. As of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, we no longer observed these internal consistency violations ( #90 ). 3.5 Joins ParticleDB struggled to join tables together. The following issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults. 3.5.1 Canât Join Integers to Floats (#58) Even after agreeing that 2.0 = 2 , ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 refused to join two tables on an int and a real column: root => CREATE TABLE t (a real ); root => CREATE TABLE u (a int ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 2.0 ); root => INSERT INTO u (a) VALUES ( 2 ); root => SELECT t.a FROM t JOIN u ON u.a = t.a; ERROR: join key must be integer type Databases like Postgres would return a single row here, since 2.0 = 2 . ParticleDB gained the ability to join floats to integers ( #58 ) by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 3.5.2 Incorrect Column Names (#54) Because two tables can have a column with the same name, SQL databases generally return both table and column names, so you can tell which column belonged to which table. ParticleDB, with both the ParticleDB and Postgres interfaces, neglected to return table names. Instead, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 renamed column a in joined tables to right.a , right.right.a , and so on. Consider the following simple join across two tables t and u , both with an integer column a : SELECT * FROM t FULL OUTER JOIN u ON t.a = u.a; In Postgres this produced rows like: [{ :t/a 1 , :u/a 1.0 } { :t/a 2 , :u/a 2.0 }] Here the expression :t/a denotes column a of table t . In ParticleDB, this same query returned: [{ :a 1 , :right.a 1.0 } { :a 2 , :right.a 2.0 }] The table names are completely missing, and ParticleDB has altered the name of column a to right.a . Programs which expected typical SQL behavior would throw an error as they attempted to read columns which were not present, or could silently read null values. ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 no longer munged columns, but the database still omitted table names. The resulting name collisions destroyed information. [{ :a 1 } { :a 2 }] While Jepsen has not had a chance to test this version, Orkes claims this issue ( #54 ) was resolved by version 1.1.19-rc.13. 3.5.3 Coercing to Strings (#76) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, joins would coerce some values to strings in ParticleDBâs Postgres interface. For example, consider the following join: CREATE TABLE t (a int ); CREATE TABLE u (a real ); INSERT INTO u (a) VALUES ( 3.2 ); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 5 ); SELECT u.a FROM t CROSS JOIN u; With the ParticleDB interface, this produced the number 3.2 . With the Postgres interface, it produced the string "3.2" . This issue ( #76 ) seemed fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-21. 3.5.4 Missing Rows (#59) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, outer joins of a non-empty table to an empty one often returned no rows, even though the query should have produced all rows in the non-empty table. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a int ); root => CREATE TABLE u (a int ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 1 ), ( 2 ); root => SELECT t.a AS t, u.a AS u FROM t LEFT JOIN u ON u.a = t.a; t | u ---+--- ( 0 rows ) By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB correctly returned rows when joining to empty tables ( #59 ). 3.5.5 Column Confusion (#77) Many tables in real databases contain columns with identical names, like id or created_at . When asked to join two tables like this, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 became severely confused, even when all columns were fully qualified. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a text); root => CREATE TABLE u (a text); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 'this' ), ( 'that' ); root => INSERT INTO u VALUES ( 'is not the right column' ); root => SELECT t.a AS ta, u.a AS ua FROM t CROSS JOIN u WHERE (u.a = 'this' ); ta | ua ------+------------------------- this | is not the right column ( 1 row ) This should not have matched anythingâthere are no rows in table u where u.a = 'this' . Instead ParticleDB matched a row in table t which satisfied t.a = 'this' , then cross-joined it to all rows in u . To add insult to injury, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 appeared to swap around the output columns, producing the following table: ta | ua -------------------------+------ is not the right column | this If column t.a was of a different type than u.a , ParticleDB would try to coerce the types into compatible forms, producing bizarre error messages or delightfully weird results. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 was much less confused when joining tables containing the same column name ( #77 ). 3.6 Zombies ParticleDB often wound up with rows that could not be deleted or updated, or which persisted in some (perhaps mangled) form after their deletion. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults. 3.6.1 Total Recall (#26) In ParticleDB 1.1.17 through 1.1.18.8, it appeared impossible to delete rows within a transaction. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a boolean ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( TRUE ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> DELETE FROM t; DELETE 0 root =*> COMMIT ; root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- t ( 1 row ) We were unable to find a predicate that allowed one to delete records ( #26 ). Version 1.1.18.9 allowed transactions to mostly 7 delete rows. 3.6.2 Memento Delere (#45) 1.1.18.9 resolved issue #26, but deleted rows still lingered on in some capacity. While a transaction could not directly select deleted rows, it could observe them via aggregate functions and various predicates. root => CREATE TABLE t (a boolean ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( TRUE ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> DELETE FROM t; DELETE 1 root =*> SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t WHERE a = TRUE ; COUNT ------- 1 ( 1 row ) root =*> SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t WHERE a = FALSE ; COUNT ------- 0 ( 1 row ) The row must still be present in some sense, because these aggregate queries could observe its value via predicates. However, trying to read the row directly returned nothing: root =*> SELECT a FROM t WHERE a = TRUE ; a --- ( 0 rows ) Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 no longer allowed shades of deleted records to persist in aggregate queries ( #45 ). 3.6.3 Night of the Living Integers (#23) In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, updating an integer column could make rows impossible to delete. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (i int ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 0 ); root => UPDATE t SET i = 1.5 ; root => DELETE FROM t; DELETE 0 root => SELECT * FROM t; i --- 1 ( 1 row ) While this row appears to contain the integer 1 , that integer is special , since the UPDATE statement provided the value 1.5 . This row cannot be deleted. It does appear in SELECT , and is apparently equal to 1 , rather than 1.5 . Oddly, updating a row by primary key with the same 1.5 value did not create zombies; the problem ( #23 ) was somehow linked to predicates. ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 no longer exhibited this behavior. 3.6.4 Team Rocket (#84) Tables with a double precision column suffered from a similar problem: they could be updated with integer values, but doing so would produce zombie rows that could neither be updated nor deleted again. ROOT => CREATE TABLE t (a double precision ); ROOT => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 1.0 ); ROOT => UPDATE t SET a = 2 ; ROOT => DELETE FROM t; DELETE 0 root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- 2 ( 1 row ) If the double precision column was a primary key, these updates would produce duplicate copies of the updated row. This issue ( #84 ) affected ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, and was fixed in 1.1.18.11.rc-9. 3.6.5 A Ghost is Technically Not a Number (#78) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, NaN values stored in real or double precision columns could neither be updated nor deleted. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t; CREATE TABLE t (a real ); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'NaN' ); UPDATE t SET a = 5.0 ; -> # :next .jdbc{ :update - count 0 } DELETE FROM t; -> # :next .jdbc{ :update - count 0 } SELECT * FROM t; -> [{ :a ##NaN}] This issue ( #78 ) did not occur with the psql shell, but did happen with both ParticleDB and Postgres JDBC clients. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 seems to have fixed the problem. 3.6.6 Beached Strings (#74) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, fixed-width strings were unmodifiable unless created with exactly the right number of characters. While ParticleDB would correctly pad the string 'hi' to 'hi ' , the resulting row could neither be updated nor deleted. root => CREATE TABLE t (a character ( 3 )); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'hi' ); root => DELETE FROM t; DELETE 0 root => UPDATE t SET a = 'sup' ; UPDATE 0 root => SELECT * FROM t; a ----- hi ( 1 row ) If a fixed-width column was used as a primary key, it could be updated, but only once. Both old and new copies would appear as distinct rows. CREATE TABLE t (a character ( 3 ) PRIMARY KEY ); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'um' ); UPDATE t SET a = 'no' ; SELECT a FROM t; -> [{ :a "um " } { :a "no " }] Any further attempt to modify those rows would produce a duplicate key error, despite all the values involved being distinct. Fixed-width strings were also incomparable using the = operator. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 resolved these issues ( #74 ). 3.6.7 Pet Sematary (#46) In SQL, the DROP TABLE statement destroys a table completely. In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, it left a shadow of the table behind, whose rows would reappear in later tables with the same name and more-or-less compatible schemata. To demonstrate this behavior, let us create a table with a single row: root => CREATE TABLE t (a text, b real ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 'boo' , 18.83 ); root =*> COMMIT ; We then drop the table, and demonstrate that it no longer exists: root => DROP TABLE t; root => SELECT * FROM t; ERROR: table not found If we then create a new table with the same name and a somewhat compatible schema, rows from the deleted table reappear in the new one. However, the resurrected rows are not exactly their former selves. The floating-point value 18.83 has become the integer 19 . root => CREATE TABLE t (a text, b int ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t; a | b -----+---- boo | 19 ( 1 row ) This behavior ( #46 ) seemed linked to transactions, and no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-3. 3.7 State Corruption ParticleDB had many ways to create values which could not be read, alter values unexpectedly, create rows with incorrect or missing columns, or otherwise corrupt logical state. The issues in this section involved only a single server, single client, and no faults. 3.7.1 Unreadable Infinities (#15) In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, ParticleDBâs Postgres interface did not correctly serialize floating-point values like Infinity . One could write infinite values, but trying to read them would cause the client to throw an error. CREATE TABLE t (a real) ; INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'Infinity' ) ; SELECT * FROM t => PSQLException: "Bad value for type double : inf" With Postgres, this correctly returned the JVMâs Double/INFINITY value. NaN was serialized correctly. At the psql shell, stored values came back as inf , rather than Infinity . In version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB serialized infinite values correctly ( #15 ). 3.7.2 NaN Sometimes Converted to 0.0 (#21) ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 would sometimes (but not always!) convert the floating-point value NaN to 0.0 . For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a real ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 2.5 ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'NaN' ); root => SELECT * FROM t; a ----- 2.5 0 ( 2 rows ) Delightfully, whether this NaN corruption occurred depended on the order in which rows were inserted. If the first value inserted into the table was NaN , that and later NaN s would be preserved. Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to store NaN correctly ( #21 ). 3.7.3 Assignment of Incompatible Types (#7) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could update a column of one type to a column of a different, incompatible typeâproducing values like null or 0 . For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a INT , b BOOLEAN ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 2 , FALSE ); root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = b; ERROR: arrow compute : Invalid argument error: Invalid comparison operation: Int64 == Boolean root => UPDATE t SET a = b; root => SELECT * FROM t; a | b ---+--- 0 | f In Postgres, this UPDATE would throw ERROR: column "a" is of type text but expression is of type int . ParticleDB refused to compare this string to an integer (at least in this case), but was perfectly happy to make one equal to the other, resulting in NULL . Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to resolve this issue ( #7 ). 3.7.4 Insert Column Order Table Corruption (#16) In SQL, one usually inserts a row into a table using a statement like INSERT INTO people (name, age) VALUES ('xanthippe', 15) . ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored the INSERT statementâs columns, using whatever column order had been used to create the table originally. This produced rows with titillating properties. Consider the following pair of inserts: one with columns in the same order as the tableâs schema, and a second in a different order: root => CREATE TABLE t (a TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY , b boolean ); root => INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES ( 'x' , TRUE ); root => INSERT INTO t (b, a) VALUES ( FALSE , 'y' ); root => SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t; COUNT ------- 2 ( 1 row ) While ParticleDB thinks this table contains two rows, neither can be read via SELECT * : root => SELECT * FROM t; a | b ---+--- ( 0 rows ) In general, any query which happened to encounter a row inserted with a different column order would silently produce zero results. However, each row could be read by primary key! Note the different column orders in the output: root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = 'x' ; a | b ---+--- x | t ( 1 row ) root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = 'y' ; b | a ---+--- f | y ( 1 row ) In the preceding example, the two columns were of (somewhat) incompatible types. What happens if the types are compatible? root => CREATE TABLE t (a INT , b REAL ); root => INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES ( 1 , 1.23E32 ); root => INSERT INTO t (b, a) VALUES ( 2.34E32 , 2 ); root => SELECT * FROM t; a | b ---------------------+--------- 1 | 1.23e32 9223372036854775807 | 2 ( 2 rows ) Now the table is readable, but the data is corrupt. The second rowâs a value appears under b , and vice-versa. The floating-point value 2.34E32 has become the integer 2 63 â ââ 1 . If we attempt to delete every row from the table, something very strange happens. The DELETE leaves the differently-ordered row in place, and its originally inserted values now appear intact! root => DELETE FROM t; DELETE 1 root => SELECT * FROM t; a | b ---+--------- 2 | 2.34e32 ( 1 row ) A second DELETE statementânow that the table contains only rows inserted with column order (b, a) âcould successfully delete the remaining row. These column-order issues ( #16 ) no longer appeared in version 1.1.18.4. 3.7.5 Updates Can Insert Corrupt Rows (#24, #25) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, an update which matched no rows could instead create a new, possibly corrupt row in the table, with baffling effects. Consider a table mapping integer keys to integer values: root => CREATE TABLE t ( id int not null primary key , val integer ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> UPDATE t SET val = 10 WHERE id = 0 ; UPDATE 1 root =*> COMMIT ; This table was just created. It contains no rows, so the update should have affected zero, not one row. And yet it now contains a row! root => SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t; COUNT ------- 1 ( 1 row ) However, that row is invisible to typical queries: root => SELECT * FROM t; id | val ----+----- ( 0 rows ) root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 0 ; id | val ----+----- ( 0 rows ) root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE val = 10 ; id | val ----+----- ( 0 rows ) Although one cannot directly see the row by primary key, it can conflict with some inserts. root => INSERT INTO t ( id , val) VALUES ( 0 , 100 ); INSERT 0 1 root => INSERT INTO t ( id , val) VALUES ( 10 , 110 ); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint ( key = 10 ) âHang on,â an astute reader might exclaim. âThe row we supposedly updated had id = 0 and set val = 10 . Why did it not conflict with an insert of id = 0 ?â Quite right, dear reader! And why did it instead conflict with id = 10 ? These are excellent questionsâwhich we do not know the answer to. Pressing on: root => CREATE TABLE t ( id int not null primary key , val integer ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> UPDATE t SET val = 50 WHERE id = 5 ; UPDATE 1 root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 5 ; val ----- 50 ( 1 row ) root =*> COMMIT ; Within the transaction, the row produced by this update is readable by its primary key id = 5 . Although this table has two columns, the row is printed as if it had only one: val = 50 . As in #16, these corrupt rows caused queries that encountered them to silently return zero rows, even if there were other valid rows that would have matched. root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 6 , 60 ); root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN ( 6 ); id | val ----+----- 6 | 60 ( 1 row ) root => SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN ( 6 , 7 ); id | val ----+----- ( 0 rows ) Although our corrupt row had id = 5 (or perhaps 50 ), adding a second value to the IN predicate seems to have caused ParticleDB to ânoticeâ the corrupt row. It then failed to return the valid row with id = 6 . Depending on the table structure and UPDATE statement, rows created by updates might be structurally valid, but logically corrupt: root => CREATE TABLE t (a INT UNIQUE ); root => INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 1 ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> UPDATE t SET a = 3 WHERE a = 2 ; UPDATE 1 root =*> COMMIT ; root => SELECT * FROM t; a --- 1 3 ( 2 rows ) This bug ( #24 ) also allowed updates which would have left a rowâs value unchanged to instead throw a duplicate key exception, as they (presumably) conflicted with themselves ( #25 ). Both issues appeared resolved as of version 1.1.18.9. 3.7.6 Sometimes, Strings That Are Extensiveâ¦ Are Cursed (#37) In versions 1.1.15 through 1.1.17, text strings could be unexpectedly transmogrified into eight-bit integers. We encountered this in append tests using the official ParticleDB client, like this one . The append workload stores a comma-separated list of integers in an SQL TEXT column called val , and appends values to it using CONCAT . Most reads of val sensibly returned strings: [ "select (val) from txn2 where id = ? " 2946 ] -> [{ :val "1" }] However, after approximately 30 seconds, the ParticleDB client began returning eight-bit integers for key 2946 . Here, the keyâs value has become the JVM Byte 1 : [ "select (val) from txn2 where sk = ? " 2946 ] -> [{ :val 1 }] From this point on, some keys appeared as strings, while others returned integers. A read of key 2961 returned the string "2" , while key 2865 returned the integer 1 âthen moments later, the string "1,2" . Sometimes the integer values corresponded to the string value produced by earlier writes, but not always. For example, a transaction read key 2980 as the integer 0 âwhen the only elements appended to its string were "1" and "2" . Shortly thereafter, a single transaction read key 2980 twice and found a string, then an apparently unrelated integer: [ "select (val) from txn2 where id = ? " 2980 ] -> [{ :val "2,1" }] [ "select (val) from txn0 where sk = ? " 2981 ] -> [{ :val "1" }] [ "select (val) from txn2 where sk = ? " 2980 ] -> [{ :val 3 }] This issue ( #37 ) seemed to disappear by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 3.7.7 Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Table (#72) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1, append tests of the table-2pl transaction mode often threw errors like: PDB wire error 1064: SQL execution error: failed to create RecordBatch: Invalid argument error: Column âidâ is declared as non-nullable but contains null values This is odd. The append workload always picks a unique integer ID for every write, and never tries to write a NULL ID. It also never updates an IDâthey are set only once, when the row is created. Hereâs an example where a single SELECT statement, issued outside of a transaction, complained of null primary keys. This suggests that the table state had somehow become corrupt. We no longer observed this error ( #72 ) in 1.1.18.11.rc-7. 3.8 Transactions and Concurrency We found several problems with ParticleDBâs transactions and concurrency control. All of these occurred in single-node instances without fault injection. 3.8.1 Nested Transactions Destroy Ongoing Ones (#44) ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 allowed clients to begin nested transactions, instead of warning that a transaction was already ongoing. Any writes performed by the enclosing transaction would be lost, both within the nested transaction and after commit. root => CREATE TABLE t (a int ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> INSERT INTO t VALUES ( 3 ); root =*> BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t; a --- ( 0 rows ) root =*> COMMIT ; ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved this issue ( #44 ): issuing BEGIN within a transaction warned there is already a transaction in progress , and preserved the ongoing transactionâs writes. 3.8.2 Aborted Transactions Can Commit (#43) Between versions 1.1.17 and 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB handled aborted transactions irregularly. With the Postgres interface, an attempt to commit an aborted transaction would throw an error, as one would expect: root => BEGIN ; root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 3 ); root => THIS IS NOT VALID SQL; ERROR: sql parser error: Expected: an SQL statement, found: THIS at Line: 1 , Column : 1 root => COMMIT ; ROLLBACK Nevertheless, the writes performed by the aborted transaction persisted: SELECT * FROM t; -> [{ :a 3 }] The ParticleDB client had a different, also unexpected behavior: executing a COMMIT statement on a failed transaction returned [#:next.jdbc{:update-count 0}] , rather than an error. Although the transaction apparently committed, its effects were invisible. Both interfaces, as of version 1.1.18.11.rc-18, returned errors and did not expose the effects of aborted transactions ( #43 ). 3.8.3 Aggregates Sometimes Fail to Observe a Transactionâs Rows (#48) In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, transactions which performed aggregate queries, like SELECT COUNT(*) , could miss rows they should have matched, and return duplicate copies of rows, depending on the predicate and previous queries in the transaction. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a int ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 2 ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 3 ); root =*> SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM t; COUNT ------- 1 ( 1 row ) This table clearly contains two rows: 2 and 3 . Yet while the second row was visible to SELECT * , it was invisible to SELECT COUNT(*) . Oddly enough, aggregate functions which interacted with the columnâs value, like SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE a < 5 , sometimes observed correct state. In other circumstances, SELECT queries appeared to create duplicate copies of rows within the transaction, causing each query to observe more and more rows. These behaviors ( #48 ) no longer appeared in version 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 3.8.4 Double Trouble (#89) ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9 would occasionally return duplicate copies of a single row, even though the row had a primary key which ought to have ensured uniqueness. For example, take this append test , in which a read of key 10 returned two rows, rather than one. [{ :val "1,2,5,10" } { :val "1,2,5,10" }] We no longer observed duplicate rows ( #89 ) in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 3.8.5 Updates to Zero Values Sometimes Fail Silently (#91) In ParticleDB 1.1.18.4, a transaction could set all rows in a table to some value, receive an acknowledgement that every row had been updated, then read the table to find that some rows still had their previous values. This bug seemed to hinge on inserting rows with a special âzeroâ value: 0 for integers, 0.0 for floats, and '' for various kinds of string columns. For example: root => CREATE TABLE t (a INT ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 0 ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> UPDATE t SET a = 1 ; root =*> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 0 ); root =*> UPDATE t SET a = 2 ; UPDATE 2 root =*> SELECT t.a FROM t; a --- 2 0 ( 2 rows ) ParticleDB claimed that it updated all two rows in this table, but showed the original value of 0 for one of them. This issue ( #91 ) seemed fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2. 3.8.6 Tables With a TEXT Primary Key Are Mostly Invisible (#41) Version 1.1.18.9 fixed several safety issues, but also introduced new ones. For example, tables with a text primary key were mostly invisible to transactions: root => CREATE TABLE t (a TEXT PRIMARY KEY ); root => INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'mood' ); root => BEGIN ; root =*> SELECT * FROM t; a --- ( 0 rows ) SELECT , UPDATE , and DELETE were all affected. Rows were invisible to a broad variety of predicates, including WHERE a LIKE 'moo%' and WHERE a IS NOT NULL . However, rows were still accessible by primary key: root =*> SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = 'mood' ; a ------ mood ( 1 row ) Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 no longer exhibited these mostly-invisible tables ( #41 ). 3.8.7 A Thousand Tableaus (#38, #66, #68, #69) Perhaps owing to the single-threaded issues discussed above, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 exhibited frequent, profound transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. We routinely observed the loss of committed writes, internal consistency violations, G1a (Aborted Read), G1b (Intermediate Read), and P4 (Lost Update). In the append workload, successfully appended values would routinely disappear from later reads of a given key. Our test suite inferred every kind of cyclic anomaly including G0, G1c, G-Single, and G2-item, but many of these can be attributed to more basic issues, like write loss. These issues occurred with a single server and without faults, and affected every transaction mode, interface, and WAL mode tested. 8 Since we have already discussed single-threaded anomalies at length, we omit detailed discussions of these issues. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-1, ParticleDBâs most glaring examples of G1a ( #66 ), G1b ( #38 ), internal consistency anomalies ( #68 ), write loss ( #69 ), and so on were much diminished. 3.8.8 G-Single (#73) With versions 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22, we occasionally observed G-single , a violation of Snapshot Isolation, in single nodes without faults. For example, here are two transactions from an append test using transaction mode occ-v3 and WAL mode groupsync : The top transaction read key 9 and found it did not exist, then appended 8 to it. The bottom transaction appended 6 to key 9 . Since every read of key 9 observed a value like [6 8 12 ...] , we know that the append of 6 happened before the append of 8 . The top transaction failed to observe the bottom, even though the bottom must have occurred before the top. This is a similar phenomenon to P4 (Lost Update), and violates Snapshot Isolation. Similar behavior ( #73 ) occurred in zero-copy-occ and 1.1.18.11.rc-22âs occ . Orkes is investigating. Following our collaboration, Orkes reports version 1.1.19-rc.13 no longer exhibits G-Single. 3.8.9 Brazil (#67) In version 1.1.18.9, we found that queries for a specific row by a unique, constant integer ID would occasionally return the value of a completely different row. For example, consider this append test running against a single, healthy node with transaction mode occ-v3 and WAL mode groupsync . Reads of key 12 mostly observed values consistent with the appends to key 12 , but for a brief time observed nothing, and then the value of key 7 instead: Time (s) Value 6.02 1, 2, 7, â¦ 82 6.05 1, 2, 7, â¦ 82 6.17 6.22 6.24 1, 2, 7, â¦ 82, 92 6.24 6.25 1, 5, 8, â¦ 181, 86 6.29 6.29 1, 5, 8, â¦ 181, 86 6.40 6.49 6.68 1, 2, 7, â¦ 82, 92, â¦ 139, 142 The value [1, 5, 8, ... 181, 86] was consistent with reads of key 7 , not key 12 . For the remainder of the test, reads observed values consistent with the original version of key 12 : [1, 2, 7, ...] . This issue ( #67 ) did not appear in our tests after version 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 3.8.10 Lost Writes With table-2pl (#70) In versions 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, ParticleDBâs table-2pl transaction mode routinely lost committed writes during normal operation. For example this append test , using the ParticleDB Java client, lost writes to dozens of keys in just a few seconds. Here are some of its reads of key 187 : Time (s) Value 10.89 5 10.89 10.92 1, 6 10.92 10.92 10.92 1, 6, 10, 11 10.93 2 11.09 2, 13 Since the append workload only appends to rows and never deletes them, every read should have observed a prefix of the longest version of the list. Instead it appears that the append of 5 , then the appends of 1 , 6 , 10 , and 11 , were lost. Moreover, some of these writes were lost in the middle of a transaction, resulting in internal consistency errors. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-7, table-2pl no longer lost writes this frequently ( #70 ). 3.8.11 Internal Anomalies With occ-v3 (#96) ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2 occasionally violated internal consistency using transaction mode occ-v3 and WAL sync mode groupsync . For example, take this append test where a single transaction read nil , then [1, 4] for key 8 : [[ :r 8 nil ] [ :r 8 [ 1 4 ]]] At Read Atomic and above, two successive reads of the same key should not return different results. This also violates Snapshot Isolation and Serializability. This bug ( #96 ) may have been resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-19. 3.8.12 There is No Anti-Memetics Division (#65) ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-9.1 would often forget a column existed. A query like SELECT * FROM snacks WHERE sk = 4 would throw an error like PDB wire error 1064: column not found: sk . This issue ( #65 ) occurred in every transaction mode, but seemed to be resolved by version 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2. 3.8.13 Six Data Blockers and a Large Iced Coffee (#31) Versions 1.1.18.8 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 exhibited perplexing nondeterministic failures in the compare workload. Each test case established a fresh database client, created a globally unique table, and performed operations against that table synchronously. At no point should there have been two clients concurrently accessing a table. And yet sometimes, rows failed to appear in queries: root => CREATE TABLE t_876 (a boolean ); root => INSERT INTO t_876 (a) VALUES ( NULL ); root => INSERT INTO t_876 (a) VALUES ( NULL ); root => SELECT * FROM t_876 WHERE TRUE ; a ------ NULL ( 1 row ) One could update rows using the predicate WHERE NULL , which should never match anything: root => CREATE TABLE t_40 (a boolean ); root => INSERT INTO t_40 (a) VALUES ( FALSE ); root => UPDATE t_40 SET a = (a <= a) WHERE NULL ; UPDATE 1 In many cases single SQL statements threw errors complaining of concurrent updates, even though at most one client should ever have accessed a given table. root => CREATE TABLE t_101 ( a text COLLATE unicode PRIMARY KEY ); root => INSERT INTO t_101 (a) VALUES ( ' ' ); root => UPDATE t_101 SET a = NULL ; ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update on table "t_101" key " " Deleted rows could also remain visible: root => CREATE TABLE t_27763 ( a boolean , b boolean NOT NULL UNIQUE PRIMARY KEY ); root => INSERT INTO t_27763 (a, b) VALUES ( NULL , TRUE ); root => DELETE FROM t_27763; root => SELECT t_27763.a AS j FROM t_27763 WHERE t_27763.b ORDER BY t_27763.b; j ------ NULL ( 1 row ) These anomalies ( #31 ) occurred with all transaction modes and WAL sync modes, but attempts to reproduce them deterministically, or to narrow down their cause, were unsuccessful. They may be artifacts of a bug in the test suite, but we lacked time to investigate fully. After our collaboration, Orkes reported 1.1.19-rc.13 resolved this issue. 3.8.14 Read Skew With table-2pl (#106) With the ParticleDB interface, WAL mode groupsync , and table-2pl , version 1.1.18.11.rc-18 exhibited G-single under normal operation. Hereâs an example : T1: [[ :r 112 nil ] [ :append 112 1 ] [ :append 103 29 ] [ :append 67 105 ]] T2: [[ :r 110 [ 10 14 13 20 16 28 30 33 48 35 ]] [ :r 112 [ 1 ]] [ :r 110 [ 10 14 13 20 16 28 30 33 48 35 ]] [ :r 103 [ 1 4 11 15 17 20 24 25 ]]] The first transaction appended 1 to key 112 and 29 to key 103 . The second transaction observed the append to key 112 , but missed the append to key 103 . Since it observed but also failed to observe another transaction, this is A5A (Read Skew) . Since the first transaction read-write depends on the second, and the second write-read depends on the first, it is also G-single. Both are violations of Snapshot Isolation. We no longer observed Read Skew with table-2pl ( #106 ) by version 1.1.18.11.rc-19. 3.8.15 Stale Read With strict-serializable (#109) Version 1.1.18.11.rc-18 added a new transaction mode, strict-serializable , which may have been renamed to serializable in 1.1.18.11.rc-22. 9 Strict Serializability (also known as Strong Serializability) guarantees that all transactions appear to execute in real-time order: if T 1 completes before T 2 begins, then T 1 appears to execute before T 2 . However, this was not true in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. Healthy ParticleDB nodes infrequently but regularly exhibited Stale Read , even with WAL mode sync . In one of our testing environments, these anomalies appeared roughly every 300,000 transactions, using Elleâs exponential key distribution and 10 concurrent clients pushing ~80 transactions per second. Stale reads all seemed to share the same structure: a cycle comprising a real-time, read-write, then write-read edge. Hereâs an example involving a single key: The top transaction appended 66 to key 22209 , which was read by the middle transaction. After the middle transaction completed, the bottom transaction began, and read key 22209 without 66 . This is a violation of Strong Snapshot Isolation, and therefore Strong Serializability as well. After the conclusion of our testing work, Orkes reported that version 1.1.19-rc.10 no longer exhibits stale read ( #109 ). 3.8.16 Lost Writes (#110) In version 1.1.18.11.rc-18 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22, a healthy ParticleDB node running occ-v3 , zero-copy-occ , table-2pl , or serializable-ssi would occasionally discard acknowledged writes. For example, take this append test , which ran with WAL mode sync . Out of approximately 20,000 keys, 31 lost writes. Here are some of the reads of key 16647 : Time (s) Value 2798.88 2798.88 1, 2, 3 2798.88 1, 2, 3 2798.90 1, 2, 3 2798.90 1, 2, 3 2798.93 1, 2, 3 2798.96 1, 2, 3 2798.98 4, 5, 6, 7 2798.98 4, 5, 6, 7 2799.02 4, 5, 6, 7, 27 2799.02 1, 2, 3 2799.02 1, 2, 3 2799.02 1, 2, 3 2799.02 4, 5, 6, 7, 27 While the transaction which wrote 3 committed successfully, and its write was visible to several other transactions, the elements 1 , 2 , and 3 were replaced by 4, 5, 6, ... after 2799.02 seconds, and never reappeared. This occurred every few minutes in our tests, with both the Postgres and ParticleDB interfaces. When we introduced faults, new behaviors emerged. 3.9.1 Data Loss on WAL Bitflips (#108) ParticleDB uses checksums to detect corruption or incomplete writes to its Write-Ahead Log (WAL) files. Sometimes these checks prevented the server from starting up with corrupt data. In other cases, ParticleDB would discover that its data files were corrupt, then start up anyway, serving data to clients. Take this append test of 1.1.18.11.rc-18. At 09:25:09 we introduced two single-bit errors into one of ParticleDBâs .wal files. At 09:25:39 we read key 1754 and observed a list of 44 elements: [[ :r 1754 [ 3 5 7 9 12 13 18 19 20 22 24 25 28 30 31 33 34 36 35 37 38 39 42 43 44 45 47 50 51 53 58 59 62 63 64 65 67 68 69 70 73 75 79 80 ]] ... A few milliseconds later, we killed and restarted ParticleDB a few times. When the server came back online at 09:26:07, it logged: 2026-07-22T14:26:07.985223Z WARN ThreadId(01) recover_streaming{dir=/opt/particledb/data/wal}: spanner_wal::segment: checksum mismatch in segment tail, stopping read segment_id=0 2026-07-22T14:26:07.985235Z WARN ThreadId(01) recover_streaming{dir=/opt/particledb/data/wal}: spanner_wal::recovery: replaying valid prefix of already-sealed corrupt WAL segment (.corrupt marker present) and continuing with later segments of this stripe stripe_id=0 segment_id=0 corruption_offset=25184 valid_size=25184 recovered_entries=242 detail="checksum mismatch: stored 0xf3b8aa37, computed 0x4a774da2" However, the server went on to start up and serve client requests normally. At 09:26:09, we read key 1754 and found those 44 elements had disappeared: [... [ :r 1754 [ 81 ]] ...] Several other keys also lost some or all of their acknowledged writes. Orkes is investigating this issue ( #108 ). While Jepsen has not tested this version, Orkes reports 1.1.19-rc.12 detects bitflips correctly and refuses to start. 3.9.2 Total Data Loss With Simulated Misdirected Reads/Writes (#112) One of our file corruption faults divided a file into four-kilobyte chunks, then randomly replaced a small fraction of those chunks with other chunks from the same file. The goal is to simulate misdirected reads or writes , a type of silent data corruption that happens in some storage systems. In 1.1.18.11.rc-22, ParticleDB sometimes responded to this type of fault by forgetting every table and (apparently) deleting everything in its WAL file. For example, take this test run . At 09:53:56, the test harness shuffled 13 four-kilobyte chunks of the first .wal file aroundâapproximately one-tenth of the fileâs contents. It then killed and restarted the node. Although this file had hundreds of kilobytes in it, when ParticleDB started up it logged that there was no data on disk: 2026-07-30T14:53:58.715589Z INFO ThreadId(01) spanner_exec::engine::context: No data found in storage â starting fresh At 09:53:58, ParticleDB began throwing ERROR: table not found for every query. No request ever succeeded after this time. It appears that ParticleDB may have deleted the contents of its WAL file. A few seconds later, the test found its size was zero bytes, and the same held true at the end of the test. After we finished testing Orkes released version 1.1.19-rc.12; they believe it resolves this issue ( #112 ). 3.9.3 Internal Anomalies With strict-serializable and Process Kills (#107) With strict-serializable , WAL mode groupsync , and the ParticleDB interface, single nodes running 1.1.18.11.rc-18 exhibited internal anomalies with process kills.
