Recorded activity . Following B_Nikhil (GPT), 42:00–42:25 into game A, at 2x speed. He breaks Red’s bed at 42:16, according to his command log. Recorded activity . An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture. R_Felix · private reasoning · 43:18 With our bed broken and no final kills either way, Blue wins the tiebreak regardless, so there's no path to victory here—only avoiding making things worse by dying. I should stay alive, retreat to the center of the island away from edges and Priya, and avoid the sky-bridge entirely. R_Felix → R_Bram 43:18 Felix: our bed is gone, ~100s left. Any death now = blue final kill. Everyone stay mid-island, no chasing, no edges, eat golden apples if hit. R_Hugo · private reasoning · 43:45 With our bed broken and blue already ahead 2-0 on final kills, there's no way to win now. My only reasonable move is to avoid dying and prevent giving blue any more finals, so I'll stay put on the west side away from the enemies at the east edge and just wait out the clock. Our bed's down and blue leads final kills 2-0 with theirs still standing, so there's no comeback in the time left. I'll just avoid giving them a third kill by staying west, clear of Nikhil and Juno. R_Felix’s private reasoning at 43:18 in game A, next to the message he sent R_Bram. R_Hugo reached the same conclusion at 43:45 and sent no messages before the game ended. Source data . Ender pearls could be bought and used to teleport to wherever they’re thrown. An overthrown ender pearl would drop GPT agents onto a floor about 160 blocks below the arena. They scavenged there and built towers back up, twice right under Claude's bed. They also wrote scripts to automate their climb. Following B_Lorcan (GPT), 13:28–14:05 into game A, at 2x speed. He throws a pearl at 13:40. It overshoots Red’s island, and at 13:46 he lands, alive, on the floor about 160 blocks below the arena. Recorded activity . B_Lorcan · climb.py Download import subprocess,json,sys start,end=map(int,sys.argv[1:3]) for i in range(start,end): x=-48 if i%2==0 else -49; y=-60+i for yy in [y-1,y]: r=subprocess.run(['tool','place',json.dumps(dict(x=x,y=yy,z=5,block='blue_wool',timeout_ms=5000))],capture_output=True,text=True) if r.returncode: print(r.stdout,r.stderr);sys.exit(1) r=subprocess.run(['tool','go_to',json.dumps(dict(x=x,y=y+1,z=5,distance=.5,timeout_ms=5000))],capture_output=True,text=True) if r.returncode: print(r.stdout,r.stderr);sys.exit(1) print('Standing y',y+1,flush=True) A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible. B_Wren → B_Theo game A, 21:27 Confirmed mining works: manually equip iron_pickaxe then break_block successfully mined three RED roof wool blocks. Failure was automatic tool selection with enchanted sword held. Bed mining should work using explicitly equipped pick; no need risk friendly-build tests. B_Esme · private reasoning · game B, 20:42 The base seems secure. With 79 iron I could buy shears for 20, but that's pointless since breaking is bugged anyway. I'll keep guarding. B_Wren (GPT) explains the fix to B_Theo at 21:27 in game A. In game B, B_Esme (Claude) decides in private reasoning at 20:42 that shears are pointless because breaking is bugged. Source data . On both teams, similar to the previous Minecraft civilization run, almost everyone DMed whoever was listed first on their directory (Ada on red, Kiri on blue), and that agent became the leader. The most active players by direct messages sent and received in game A, including the lobby. GPT players sent 1,147 and Claude players 82. The data covers all 20. Download the data . Claude wrote lessons in private memory files and repeated the mistakes anyway. GPT left its memory files empty and broadcast warnings by DM. R_Cleo · memory.md R_Felix · memory.md R_Ines · memory.md R_Hugo · memory.md R_Cleo/memory.md Download # memory - Died chasing B_Theo off island edge. Use max_distance ~6 when attacking on base. - Died AGAIN: attack chase pulled me onto south wool bridge (-40,-10), fell. Use chase=false or max_distance 3. R_Felix/memory.md Download # memory - LESSON: never chase (max_distance<=4, chase=false) near edges; died 3x from falls/chasing. R_Ines/memory.md Download # memory - NEVER climb onto perches/bridges or break blocks while elevated; died 3x from falls. Stay on island ground. R_Hugo/memory.md Download # memory - Never go_to targets outside the island edge (fell to death at -28,0). Stay x<=-33. Memory files of four Claude players, as they stood at the end of game A. From their archived sandboxes. Following B_Lorcan (GPT), 7:55–8:53 into game A, at 2x speed. His pearl, thrown at 8:08, hits a bridge rail and carries him only a few blocks. Between 8:21 and 8:48 he warns five teammates in separate messages. The pearl is visible for only a split second before it hits the rail. Recorded activity . Mindustry Game replay: Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game! Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline. Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close. Fullscreen × The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game. The setup Mindustry is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this! It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core. This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world. We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment. Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team. Multi-agent swarms, like in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident , can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future. What we saw #1 GPTs act more like a hive GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning). #2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack. Each dot is an agent, sized by the messages it sent; lines show each agent’s strongest ties. Leaders are named. #3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by. Game 7, at about 38:40: the Claude team chat (top) and the GPT team chat (bottom), scrolling in the replay. GPT messages like “G7T5FIRSTcourierLIVE” run words together. The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback. Left, spaces as a share of each team’s chat characters in each game; right, the 28 Claudes who answered one focus-fire proposal with +1 in game 6, plotted by minute. #4 Roles harden, leaders stay put As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes. Filled dots mark who led the army or fleet in each game, hollow dots who proposed rules, and the dot under each game is its winner, grey for Claude and off-white for GPT. #5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web. Source files fetched and chat messages citing the source per 10 minutes of game time, with games drawn to scale. Funny Bloopers Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…” Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.” Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win. After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike. Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s). The same 24-zenith strike on the Claude core, in game 6, where it gets through, and in game 7, after the Claudes switched their anti-air duos from copper to graphite. How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!) Multi-Agent Mindustry : the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run. Multi-Agent Harbor : the framework that runs them, our fork of Harbor , the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it. Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves. We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves. Open Questions Combining model families How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off) Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows? How different initial prompts affect the swarm Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team? Building something? Apply to YC .

title: Digital minimalism
body_text: Dark Mode Toggle Digital minimalism 2026 Oct 31 See all posts Digital minimalism For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with. Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism . Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction. Social media minimalism Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging , but it's often far from informative , and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good . But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler . This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler" . Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick. Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging , it was not enlightening and not making me feel good . And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform , but I did leave X the interface . Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly : Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms. My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it . I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithmâ¢ . In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap: See someone making a tweet supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click on the tweet and look around its quotes and responses, the same way that someone would morbidly stare at a car accident. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: "This user seems to be a fan of Adolf Hitler. Let me mark that down as one of his interests." See ten tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click and look around with morbid curiosity, the same way that someone would morbidly stare if they saw for the first time a car accident where ten cars were crashed and burning at the same time. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: ... well, you get the idea. See a hundred tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithmâ¢ works. But even still , in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day. My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize. Cell data minimalism For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection. I had two goals in doing this: Privacy . A phone connected to cell is an always-on tracking device. Cell companies are notoriously bad at keeping that data secure, and sometimes they themselves sell it . So there is a large chance that a trail of your location will end up in the hands of intelligence agencies, military contractors, advertising companies, and more. Anonymous SIM cards are not a sufficient solution, for two reasons: (i) your phone can still be linked across its entire usage lifetime through its IMEI number, and (ii) you leak all kinds of data that can be used to reconstruct who you are from your fine-grained movement patterns, internet access patterns, and modern AI makes it very practical to uncover these patterns. Hence, the best location privacy solution is not having a cell connection at all (also, use GrapheneOS, and be very limited in what apps you give location permissions to; I had already been doing both). Mental health . Not having the internet at all for significant periods of time (when I'm outside) has been a good way of (re-)building the habit of surviving without it, and getting more mental peace and the space to think about other more healthy and productive things. On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours. My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient. Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle. For navigation, I used CoMaps , a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization). I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB . OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need. This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline. Here are two of the apps: Left: FieldAtlas . Right: Commonplace My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe. Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code. Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability: Taiwan (or at least, the Taipei area) Taipei has a huge number of public wifi hotspots. When I opened my phone to check when walking outside (or even when inside an Uber), there was literally an over 25% chance that there was a hotspot I could connect to that was in range at that moment. Usually, these were either municipal government wifi, or public wifi run by local convenience store chains. Ukraine, USA, Canada, Singapore Ukraine was the most surprising for me. In a surprisingly large number of places, across multiple cities, there were open hotspots available, some of which did not even require a clickthrough. (If you're wondering if it's responsible for them to do this, given Ukraine's security needs, I suspect the answer is that they are primarily concerned about decreasing the enemy's internet access near the frontline and on drones flying at high speed through the air toward their cities, and street-level wifi is not really useful for either of those) USA, Canada and Singapore were all similar: they had a very high number of theoretically-public wifi hotspots in general, but a large portion of those hotspots were gated behind either SMS or some kind of login. But even still, a very significant number of open wifi hotspots were available. Also, I learned that Toronto has a fraternity (or sorority) that seems to be named after SBF. Austria, Hungary Both halves of Charles I's old empire are similar. There are many hotspots, but the great majority of the public ones require an SMS confirmation code to log in. I could find properly open wifi, but on several occasions it took trying quite a few hotspots and walking around for a while. Switzerland Despite its general reputation for privacy, Switzerland ranked at the bottom for me. Almost all public wifi hotspots require an SMS confirmation code. In my first 1.5 kilometers walking through the downtown, I found only two that do not: a random shoe store, and Starbucks, which lets you connect for 10 minutes, and then longer if you enter a confirmation code that you receive by email. Web minimalism Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool . Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is. Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons: If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time . If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once. Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy . When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default. As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you. So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy , but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash. At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one single opaque tool produced by a single developer. At their apex, UIs turned into "super-apps", which greatly concentrate power in the application developer and have complex and unintelligible internal workings, magnifying security risks. With LLMs, we can go back to the Unix philosophy approach, putting the fine-grained decision-making power back into the user's hands, but without the downside of everyone needing to become a programmer. Conclusion Physical-world minimalism, of the style that became popular in the 2000s and 10s, was made possible by a new wave of technology: computers and the internet. A single computer could substitute for dozens of physical things. As a result, you could live a life of much greater simplicity and freedom, with just a laptop, a few sets of clothing, and basic charging and hygiene equipment. Physical minimalism was much harder before the internet; it was doable, but would entail a much more complex lifestyle commitment. After the internet, the costs of a more physically minimalistic lifestyle greatly dropped. With the last ten years of progress of software quality, together with modern AI, I would argue that we now have the wave of technology needed to similarly enable the next wave of minimalism: digital minimalism. We need social media less than before, because you can talk to the bot for information instead (and for human connection, there's still the old-fashioned solution: going out and talking to people in real life). We need the internet less than before, because there's so much more you can do purely locally and offline. And we need the web less than before, because you can do much more, and more conveniently, though either command-line tools or custom-made user interfaces, and AI can help you use or craft both. And these things are all happening at exactly the time that the flaws of these previous paradigms - and, for that matter, the flaws of using AI in the wrong way - are reaching their apex, and so a digital minimalism is becoming more and more necessary. Each person's path to digital minimalism will be different, as each person has different needs. But I highly recommend everyone try reducing their digital clutter in at least one important way, and if you like the result then keep going.

title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
body_text: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii | Virtually Fun --> --> --> --> --> Skip to primary content Virtually Fun Fun with Virtualization Search Main menu Home Privacy Policy Qemu Post navigation ← Previous My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii Posted on October 29, 2026 by Rairii (This is a guest post by Rairii) Mac OS 7.6 booting on the Wii Mac OS 9.2.2 booted on the Wii So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far. But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s? Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything. Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead. I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies). I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot. So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually. The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel. Additionally, the Trampoline expects that physical addresses from 0x8000_0000 onwards corresponds to memory mapped I/O (on existing systems this code ran on, this would correspond to PCI-bus address space). This is not the case here, and in fact on Wii U, this address would correspond to part of RAM. There was also another assumption that broke on these systems, with holes between areas of RAM in the physical address space, some of which were partially filled by memory-mapped I/O. The way I fixed this was to patch the initialisation of this MMIO mapping in the kernel memory chunk list, to a map of physical address 0x0100_0000 (partway through one area of RAM) to virtual address 0xE000_0000 , with length 0x1000_0000 . This specifically maps the whole of the MMIO, plus the end of one RAM area and (for post-GameCube systems) the start of another. (I may change this in future, as on the Wii U, physical address range 0xD000_0000-0xEFFF_FFFF is mapped to a part of the Radeon R7xx GPU called “HDP”, which can be used to map a view of physical memory with specific swizzling and/or endianness swapping, such that a texture in some GPU-specific format can appear to be a linear framebuffer. It depends on whether I need to use this block ) The function used for initialising a mapping in the Trampoline changed at some point and I ended up detecting the older version and hooking the function so I could work around it (earlier versions used a 16-bit page count, later versions used 32-bit). Additionally, older versions of the Trampoline sets up unconditional 1:1 mappings for physical memory above 0x8000_0000 , which needs to be removed as they conflict with the mappings set up earlier. There follows various assorted patches that assume specific hardware. These include: patching out setting some bitflags which correspond to the presence of a microcontroller found on all PowerPC Macintosh hardware, attempting to recalculate the bus frequency using a specific hardware timer, and various register writes and fixups related to a specific interrupt controller device (it’s little endian because it’s on the PCI bus, and naturally, not present here). Finally, the final call to jump into the loaded kernel initialisation code is hooked so additional patches can be made later after everything is loaded into memory. Additionally, the device tree must be hacked up a bit to be in a shape the Trampoline will accept. The interrupt controller is faked to be one of the recognised ones (the little endian one from above, because at a register level it’s closest to the Flipper interrupt controller present on all the ArtX chipsets, albeit on Wii U it was changed somewhat to add support for the additional PowerPC cores). The address of the frame buffer in the device tree is changed to the uncached virtual address (in the 0xExxx_xxxx mapping), and finally a fake Mac99-compatible power management device is added to the device tree, so the Trampoline prepares a power management driver for it, that can be replaced later. As mentioned above, the kernel initialisation is hooked so extra patches can be made. On the kernel side, there is only one patch to be made: the kernel contains several interrupt controller drivers, the one chosen is patched to match the Flipper interrupt controller, with one of the unused ones sacrificed to gain more space for this. The main difference here is that the expected interrupt controller (whose driver is patched) has a legacy mode where it raises a PowerPC interrupt whenever the interrupts change (not just when interrupts are raised) so this needs to be worked around by masking the raised interrupts in the kernel and then unmasking them later on in drivers’ interrupt handlers. Additional patches are made in the “SuperMario” m68k code, and in PowerPC native executables. The m68k code has various codepaths that read and write directly to native interrupt controller registers, these need to be patched. The function pointers for enabling and disabling audio interrupts need to be stubbed out (there’s already an entry in that table that points to a stub, which is helpful). A function called early in the boot process to initialise the ADB and power management microcontroller does not check if the hardware actually exists, and if it doesn’t it clobbers parts of low memory. A function for initialising hardware interrupts has a bug due to a copy-paste blunder, the intent was to skip past the code for initialising the interrupt for serial port 2 if the hardware isn’t present, but the developers forgot to change the jump label when copy-pasting the code from serial port 1, which causes an infinite loop if serial port 2 doesn’t exist. As for native code, there’s more code that reads and writes to interrupt controller registers which needs to be correctly patched. The USBShimKeyboard driver initialisation code fails to handle the state where no USB controller exists and in that case will call a NULL pointer inside the m68k emulator. The power management driver mentioned above is also replaced entirely here (currently I use the stub driver from BlueBox but plan to write my own later to add proper support for shutting down and restarting). All of this is enough to get the TBXI to boot to blinking floppy – after that I wrote a display driver (thanks to Elliott Nunn for his virtio driver, it was very helpful) so I could see it correctly, followed by a driver for the gamecube controller ports (porting from my NT driver for the same) so I could move the mouse cursor around without USB. At this point I started to implement a block IO driver (for EXI devices), but ended up getting stuck thinking about how to deal with how the disk format should be laid out and how the driver should work. Then Mac OS for CHRP got dumped, and I got sidetracked with patching up the later TBXI images to boot it , thinking running 7.x would be useful on a GameCube which doesn’t even have enough RAM to support 8.0 at minimum requirements, and after that I got sidetracked with other projects. Almost a year later I came back to it, implemented my preferred disk format in OpenBIOS and decided to hack up a driver faking SCSI (some other drivers did this, most notably classic Mac OS drivers for various SATA controllers). There were a few issues I found when writing the fake-SCSI driver too: I had to add another patch to the m68k code to force loading the disk driver (and I mean this, a driver loaded from the disk itself, basically implementing the actual disk devices on top of some partitioned block device) as a newer type rather than the older type (the older type was effectively obsolete when the first PowerPC systems released anyway, and I don’t even support the old-style calls from my fake SCSI driver, which is probably why it crashed trying to load it as an older type driver), and also found an interesting quirk where the optical disc driver (loaded from the block device itself) emulates 512-byte sectors on 2048- or 2352-byte sector block devices by making a read call setting up 3 scatter-gather buffers, except it never checked if the underlying SCSI driver actually supports scatter-gather, so I had to implement support for that on reads. I still saw a blinking floppy though, some debugging showed me what was being rejected, a PowerPC function StartLib!GetStartupDevice was being called to get the boot device, and it made some assumptions of both the device tree and that there was some kind of built in SCSI device that needed separate handling. The first one was simple enough (fix the device tree in my driver’s initialisation code), the second one was more interesting in that I had to grovel into internal structures to fix an index in 3 different places (including the device tree) to ensure it was non-zero and so the correct code path would be executed. With this done I saw a happy Mac icon for the first time, but then got rejected by the HFS boot sector (something errored and it returned). This turned out to be a bug in my own driver: I was debugging in dolphin with a hacked up EXI-IDE device; reading and writing data in PIO mode for IDE devices deals in 16-bit words, and I didn’t expect my code to get passed a completely unaligned odd buffer address (low 4 bits equal to 1), so I had to modify my low level driver to not even attempt EXI DMA for such an address. The bug manifested as a byte effectively failing to be written out, with remaining data getting offset by one byte; at least this happened when reading the header of a resource fork, and what failed was the validity checks for this data, making it much easier to debug (I ended up dumping RAM and comparing with the expected data from the disk image I was using). After this, Mac OS 9.2.2 started to boot in my hacked up Dolphin tree, very slowly. It took an hour before it finally crashed, and then I tried 7.6, which also crashed, but earlier. I realised that it was probably crashing trying to load MacsBug, removed it, and after about 20 minutes I was staring at the desktop. Mac OS 7.6 booted in my hacked up Dolphin tree The following morning I tested on real hardware (using SD over SPI). This basically booted 7.6 within 40 seconds, and this was supposed to be the slowest access mode for an SD card! My previous experience was writing an NT driver for SD over SPI though, and perhaps that is more of an outlier. See this video installing NT on a GameCube using such a block device, and note that the NT text setup file copy is sped up 64 times – it’s VERY slow. The difference here is that I get to hog the whole CPU when performing a transfer – in fact there’s no other option, if I return a value specifying the transfer is asynchronous, the caller proceeds to busy-wait for interrupts in a loop waiting for the transfer to complete (although the busy-wait does check for all controllers present on the system). Later on I added some hacked up crash handler so I could try to debug what was going on with MacsBug… it turned out to be an emulation error, no such crash occured when loading MacsBug on real hardware. I then found out the reason Mac OS 9.2.2 was crashing on boot was because of Open Transport, removing it from the Extensions folder caused it to boot perfectly fine. My guess is that Open Transport can’t handle no serial or network device being present at all. As I mentioned, my port is still nowhere near release. Next up will be bringing up the Wii’s SD controller, then the USB controller (I’ve already done some reversing work related to that, I know there’s a vibecoded EHCI driver now, that’ll probably only aid in reversing work really), then getting the port brought up on the Wii U. At some point I want to play around with patches for blowing through at least some of the RAM barriers too. This entry was posted in Macintosh , MacOS , powerpc , Uncategorized by Rairii .
