title: Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man
body_text: Remembering Patrick Stewart: What Captain Picard taught us Skip to main content Sections Epaper Sports Red Sox Patriots Celtics Bruins High Schools Colleges Women's Sports TV & Radio Metro Weather Politics Transportation Education Cambridge & Somerville Around Mass. Investigations Obituaries Death Notices Games & Puzzles Align Crossword Mini Crossword KenKen Sudoku Word Flower Horoscopes Business Technology Economy Housing Real Estate Biotech The Fine Print Bold Types Politics Money, Power, Inequality Climate Spotlight Opinion Ideas Columns and Op-eds Editorials Letters Cartoons Say More podcast College Town New Hampshire Business Politics Education Crime Health Commentary Rhode Island Things to Do Rhode Island Podcast RI Food & Dining Politics Business Arts Crime World COVID Globe Magazine The Big Day Dinner with Cupid Perspective Connections Lifestyle A Beautiful Resistance Food & Dining Comics Games Travel Pop Culture Relationships Love Letters Real Estate Arts Books Movies Music TV Visual Arts Performing Arts Cars Real Estate Events Share a News Tip or Story Idea Search Podcasts email Created with Sketch. Newsletters More Print this Article View Comments Metro Weather Politics Sports Business Puzzles Rhode Island Globe Magazine Opinion Health care Arts Lifestyle Education Cambridge & Somerville Money, Power, Inequality Spotlight Technology Climate Cars Real Estate Events Appreciation Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man Print this Article View Comments Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. GLOBE PHOTO/ELLIOTT MARKS Patrick Stewart died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him. For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family. Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy. Two of the Globe’s dyed-in-the-wool Star Trek fans share what Captain Picard, and Patrick Stewart, meant to them. John Hilliard: For a younger, and likely wiser generation, stanning a bald middle-aged English actor who played a French guy on a spaceship may be a questionable life choice. But here is the thing: What made Stewart resonate as Picard was how he rooted the character, as in the best of fairy tales, in emotional truth. Jason Laughlin: I agree. Picard seemed as real as the complex characters that would start to populate prestige TV a decade later. But unlike anti-heroes such as Tony Soprano and Walter White, Stewart gave us a nuanced character we actually admired. He loved his job. He had passions like archaeology , Shakespeare , and music . He held to his ideals even when it meant terrible personal sacrifice. In the mess of American politics over the past 20 years, there have been so many times I’ve longed for a Picard-style speech that makes right and wrong crystal clear. “You know, there are some words I’ve known since I was a schoolboy,” Picard said when a Joe McCarthy-esque admiral began witch hunting on the Enterprise. “With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably.” His character’s moral clarity, and Stewart’s conviction in delivering it, put an end to the admiral’s reign of terror. If only real world oppression could be dispelled so easily. For decades, Patrick Stewart was a star of stage and screen, but no role defined him quite like the noble space captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek: The Next Generation. STEVE FORREST/NYT JH: Full disclosure : Star Trek is a show, which Youtube will prove, that leaned hard on latex foreheads and sometimes-flimsy production to tell stories of intergalactic scallywags known as Klingons and Borg, Romulans and Cardassians. Like free office coffee, it’s an acquired taste. JL: One of my friends has a theory that if you didn’t get into Star Trek before you’re 18 years old, you’re never really going to get it. To me, what’s so accessible, and radical, about Stewart, though, was his ability to convincingly portray vulnerability while still maintaining Picard as a credible leader. One episode saw Picard return to his home village in France to heal from a traumatic assault. At the conclusion, Stewart surrenders the control that was his character’s hallmark and falls into the mud, sobbing, over his failure to fight off his assailants. It’s a raw, real, depiction of a broken man. Stewart shifts from total collapse into slow recovery by reconciling with his brother. Grief is replaced by warmth, and Stewart sells it perfectly. JH: Totally. He knew how to make that show work for him. That’s despite an episode where he faces off against a giant, talking tar pit . Or the one where he sells eating a sandwich in the sci-fi version of the family station wagon. Or when he chugs Ecto Cooler (remember Ecto Cooler?) with a depressed Scotty , from the original Star Trek, and shares stories about first jobs and first girlfriends. He even shows up in tights, as discount Errol Flynn Robin Hood. As a kid raised on television before there was an Internet, Stewart plugged into a world where figures like Mr. Rogers and Bob Ross presented a model for manhood that was gentle, patient, and a teacher. Stewart played Picard in a similar vein, basically everyone’s Space Dad. Even as recently as last month, Captain Jean-Luc Picard appeared on Star Trek Day in the London Underground. Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for Paramount+ JL: This is embarrassing, but the first TV episode that moved me to tears was from The Next Generation. “ The Inner Light ” has Picard experience an entire lifetime as a different person on an alien planet. Again, the actor found his character’s humanity through slow revelation that perhaps a life with a wife and children is just as big an adventure as exploring space. “Seize the time,” Picard says to his daughter in this other life. “Live now! Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.” At the end of the episode, it’s revealed the decades he spent in that other life were an illusion he experienced in less than an hour. The only tangible thing he has from that world is a flute he learned to play in that other life. In the final moments, Picard plays it again, and without saying a word Stewart plays absolute heartbreak. Seeing a strong, confident leader who was able to express regrets, sadness, and heartache left a lasting impression. Well into his 80s, Patrick Stewart was playing the character he became best known for. Richard Shotwell/AP Photo/Richard Shotwell JH: Imagine you’re a kid watching TV, and you feel kind of alone, unsure of yourself. And then there’s Stewart, in full reassuring teaching mode. It’s the episode where Wil Wheaton’s character is struggling with tremendous guilt as he tries to hide his complicity in the death of a friend. Stewart, as Picard, is on to him. Wheaton’s character, Wesley Crusher, is as close to a son as Picard will likely ever have, and Stewart leans into Picard’s grief, grief from knowing that doing the right thing will likely destroy the younger man’s future. “A lie of omission is still a lie,” Picard tells Wheaton. Stewart’s voice cracks as Picard remembers meeting Wheaton’s character for the first time. He sat in Picard’s chair. He knew every button on the ship, every function. He was annoyed, Picard growls. Stewart pulls back. Picard never had any doubt that Crusher would grow up into an outstanding officer. Until that moment. “The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it’s scientific truth, or historical truth, or personal truth,” says Picard, who then delivers the gut punch. “If you can’t find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don’t deserve to wear that uniform.” It doesn’t matter if you know what a Starfleet is, or if someone can be an officer of one. Stewart always finds a way to connect his audience to the emotional truth. When you’re a kid, you’re looking for lessons, even if you don’t want to admit it. Stewart, as a master of navigating the human heart, understood the moment and his character. Ultimately, Picard was a teacher, and a guide, not just for the characters with whom he shared a scene, but for the audience as well. JL: Stewart was 47 when he began playing Picard. I’m just a year older than him now, and the very best of his episodes have taken on new resonance. Family tensions are real and devastating. Professional choices have lasting consequences. The melancholy of middle age lingers on the periphery of every happy moment. Patrick Stewart’s Picard still serves as a role model. He showed how to face those moments with dignity, optimism, and a belief in the enduring capacity to be our best selves. Jason Laughlin can be reached at jason.laughlin@globe.com . Follow him @jasmlaughlin . John Hilliard can be reached at john.hilliard@globe.com or on Signal at john_hilliard.70. Follow him on Bluesky at iamjohnhilliard.bsky.social. title: Azure's Weakest Link – Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises
body_text: Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Azureâs Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises | Binary Security AS Home About Careers Services Penetration Testing Application Security Security Engineering Posts Contact Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Posted by Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud on October 02, 2026 · 18 mins read In my previous blog posts, Azureâs Weakest Link? and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , I gave an overview of the severely insecure architecture behind API Connections in Azure, a part of Azure Logic Apps, and an instance of a full cross-tenant compromise using these inherent flaws. Now I am back with some more vulnerabilities in this system, each giving the same primitives to the attacker. In total, the vulnerabilities here netted me a cool $200,000. I also held a talk detailing this at Blue Hat Asia 2026, and when the recordings are out, I will add a link here. TL;DR API Connections allow anyone to fully compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend. This includes cross-tenant compromise of Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, as well as any other externally connected service, such as Jira or Salesforce. The only thing stopping exploitation is really the layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, but as you will see, it is really difficult to catch all the edge cases here. Architecture If you havenât read the first parts of this series, I would recommend checking those out first, Azureâs Weakest Link? - Part 1 and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , but if you donât care, I will go through the most important parts of the architecture first. From Microsoftâs documentation , we see a quite intriguing diagram of how the API Connection architecture is built. This basically spells out all that is needed to understand how the system operates, kudos to whoever made it! It works like this A logic app, the symbol on the bottom left, queries a shared Azure API Management instance The API Management instance first checks the swagger (OpenAPI) definition of the connector type and checks that it is a valid action A sort of key exchange happens where the input token, or key, is exchanged for the configured token for the backend service The API Management instance finishes the call with this new token to the backend instance. From this, we can surmise that if we are able to trick the API Management instance to operate on a different connection than the ones we own, we would be able to effectively use the configured token for a victimâs connection on their backend service. This service can, in effect, be anything. As you can see here , the list of backend services is effectively unbounded and includes a number of Azure services. However great the diagram is, there is one crucial omission, which we have already used to great effect in part 2 of this series. By using the ARM REST API DynamicInvoke or /extensions/proxy/ endpoints, we can directly query the APIM service through ARM. I have taken the liberty of updating the diagram to match this. Considering this, and the fact that, as a resource manager, ARM basically has full access to everything, our exploitation pathway becomes clear. We must trick the calling service into querying a different connection than ours, and thus get full control of the backend service. Caveat: It is, of course, possible for the people who set up these connections to scope their access tokens or keys so that the API Connection has minimal privileges in the backend. I would guess, however, that this is rarely done. In the case of OAuth connections, it will surely always be the token of the person who initially made the connection. And for the API key case, well, who cares enough to scope such things minimally? Microsoft doesnât, at least. Initial Exploitation The first cross-tenant exploitation I achieved in API Connections, and in fact in Azure as a whole, has already been described in part 2. As a recap, here is an example payload using the DynamicInvoke endpoint of my own connection to read the Key Vault of a different tenant. POST /subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom2/DynamicInvoke?api-version=2018-07-01-preview HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Type : application/json Content-Length : 147 { "request" :{ "method" : "get" , "path" : "path/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value" }, } HTTP/2 200 OK Cache-Control: no-cache Pragma: no-cache Content-Length: 1329 { "response": { "statusCode": "OK", "body": { "value": "dontreadme", "name": "victimsecret", "version": "7914d45aa60342809fb8cc12dc68b10e", "contentType": null, "isEnabled": true, "createdTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "lastUpdatedTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "validityStartTime": null, "validityEndTime": null }, "headers": { <Headers> } } } As you can see, itâs a pretty clear path traversal vulnerability. This implies what we already assumed: When the request fires from ARM to the APIM instance, it has rights to all connections, regardless of what it operates on. Further exploitation A couple of weeks after I reported this vulnerability, it got marked as fixed, and when I tried it again, the following error message greeted me: Now, I considered whether or not this was a sufficient fix. It seemed to restrict the paths allowed, rather than the underlying token issue, so I guessed there would be ways around it. An interesting little fact about the ARM API is that, in some cases, it might not be as much of a black box as you assume. The relevant code can sometimes be found within the resource types themselves. I do not know whether this code actually executes on these machines or is merely included as an artifact, but it is a gold mine of interesting information. So, I created a Standard Logic App, which provides a fully dedicated host, SSHed into it, and extracted the code. Lo and behold, look what I found: Can you see the fix they implemented? What was even more interesting here actually was something I found, and was not really even looking for. When searching for the actual DynamicInvoke code, what greeted me was not actually just this one public function, but four: These functions are completely undocumented, and I could find no reference to them anywhere. However, they were reachable and located along the same path. So, for instance, to hit DynamicList here, simply change dynamicInvoke in your URI to DynamicList . Knowing that the slap-dash blacklisting fix that they implemented only applied to DynamicInvoke , I assumed that these would all be vulnerable in the same way if they had the same functionality. Without boring you too much with the required arguments and return values here, the exploitation method is really quite the same, although the payload is a bit more involved. For DynamicList , you need to specify each path parameter on its own and do a bit of work to get a result, but the same logic applies. To achieve, for instance, a cross-tenant write on a victimâs SQL server through their connection, a payload like this works: POST /subscriptions/162fc6db-03cd-4fe8-ab44-dc0a947e74af/resourceGroups/api-connection/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom_validator/DynamicList?api-version=2018-07-01-preview&_=1765372176638 HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Length : 524 Content-Type : application/json { "dynamicInvocationDefinition" : { "operationID" : "nine" , "parameters" : { "one" : { "value" : ".." }, "two" : { "value" : ".." }, "three" : { "value" : "sql" }, "four" : { "value" : "88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c" }, "five" : { "value" : "v2" }, "six" : { "value" : "datasets" }, "seven" : { "value" : "victimservice.database.windows.net,VictimDatabase" }, "eigth" : { "value" : "query" }, "nine" : { "value" : "sql" }, "query" : { "value" : { "query" : "Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3)" } } }, "ItemsPath" : "ResultSets/Table1" , "ItemValuePath" : "secrets" , "ItemTitlePath" : "value" } } You can quite easily see that the first parameters here execute the path traversal and then perform an arbitrary SQL query on the database. I reported only the DynamicList case first, in the hope that they would perform a similar fix to DynamicInvoke and I would get to report on the other two as well. Sadly, their fix involved simply blocking all these endpoints. No other mitigations seem to be in place, however, so if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable. Further exploitation Messing around with paths in these dynamic calls seemed to have reached its conclusion: I couldnât get past the path limitations on DynamicInvoke , and all the other endpoints were blocked. What I needed was a different way in. As I was trying to sleep one day, it occurred to me that I had overlooked using the Logic Apps themselves. I realized that there was, in fact, a significant difference between the Consumption and Standard Logic Apps connection-creation flows. The most glaring difference is that Consumption Logic Apps, where your workflow is co-located with a bunch of others, create a Version 1 connection, while the dedicated-host Standard Logic Apps create a Version 2 connection. The following diagrams make a more subtle difference between the flows clear: Do you see the difference? Obviously, when itâs spelled out like that, itâs pretty clear what the point is. Using a Standard Logic App, after we have created the resource and added whatever authentication to the backend server we need, we authorize that specific logic app to access it using its managed identity. However, when we have a Consumption Logic App, we donât have any such identity to authorize because we donât control it. This perhaps makes some sense: we canât authorize it, so we donât. I realized that this must imply that every Consumption Logic App has implicit access to every Version 1 API Connection; the only thing stopping us from exploiting this must be some sort of input validation. The classic view of a Logic App workflow is quite restrictive in its input, but there are both the API endpoints, and the Code view in the GUI that allow us to play around a bit more with the inputs. This allows us to see the inputs in more detail, edit them, and even add more. The obvious trick of changing the referenced connector to a victimâs connection fails, as the runtime performs extensive validation that you own the connection. We have the codebase, though, so we can try to find all the valid parameters. It did not take much searching for me to discover the host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter. I canât quite get my head around why this parameter is included, nor why itâs still accepted to this day, but it works in the way you would expect. After performing a series of validations on the connection referenced in host.connection , you can specify that it should use something completely different instead of the runtimeUrl baked into that connection. As long as the host ends with azure-apihub.net , it will also include the required Authorization header. What happens when this workflow is run then? The keen-eyed reader might notice that the runtimeUrl used in the exploit is not just the connectionId . This is because some extra elements get added to the URI, but it is of no consequence to us; the exploit works fine. Manna from the heavens I, of course, reported this to Microsoft again, and they spent some time working up a fix. When it finally came through, the exploit returned an error message: The host API runtime URL is not valid for the API connection '/subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/keyvault-1'. The runtime URL path must match the expected API endpoint 'https://logic-apis-norwayeast.azure-apihub.net/apim/keyvault/cbfb0f4313144117a7440368902bb871?' for the referenced connection. Either omit the 'host.api' input property, or correct the runtime URL to match the API associated with the connection. Except for the excessive length of this message, it seems like quite a suitable fix. The runtime URL must exactly match what is expected; otherwise, no dice. Apart from just removing the parameter altogether, itâs quite sane. Unless, of course, it checks that value at the wrong time: This works again, with the same result. Whatâs going on here is that the validation happens before the path is normalized, so the runtime thinks the URI is pointing to my referenced connection, but the APIM instance sees it differently. And just like that, I got another critical vulnerability. The fun does not stop there. When Microsoft managed to scrape together a fix for this path traversal, a surprising thing happened. The original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated, and as a result, you could perform that attack again. I would include some pictures, but they would be the same pictures as above, so you can just imagine them. Reporting and rewards Altogether, API Connections have netted me five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in Azure, which is perhaps more than expected. All vulnerabilities reported here were fixed within a reasonable time after I submitted the reports, and while there were some disagreements with MSRC along the way, overall, I am quite happy with the results. title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
body_text: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dhruv Mehrotra Maddy Varner Dell Cameron Security Oct 28, 2026 4:00 PM Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents The leaked records include the locations of ICE and CBP facilities, workers’ cell phone numbers, and the members of groups tied to wiretap programs, Palantir software, and xAI’s Grok chatbot. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents , including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119 , a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool. “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.” Updated 10/28/2026 at 8:02 pm ET: Added comment from DHS. Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: Go inside the world of digital security with Kernel Panic We sexted with a Muse AI agent —and Meta says that’s totally fine Big Story: Meet the DEA’s premier crypto detective OpenAI is pissing off mathematicians Want better search results? Ali Winston Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records Bluesky tells WIRED it blocked links to a leaked archive of information on 41,000 ICE, CBP, and other DHS workers because it contains people’s contact information, shared without their authorization. Dhruv Mehrotra ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud Documents obtained by Democracy Forward show that ICE looked into feeding voter roll data into the ELITE tool, normally used to identify targets for deportation. David Gilbert Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists Despite Illinois’ sanctuary laws, local police in and around Chicago helped ICE investigative agents track activists engaged in First Amendment–protected activities. Ali Winston The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. Vittoria Elliott Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy As a recent government report on DOGE shows, even getting basic information out of the Trump administration will put a new Congress to the test. Vittoria Elliott Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls From heat maps to Signal chats to war rooms, volunteers across the US are ready to act if federal immigration agents show up on Election Day. David Gilbert ICE Agent at NYC Shooting Has History of Alleged Violence and Illegal Arrests Brenden Cuni, an ICE supervisor, has been accused of excessive force and tackling a pregnant woman to the ground. Several of his arrests were later found to be unlawful in federal court. Dhruv Mehrotra Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer Investigators also sought permission to use an invasive surveillance tool called a cell-site simulators against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate. It’s not clear he had the legal authority to do so. Molly Knight Raskin A Mysterious Nonprofit Run by SpaceXAI’s Top Lawyer Is Paying the Salaries of Government Workers The National Design Studio has been something of a successor agency to DOGE. A WIRED investigation finds some of its members are on loan from a nonprofit run by SpaceXAI’s general counsel. Vittoria Elliott WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original. This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life. What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Try it in your browser . The playground sets a page as a printer's proof, grows its margin with the same Lua, and hands it back as an SVG, a LaTeX preamble or a Typst page setup. Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free. Two documents share one package, and two more ( showcase.tex , spread.tex ) show what else it does: florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex composition authored : stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown : a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page preview PDF florilegium.pdf florilegium-grow.pdf Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn. Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below. 300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems. Watch it grow as it grows with the free space it fills Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives. The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way ( build/grow-6.gif and .mp4 , about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles. The margin reads the text showcase.tex , "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows. Download showcase.pdf . The grown margin can respond to the document around it: Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". Flowers at the headings. With the option sections , every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. Seasons. With the option aging , the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead. One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where. Visitors Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out. Any ink The whole palette comes from one color, ink : Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray. Themes Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric , and with theme=math . The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, florilegium-theme-<name>.lua , that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own. theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes ( florilegium-theme-geometric.lua ). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page. theme=math is no plant at all ( florilegium-theme-math.lua , drawing from florilegium-figures.lua ): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families , figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is. \usepackage [ grown,theme=geometric ]{ florilegium } % or theme=math; the whole document \florilegiumtheme {math} % or from the page this stands on A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed. Less in the margin Seed 6 at density=1 , 0.5 , 0.2 and 0.05 , and at intensity=0.5 . A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme: density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things. intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail. \usepackage [ grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6 ]{ florilegium } At the defaults ( 1 and 1 ) every page is exactly the page it was before. One ornament in the text Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one. \usepackage [ nomargin ]{ florilegium } % ornaments only, no garden in the margin \florilegiumornament {leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf. \florilegiumornament [size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower} Any primitive works ( leaf , leaflet , flower , blossom , bud , bell , lily , cyme , umbel , butterfly , bee , bird , hedera , sparkle , ...), and so do the current theme's ( crystal with geometric ; knot , polyhedron , koch , ... with math ). Both sides of the page spread.tex , pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme. Download spread.pdf . The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document ( twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left. SVG, Typst and the browser The playground , seed 12 in autumn on a last page. The page is a proof, and its colophon, the note a book keeps about its paper, ink and printing, is the set of controls: every copper word in it can be changed. The same Lua can draw a page without TeX. florilegium-svg.lua runs the package's own code with a small stand-in for the few parts of TeX it touches (the page's lengths, the page number, and the node a drawing goes into), takes the PDF drawing commands that florilegium-ink.lua writes as it always does, and rewrites them as SVG. Nothing in the drawing code changes, so the garden is the one LuaLaTeX would draw, not an imitation of it. texlua florilegium-svg.lua --seed 7 > margin.svg # page 1 of a document with \def\florilegiumseed{7} lua florilegium-svg.lua --seed 7 --season autumn --ink 5B2A1F --left 25mm --right 65mm > margin.svg texlua florilegium-svg.lua --help # paper, margins, two-sided pages, the last page, themes... make svg SEED=7 # -> build/svg-7.svg Any Lua 5.3 or 5.4 runs it. Lengths are read the way TeX reads them and colors are converted the way xcolor converts them, so --seed 7 with the default margins gives, byte for byte, the drawing on page 1 of florilegium-grow.tex built with seed 7. The SVG is a whole page with a transparent background, which makes it a page background anywhere. In Typst: # set page ( paper : " a4 " , margin : ( left : 68mm , right : 22mm , top : 32mm , bottom : 30mm ), background : image ( " margin.svg " , width : 100% , height : 100% )) The playground runs the same files in the browser with wasmoon , Lua 5.4 compiled to WebAssembly, in a background worker, and a page grows in about a second. Seed 7 there is seed 7 here. The proof is the control surface as much as the colophon is: the measure above it sets the margin, and dragging the foot of the text up makes a last page. The text on the proof describes the garden that just grew, from the counts the growth loop keeps. Under it, the page can be seen as readers with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia see it, with the distance between the ink and the accent measured for each (Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes's model, distances in Oklab); a pairing that is hard to tell apart is flagged when you choose it. Next to the download are the LaTeX preamble, the Typst setup and the command line that make the same garden, and the address bar keeps every setting, so a garden can be shared as a link. To run it from a clone, serve the repository with make playground and open http://localhost:8000/web/ . The math theme works too. Its figures come from the same Lua; its equations and symbols, which TeX sets in a PDF, are set in the playground by MathJax in the same Computer Modern, and the command line leaves them out. The fonts are served with the page (IM FELL DW Pica, and Latin Modern renamed as its license asks), so nothing is fetched from a font service. In PostScript postscript/florilegium.ps : the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how. The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from florilegium-ink.lua , florilegium-flora.lua and florilegium-grow.lua , procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file: gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden -dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the interpreter's calendar picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map: Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end. Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY . Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition. postscript/README.md describes every option, how a seed is chosen when none is given, what to know before porting the file further, and the tests that postscript/check.sh runs on it. The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps , with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency. Build LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex , whose seasons need the page count). make # the four PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* make svg SEED=7 # the same page as SVG, without TeX -> build/svg-7.svg make playground # the browser playground at http://localhost:8000/web/ No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it: docker build -t florilegium-tex tools make RUN=tools/in-docker Or paste florilegium.sty , the .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX. Use it in your own document: \usepackage [ grown ]{ florilegium } % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math, % density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6 % two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin \definecolor {ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor {accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ... \florilegiuminitial [4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T. ... a flower in the margin beside this line \florilegiumbloom ... \florilegiumage {0.8} % grown only: autumn from here on \florilegiumtheme {geometric} % another theme, from the page this stands on \florilegiumornament {leaf} % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter \florilegiumtextend % grown only: at the very end of the text A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}" . Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale: \begin { tikzpicture } \begin { scope }[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20] \florilegiumdraw {flower}{1.3} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(5,0)}] \florilegiumdraw {leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(8,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(11,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {butterfly}{1.5} \end { scope } \end { tikzpicture } With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex ), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math . How it works Drawing ( florilegium-ink.lua ). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink : navy to mist at the hue of ink , interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons. Primitives ( florilegium-flora.lua ). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost. Authored composition ( florilegium-authored.lua ). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root. Grown composition ( florilegium-grow.lua ), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with \pagetotal in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation. Reading the page ( florilegium.lua ). A heading or \florilegiumbloom leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink. Initials ( florilegium-initial.lua ). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper. Procedural ≠ random. The seed is derived from the page number, so page n always gets garden n . Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset. See CLAUDE.md for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done. Credits The Reddit post that asked the question (see Origin ). The growth loop follows Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The tone ramp is computed in Oklab , Björn Ottosson's perceptual color space; the conversion matrices in florilegium-ink.lua are his, released into the public domain. The random numbers come from mulberry32 , Tommy Ettinger's public-domain generator. The PostScript port uses the "minimal standard" generator of Park and Miller (Communications of the ACM, 1988) by Schrage's method (ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 1979). \florilegiumornament , its ink and seed=random keys, and the density option answer issue #4 from rubyFeedback. The playground runs the Lua in the browser with wasmoon (MIT) and typesets the math theme's equations with MathJax (Apache 2.0), both loaded from jsDelivr. It is set in Igino Marini's IM FELL DW Pica (SIL OFL) and Latin Modern (GUST e-foundry, GUST Font License); see web/fonts/README.md . Its color-blindness views use the model of Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes, A Physiologically-based Model for Simulation of Color Vision Deficiency (IEEE TVCG, 2009). The math theme's figures keep the names of the people they come from: Maurer's roses, Vogel's model of the sunflower, Temple Fay's butterfly curve, the Petersen graph, Koch's snowflake, Hilbert's curve, Lissajous figures, the gasket of Apollonius. title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
body_text: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. Observability Real Talk Subscribe Sign in AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Elizabeth Feb 28, 2026 30 6 5 Share 💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz! This newsletter is a n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between! & This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚 Subscribe There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days. The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering , that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027. Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient. The Ironies of Automation: Part-I Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉). In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation . It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today. Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for. Ring any bells yet? 🙂 Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems. The exact problems that require deep expertise , the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising. Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing. Current State of AI in SRE Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering. What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted? Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today. What’s on the horizon? Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks. PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model. Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated. Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation. Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context. But here’s the catch. If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down. Subscribe if you wish to read some more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe The Crisis of Deskilling This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture. In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill. In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect. Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always . My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust . We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening . It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied. For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated. But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling . Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing. The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing . SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult. What Can We Do About It? We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward. A few approaches worth considering: Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities . This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged. Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture. The Bigger Picture Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply. We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz . We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product. Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned. One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would. And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure. The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts. Here’s the LinkedIn post our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this. Thanks for reading Observability Real Talk! Subscribe if you wish to read more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe 30 6 5 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Tim 2d The US navy also went through this 50+ years ago. They had the ability to automate nearly everything, but the admiral in charge of the project wisely said that a machine could suggest what to do, but there must always be a human in the loop to actually carry out the action, or we would lose our ability when the machines failed. Reply Share Piotr Zakrzewski 2d Also in novel incidents you are not left on your own with just your (rusty) skills. It is still AI plus you, even if AI cannot solve it on its own, you can still iterate during the incident, making observations, using AI to ask questions and dissecting the problem to eliminate root cause candidates. This is how it goes for me at my job. I am much more confident going into a SEV response knowing I have well integrated AI on my side. Reply Share 4 more comments...
