Dismiss alert {{ message }} chris124567 cfsolve Repository navigation Code Issues Pull requests 3 ( 3 ) Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items cfsolve Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 55 ( 55 ) Star 494 ( 494 ) You must be signed in to star a repository About Cloudflare turnstile and challenge page solver in Rust (full reverse, request based) Resources Readme MIT license Activity Stars 494 stars Watchers 1 watching Forks 55 forks Report repository master Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 11 Commits 11 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date examples examples profiles profiles src src vendor vendor .gitignore .gitignore Cargo.lock Cargo.lock Cargo.toml Cargo.toml LICENSE LICENSE README.md README.md rust-toolchain.toml rust-toolchain.toml rustfmt.toml rustfmt.toml View all files Repository files navigation README MIT license More items cfsolve cfsolve is a Rust library and command line tool that solves Cloudflare Turnstile widgets and challenge pages without a headless browser. It returns a Turnstile token for widgets or a cf_clearance cookie for challenge pages. Turnstile widgets can be solved using the page URL, the sitekey, and optionally the page's HTML (this should not be required in most cases). Challenge pages require a direct fetch or the HTML of the page. Browser profiles cfsolve impersonates a specific browser, described by a profile file. One is included: profiles/safari-26-ios.json (Safari on iPhone). Each profile references recorded responses to the challenge's browser checks, stored as JSON in a directory. Keep each profile with its directory when you copy. Producing these files requires some manual (or AI) effort though it can be greatly aided by solving challenges in a real web browser with the proxy set to the address of a running capture-proxy , which records the decoded payloads sent to Cloudflare. Currently only Safari and Chrome(ium) profile types are supported. Building You need the Rust version pinned in rust-toolchain.toml , plus CMake, a C/C++ compiler, libclang, and Git (to patch and build BoringSSL). cargo build --release --bin challenge Command line tool ./target/release/challenge --page ' https://example.com/login ' /tmp/solve \ --solve --fingerprint profiles/safari-26-ios.json On success it prints the token (or cf_clearance=... ) and sends progress to stderr. The directory argument holds all requests and responses for debugging, so it must be empty or not exist yet. By default it solves the first Turnstile widget on the page, or clears the challenge page. To pick one widget when the page has several, pass its sitekey, with its action and cData when the site sets them. With --sitekey , it fails on a challenge page. ./target/release/challenge --page ' https://example.com/login ' /tmp/solve \ --solve --fingerprint profiles/safari-26-ios.json \ --sitekey ' SITEKEY ' --action ' login ' --cdata ' CUSTOM_DATA ' If you only have a sitekey, add --blank-page and set --page to the site's real URL. Option Description --fingerprint <file> Browser profile file to use. Required. --page <url> The page with the widget, or the challenge page. --solve Solve the widget or challenge. Without this, cfsolve stops after sending the widget's first payload. --sitekey <key> Select a widget by sitekey. --action <value> , --cdata <value> Override the widget's action and cData. This needs --sitekey . --blank-page Skip loading the page. Render the widget on a blank page at the page URL. This needs --solve and --sitekey . --proxy <url> Send every request through an http:// , https:// , socks5:// , or socks5h:// proxy. Put credentials in the URL, as in socks5h://user:password@host:1080 . -h , --help Show help. Library Add cfsolve as a path dependency and copy its [patch] section, since Cargo only reads patches from the top-level Cargo.toml : [ dependencies ] cfsolve = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve " , default-features = false } tokio = { version = " 1 " , features = [ " macros " , " rt-multi-thread " ] } [ patch . crates-io ] btls-sys = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/btls-sys " } wreq = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/wreq " } http2 = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/http2 " } default-features = false turns off the internal tools so only the solver remains. Use the Rust version in rust-toolchain.toml or newer. use cfsolve :: { Browser , Options , PageSource , Turnstile } ; # [ tokio :: main ] async fn main ( ) -> Result < ( ) , Box < dyn std :: error :: Error > > { let browser = Browser :: read ( "/path/to/cfsolve/profiles/safari-26-ios.json" ) ? ; let options = Options :: default ( ) ; let turnstile = Turnstile { url : "https://example.com/login" . parse ( ) ? , page : PageSource :: Navigate , widget : None , } ; let token = browser . solve_turnstile ( turnstile , & options ) . await ? ; println ! ( "{token}" ) ; let cleared = browser . clear ( & "https://example.com/" . parse ( ) ? , & options ) . await ? ; println ! ( "cf_clearance={}" , cleared . clearance ) ; println ! ( "{} cookies; protected page: {}" , cleared . cookies . len ( ) , cleared . page . url ) ; Ok ( ( ) ) } Load a Browser once and share it. Concurrent operations each get their own connections and cookies. Send the cf_clearance cookie from the same IP address and user agent as the profile, or Cloudflare will reject it. Turnstile with a sitekey or your own HTML PageSource::Navigate fetches the page. With only a URL and sitekey, use PageSource::Blank and specify the widget: use cfsolve :: { PageSource , Turnstile , Widget } ; let turnstile = Turnstile { url : "https://example.com/login" . parse ( ) ? , page : PageSource :: Blank , widget : Some ( Widget { sitekey : "SITEKEY" . into ( ) , action : Some ( "login" . into ( ) ) , cdata : None , } ) , } ; let token = browser . solve_turnstile ( turnstile , & options ) . await ? ; Set action and cdata to the values the site uses, or None when the site doesn't set them. You can also pass a Widget with PageSource::Navigate to pick one widget out of several or to supply one the site adds with JavaScript. For a page you have already loaded, such as one behind a login, pass its URL and HTML: PageSource :: Html { html : std :: fs :: read_to_string ( "account.html" ) ? , referrer_policy : None , // Or the response's Referrer-Policy header. } The widget runs in a cross-site iframe, so you don't need your login cookies. With Html , widget: None solves the first widget on the page, while Blank always needs a Widget and renders it on a blank page at the site's URL. Challenge pages browser.clear(&url, &options) fetches the page and clears the challenge. The Clearance it returns contains the cf_clearance cookie, all cookies for the page, and the protected page. It fails with Error::NotChallenged when there's no challenge. If you fetched the challenge page yourself, pass the response as a FetchedPage to browser.clear_fetched(page, &options) . Use the same IP and user agent as the profile. If you don't know whether a URL shows a widget or a challenge page, use browser.solve , which covers both cases: use cfsolve :: Outcome ; match browser . solve ( & url , & options ) . await ? { Outcome :: Token ( token ) => println ! ( "{token}" ) , Outcome :: Cleared ( cleared ) => println ! ( "cf_clearance={}" , cleared . clearance ) , } Options Set a proxy per operation through Options , using HTTP, HTTPS, or SOCKS5: let options = cfsolve :: Options { proxy : Some ( "socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080" . into ( ) ) , .. Default :: default ( ) } ; Library operations are silent by default. For progress messages and debug files, implement Sink and set options.sink to Some(Arc::new(your_sink)) . Errors Error Cause Retry? Error::Network Connection failed. Yes Error::Rejected Cloudflare rejected the solution. Yes Error::Blocked The site returned an error page instead of a challenge. No Error::Challenged You asked for a Turnstile token but got a challenge page. Yes, after clearing it Error::NotChallenged You asked for a challenge clearance but there was no challenge. No Error::Config Invalid profile or options. No Error::Unsupported Any other failure, such as a new challenge build or a page with no widget. No License MIT, except for the patched dependencies in vendor/ , which keep their own licenses. The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt. nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal , which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory. Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level) Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked ). Quick start 1. Folder layout Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it: nesformer/ <- run commands from here ├── nesformer/ <- the Python package ├── chipformer/ <- Qwenputer's compiler ├── roms/ <- test ROMs (put your own here too) ├── examples/ <- sample GIFs and frame sheets ├── tests/ ├── LICENSE ├── LICENSE.chipformer ├── README.md ├── pyproject.toml └── weights/ <- from nesformer-weights.zip ├── config.json ├── generation_config.json ├── model.safetensors ├── nesformer.json └── SHA256SUMS The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere, pass --weights /path/to/weights to run , check or trace , or give the path to info . To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the top folder. 2. Install You need Python 3.11 or newer. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install numpy scipy numba pillow 3. Play a game python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593 " --show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif ) in the current folder. Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba. After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around 25 minutes. Playing your own ROMs Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely licensed test ROMs in roms/ . python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555 " That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations . Controller scripts --buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined by + , then @ , then one or more frame ranges joined by + : start@60-65 press Start during frames 60 to 65 right@200-600 hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600 a@250-265+300-315 press A twice right+b@200-600 hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.) The buttons are a , b , select , start , up , down , left and right . Frames count from power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer A press makes a higher jump. Commands Command What it does python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens) python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds) python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint Options for run : Option Default Meaning --frames N 120 Stop after N frames --buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above) --show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal) --gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF --png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both. --every N 1 Keep every N-th frame --scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times --engine fast fast (numba), numpy , or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s) --no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames) --max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens --trace FILE none Save the token ids run , check and trace all accept --weights , --engine , --buttons and --no-skip . check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/ . How it works What's in the weights, and what isn't In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host ( nesformer/host.py ) The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette 2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored) 32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace. The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows. The checkpoint weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code. Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM , with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216) Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs Hidden size 768 Vocabulary 263,808 tokens Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero , so the weights zip to 3.3 MB nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily. Layer plan Layer Attention (state) MLP 1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y 2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2 3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target 4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores 5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode 6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets 7 — the next token The trace Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it. As in Qwenputer's RISC-V core, the PC is implied rather than written: each final token carries its instruction's length, three DeltaNet counters tally the instructions of each length since the last jump, and the PC is the jump target plus that offset. Excerpts from Full Game: SEI P(000100 px0 L1) LDX #$40 X($40 c0 v0 px0 L2) STX $4017 IOW($4017=$40 L3) TXS S($FF L1) BIT $2002 IOR($2002) IN($00) P(000110 px0 L3) <- the host injects IN BPL $8017 J($8017) JSR $8279 PSH($FE) PSH($FD) J($8279) <- the return address is pushed in-circuit RTS PUL($FC) LO($7B) PUL($FD) J($827C) STA ($72),Y LO($08) HI($03) ST($00 a7=0 L2) <- pointer bytes latched, then the store STA $4014 IOW($4014=$02 L0) DM(0:$FF) … DM(255:$00) NT(L3) <- OAM DMA Most instructions take a single token; real game code averages 1.1–1.3 tokens per instruction. nesformer/spec.py documents every token family. How it was checked The reference CPU ( nesformer/cpu.py ) matches nestest's golden log for 3,348 instructions, and the py65 emulator on 5.7 million instructions of game code. The exact circuit , run in Qwenputer's evaluator with its bf16 exactness checks, predicts every reference token: all of nestest plus 283,610 positions of two games' boot sequences. The checkpoint in stock transformers (bf16, CPU) predicts 2,651 positions of nestest and Full Game with no mismatches. The weights, free-running , generate traces identical to the reference CPU's: Run Tokens Frames NES time Result nestest (official opcodes) 4,586 — — identical, ending in the expected HALT Thwaite, check 700,000 271 4.5 s identical trace and frames Thwaite, run 1,916,527 600 10.0 s all 300 saved frames match Full Game, run 2,645,885 420 7.0 s all 210 saved frames match The idle-loop skip changes nothing visible: frames and I/O writes, cycle timestamps included, match a run without it. Speed The default engine computes Qwen3.5's forward pass from model.safetensors , compiled with numba and skipping the all-zero blocks. It ran at about 1,650 tokens/s on one CPU core of the machine it was built on. The plain numpy engine does about 210, and stock transformers about 10. A real NES would need about 700,000 tokens per second. Games spend most of each frame in a loop that waits for vblank. When the host sees a loop body repeat exactly, with no RAM or I/O writes, it advances the clock to just before the next PPU event, and the remaining iterations still run. That cuts the token count by 2.6× to 4.2×. Overall, nesformer runs 150–290× slower than the real console. Limitations NROM cartridges only (iNES mapper 0). The CPU can address only 32 KB of program ROM at a time. Bigger games carry a bank-switching chip (a mapper , such as MMC1 or MMC3) that swaps which part of the ROM the CPU sees. nesformer's ROM reads happen inside the model, from a fixed 32 KB table, so it can't follow a bank switch yet. Supporting a mapper means storing the whole ROM in the state, keeping the bank registers there too, and adding one stage that turns each CPU address into a ROM address. Official opcodes only. An unofficial opcode emits HALT . Code must run from the cartridge ROM. A jump into RAM emits HALT . No IRQs (APU frame IRQ, DMC). BRK and NMI work. Read-modify-write instructions on I/O registers don't produce an I/O write, and $4020–$7FFF reads as 0 (no PRG-RAM). The PPU and APU aren't in the weights. The PPU renders one scanline at a time, so mid-scanline effects aren't reproduced. Sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there's no sound. Tests pip install pytest py65 python -m pytest -q tests The tests take a few minutes. They check the reference CPU against nestest's log, the circuit against the reference, the weights free-running against the reference, and the idle-loop skip. Running the checkpoint in stock transformers pip install " torch>=2.6 " " transformers>=5.22 " python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 3 --engine hf nesformer/hfcheck.py shows the whole procedure: load the checkpoint, decode one padding token, write the machine's state into the cache's DeltaNet states, then feed tokens one at a time. Files Path Contents nesformer/spec.py token families and records nesformer/cpu.py the reference 6502 that writes the trace nesformer/host.py everything around the CPU: PPU, controllers, NMI timing, cycle counting, idle skip nesformer/core.py the circuit and the state snapshot nesformer/weights.py the emitter that turns the circuit into a Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint nesformer/engine.py , fastengine.py run the weights (numpy / numba) nesformer/hfcheck.py run the weights in stock transformers nesformer/run.py , check.py , cli.py , __main__.py drivers, the teacher-forced check, the CLI chipformer/ Qwenputer's q35 compiler ( q35/ emitter and primitives, dsl/ graph) weights/ the compiled checkpoint and its SHA-256 checksum roms/ test ROMs; roms/SOURCES.md lists their authors and licenses examples/ GIFs and frame sheets from the runs; demo.gif is the Super Mario Bros. run shown at the top tests/test_nesformer.py the test suite Credits Qwenputer and its chipformer compiler: MIT, © 2026 Divyansh Agrawal ( LICENSE.chipformer ). That license also covers the code adapted from Qwenputer in nesformer/core.py and nesformer/weights.py . Its last paragraph refers to Qwenputer's CHIP-8 ROMs, which this repository does not include. Test ROMs: nestest by Kevin Horton; Full Game by Doug Fraker (MIT); Thwaite by Damian Yerrick (GPL-3.0, source at pinobatch/thwaite-nes ). License nesformer is released under the MIT License (see LICENSE ). The ROMs in roms/ keep their own licenses, listed in roms/SOURCES.md . title: We won't "just hang out"
body_text: We Won’t “Just Hang Out” Home ❖ Blog We Won’t “Just Hang Out” 28 October, 2026 Detail from Wall Street , Paul Strand , 1915. What will we do after the Singularity? The standard answer is: “we’ll just hang out”. The infinite vacation, as in the Culture novels. I think this won’t work. “Hanging out” implies: Other people exist. They want to hang out with you. You want to hang out with them. And the post-scarcity, infinite vacation AI utopia undermines all these assumptions. Other people exist The social processes by which people come together and build relationships will disappear. Work, obviously, is pointless in a world of cheap superhuman intelligence. University (really all education beyond teaching people to speak) will be pointless because there’s no work to do and because growing your human capital doesn’t change your life outcomes: you get the same UBI whether you’re illiterate or a PhD. I met a lot of my friends by writing open-source code, and participating in the community of software engineers. AI is dissolving that community by making human contributions superfluous . If Claude Code has existed when I was starting out, nobody would have cared about Austral or my other open-source projects or my technical blog posts. As a teenager I tried to install Linux, ran into all kinds of problems, and went on the IRC chatrooms to get help. And in the process I made friends. Today, I would just ask Claude. AI disintermediates everyone, so that we no longer need each other. I still have friends, but I’m running off this pre-AI supply of friends I met through communities of practice. Young people don’t have that privilege. What even is the point of cities in a world without work? If there’s nothing to do, there is no need to bring people together geographically. They want to hang out with you The BATNA to hanging out keeps getting better, cheaper, and more convenient. When people’s sensorium becomes an infinite firehose of AI-generated superstimulus, why would they hang out with anyone? This is less about AI and more about the trajectory of consumer technology, since many people already live like this: they go to work and watch TikTok. After work, they will just watch TikTok. You want to hang out with them As Gregory Conti explains : [Under] ASI this endless leisure will be passed in diminished, tiresome company, since we will lack the experiences of struggle and striving that generate interesting personalities. Our minds will have atrophied. We will have little of note to say to one another. The people in the AI utopia will have no skills, no education, no accomplishments. We’ll be lucky if they are even literate. They will not be worth talking to, and you won’t want to hang out with them. Maybe you and I can hang out with our existing friends. But just iterate this a bit. What about the next generation? How are they going to build meaningful relationships where the social processes that built those relationships are all in the past? If we get radical life extension, there’s the problem of attrition over the long term: people will drift apart, drop out of society to enter the experience machine, die in accidents, or end their lives out of ennui. So your social network might be a non-renewable resource that gets exhausted over time as your pre-Singularity relationships attrite and can’t be replaced for the reasons above. I would love to hear from you. © 2014–2026 Fernando Borretti

title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
body_text: Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5 - Divyansh Agrawal d ↗ My writing Series Attention Lab Chipformer My work About Résumé ↗ Contact ↗ ← My writing COMPILED WEIGHTS Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5 A stock Qwen 3.5 4B with a RISC-V CPU compiled into its weights, running on its own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM. Series Qwenputer Part 1 of 3 ↗ By Divyansh Agrawal 22 October 2026 9 min read Markdown version 👏 ... Save Email address Subscribe On this page I can't believe it's not silicon The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Compiling a computer into layers The CPU How Qwen uses it Does it work? A hard drive? In this economy? Limits and what's next Beyond arithmetic Try it Get new articles by email I can't believe it's not silicon Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide .) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever. To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage. I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with . Qwen hands a multiplication to the RISC-V CPU inside its own weights; the CPU's RAM is Gated DeltaNet state You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope , and the code is on GitHub . The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism ( more on that here ). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated. Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1, 1 1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1, 2 2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding, 3 3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache. Gated DeltaNet state used as RAM: a one-hot key overwrites one row, a one-hot query reads it back, and the CPU keeps its registers, memory and program counter in those rows The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights". 4 4 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it. This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment. Compiling a computer into layers Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes. Each instruction becomes a few generated tokens: one names the memory row to write (ADDR), the next carries the value (VAL), and a STEP token ends the instruction. Those tokens are the CPU's execution trace, so while Qwen is generating them, the CPU is actually running. The CPU The CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus the Zba extension and a small bignum unit for big-number arithmetic), and it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32. As it stands, it passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error. 5 5 Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps. This CPU can also run C and MicroPython code in the forward passes quite well (although a bit slowly). It is not a Linux-class chip yet, but it implements the full RV32IM instruction set. How Qwen uses it Qwen 3.5 4B is able to use this CPU quite well, without any post-training required. The CPU is used completely internally, and not invoked through any external tool calls. In order to make the model use this reliably, I decided to go the cheap way: by piggybacking on the tool call format that models are quite well-trained on, Qwen sends the CPU its instructions and reads back the results. No external tool calls or runtime are used. Once our CPU receives the instructions, the computer layers run, and then write the tool response. We use a small driver called RvChat to load the firmware into the GDN state, and this keeps the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers. Qwen's original weights stay exactly as they are. The computer weights are added on top of them, in extra dims and layers. Does it work? I think the main question here on your mind after reading through my incessant ranting will be: does this actually work? Accuracy of base Qwen3.5-4B, Qwenputer and base Qwen with a Python tool on NUPA and DeepMind arithmetic sets On the DeepMind sets: div_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 95% by giving Qwen 3.5 4B a Python tool and 72.5% for base Qwen. mul_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 100% with a Python tool and 55% for base Qwen. mul_div_multiple_longer: Qwenputer scores 100%, versus 97.5% with a Python tool and 90% for base Qwen. add_or_sub_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, the same as with a Python tool, and 87.5% for base Qwen. On NUPA's long-integer arithmetic, Qwenputer goes from 48.6% to 100%, the same as giving Qwen a Python tool. The numbers the CPU prints are exact, too: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions against a reference machine and found zero mismatches. And bolting a computer onto Qwen doesn't change how it talks: its normal text stays within noise of base Qwen (KL 6e-4, against a noise floor of 5e-4). A hard drive? In this economy? Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too. Since we already have a functional RAM, this was mostly trivial. On the model side, it's exposed via internal put / append / get / list / delete operations. Once again, no actual tool calls. When Qwen 'saves' a file, the compiled layers hash its name into one of 1,024 slots in a directory kept in the DeltaNet state, and store the text itself in other heads, with eight tokens per row, chained together. In scenarios where two names end up landing on the same slot, it just checks the next one. Finding a file again takes roughly two or three steps instead of a scan, and it holds up to 512 files, which comes out to about 53,000 tokens of text. Fun thing is, this is quite persistent. You can save the state at the end of a conversation, load it into the next one, and the files are still there. Using this filesystem, Qwen gets facts that changed between chats right 90% of the time, against 30% when you paste the old chats back in, and it's on par with giving Qwen memory tools run by Python (83.3% vs 78.9%). This one is still experimental, and its code lives on the rv-store branch , with the model on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Limits and what's next Qwenputer is very much an experiment, so a few limitations. The extra layers and wider hidden size make the checkpoint 18.8 GB, roughly double base Qwen, although most of it is zero padding. It also needs a small driver (RvChat) to boot the firmware and keep the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers, so it doesn't run with a plain generate() call yet. And it's a bit slow, with every CPU instruction costing a few decoded tokens, so a big calculation takes seconds rather than milliseconds. The batched executor I used for the benchmarks runs about 3,200 CPU tokens a second on an L4. Next up, I want Qwen to write Python and run it on the MicroPython inside its own weights, through a python() tool that works the same way calc does. Making the CPU faster is the other big one. Beyond arithmetic Exact control over the RNN layers is useful for a lot more than arithmetic. It also makes Qwenputer a really nice testbed for AI safety research, and I wrote up two follow-ups: how hybrid models like Qwen 3.5 can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights can work as monitorability tools , like an in-weight monitor the model can't switch off, or answer keys for interpretability. Try it If you want to play with it yourself, the model runs on a single 24 GB GPU. You'll need uv and the Hugging Face CLI. You don't need a tool server or a Python sandbox for the calculations: the CPU runs them inside the model. git clone https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer && cd qwenputer/experimental/riscv && uv sync --extra hf hf download divagr1925/Qwen3.5-4B-Qwenputer --local-dir qwenputer-rv uv run python -m chipformer.rv.chat qwenputer-rv --firmware tests/data/rv/calc-bridge.elf \ --ask "Use calc: what is 123456789 * 987654321?" Everything is open: the code on GitHub , and both models on Hugging Face ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ) and ModelScope ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ). If you use it in your work, you can cite it as: @software{agrawal2026qwenputer, author = {Agrawal, Divyansh}, title = {{Qwenputer}: a computer compiled into the weights of a pretrained language model}, year = {2026}, url = {https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer} } Notes Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. ↩ After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. ↩ A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. ↩ Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. ↩ Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps. ↩ Get new articles by email Email address Subscribe ← My writing Newer article Hybrid models can hide reasoning in their RNN state Older article Consensus Is Not Corroboration RELATED POSTS Building oversight tools into a model's weights ↗ Hybrid models can hide reasoning in their RNN state ↗ GET IN TOUCH [email protected] ↗ © 2026 DIVYANSH AGRAWAL GITHUB · X · LINKEDIN BACK TO TOP ↑

title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS
body_text: SMS of Death: zero-click Android telephony DoS SMS OF DEATH Vulnerability Impact Why it matters PoC Android Telephony Â· Zero-Click Â· Remote DoS SMS of Death A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls ( including emergency calls ), with zero interaction from the victim. Download APK Source â Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading. Component WapPushOverSms frameworks/opt/telephony Interaction None zero-click, silent Vector Remote SMS WAP Push, port 2948 Affected Android 12â17 patched in 14â17, Oct 2026 update Reporter Mark B Reported 5 May 2026 Android & Devices VRP Disclosed 29 Oct 2026 public writeup Recovery ADB only normal user: bricked 01 / The vulnerability An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar . The value comes back as a long , is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array: // WapPushOverSms.java:217 header length read as long, cast with no bounds check int headerLength = ( int ) pduDecoder.getValue32(); ... // WapPushOverSms.java:244 the cast value is used as an array size byte [] header = new byte [headerLength]; A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000 . Cast to a signed 32-bit int , that is -2147483648 . Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone : E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648 E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244) E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627) The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number. Affected versions. The code sits in Android's core telephony framework and has shipped in many releases. The crash has been reproduced from Android 12 (the reboot loop in issue #2 ) up to Android 16 . Google's October 2026 fix was released for Android 14 through 17 , so devices on older versions outside the security-update window, such as Android 12 and 13, run the same code and do not receive the fix. 02 / Impact Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort Zero-click. The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification. Silent. Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown. Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Telephony blackout. 1-2 seconds of no service per message while com.android.phone restarts. Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing. ~20 messages render the device unusable for an extended period. Persistent denial of service. The malformed message stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below). Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate. Recovery over ADB, contributed by @sakisdog After hitting the reboot loop on Android 12 , @sakisdog documented a less destructive recovery ( issue #2 ). The poison messages sit in the pending inbound queue ( content://sms/raw ) and are retried on every boot, so Android's RescueParty reboots the device into recovery roughly every 90 seconds. Deleting just those rows over ADB, in the short window after boot completes, breaks the loop with no factory reset: # while sys.boot_completed == 1: find the WAP Push rows (destination_port=134020), note the address adb shell content query --uri content://sms/raw --projection _id:destination_port:date:deleted # let the shell edit SMS storage, delete only those rows, then reset the permission adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS allow adb shell "content delete --uri content://sms/raw --where \"address='<SENDER>'\"" adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS default # last resort, erases ALL SMS/MMS and APN settings: adb shell pm clear com.android.providers.telephony Recovery credited to @sakisdog . It still needs a computer and ADB, and you should not choose "wipe data" at the recovery prompt, so for a non-technical user mid-loop it remains out of reach. This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service that, left untreated, reboots the phone into a recovery wipe-data prompt every ~90 seconds, driving a normal user to a factory reset to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's published rules. 03 / Why this is serious A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or stuck in the reboot loop, it cannot reliably place a call to 000 . The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing. Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination , administered by the ACMA , carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset . Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days. The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network , not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until it is updated. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand. The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces. Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination Â· Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination Â· Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis 04 / The fix One bounds check The remedy is a range check before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (line 217) , provided to Google on the day of the first report: long rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32(); if (rawHeaderLen < 0 || rawHeaderLen > pdu.length) { result.statusCode = Intents.RESULT_SMS_GENERIC_ERROR; return result; } int headerLength = ( int ) rawHeaderLen; What Google shipped Google fixed this crash, but not with the bounds check above. On 15 June 2026 an Android engineer authored commit 735d967 , "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," which shipped in the October 2026 Android security release for Android 14 through 17. Rather than validate the length, it widens the caught exception so the crash is swallowed, and deletes the triggering message so it cannot re-crash on carrier redelivery or on boot: // WapPushOverSms.java: widen the catch to cover NegativeArraySizeException - } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aie) { + } catch (RuntimeException e) { // InboundSmsHandler.java: a failed decode now deletes the poison message + try { success = processMessagePart(tracker); } + catch (RuntimeException e) { deleteFromRawTable(...); } // breaks the boot loop This fix is part of the October 2026 Android security update. Devices updated to the October 2026 patch level or later are protected; devices on earlier patch levels remain vulnerable. 05 / Proof of concept Source & APK The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number. Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing. Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries. The software is provided "as is", with no warranty, under the Apache License 2.0 . The author accepts no liability for any use, misuse, or damage. By downloading the APK or the source, you accept full responsibility for what you do with it. Download APK Source on GitHub Full disclosure by Mark B Â· @sourone github.com/MarkBlah/smsofdeath Â· Apache 2.0 Â· 2026

title: The federated code forge
body_text: The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog The federated code forge Anirudh 30 October 2026 For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation. But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however. ’05 Mail + Git ’09 GitHub + Git ’25 AT Protocol + Git Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge. It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose , you can still talk to everyone else. Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack . Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge. Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly . The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become y o u r c o d e f o r g e f o r t h e n e x t d e c a d e . Product updates A fresh look! The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans . A bobbin near you Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden. This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin . Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance. The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services. The new data model and repo-owned data First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.* , replacing the old sh.tangled.* records. Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary. With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way. In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose. But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability. If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification! Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide . Organizations Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs . Stacked PRs for everyone Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well. Launch weeks ahead This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent. Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally. Your code, your network. Come build with us on Tangled. Sign up © 2026 Tangled Labs Oy. Tangled Docs Source Discord Bluesky X/Twitter Terms Privacy

with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
body_text: H.264 is magic: a technical walkthrough of a remarkable technology. Sid Bala Home LinkedIn GitHub Sign in Subscribe H.264 is Magic Sid Bala 02 Nov 2016 • 10 min read Share H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now. H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video. Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264. Why even compress anything? A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue). 1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ 370 MB/sec of raw data. This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1]. So yeah. We need compression. Why H.264 compression? Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage: I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files: PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB 5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched. No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB. It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG. How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick? There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones. Shedding weight Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that. You remove everything except the things that matter. This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits. PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image. Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important? There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this. What does H.264 actually do? H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard. See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs! 7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that? For this we need a quick math lesson. Information Entropy Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset. For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense? Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy . The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data. Frequency Domain Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok! Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough. Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY? freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain: The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense? In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image. Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this? Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be. Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied. The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs! So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization [^3]. Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got? Chroma Subsampling. The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight. In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy. Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you? Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally. But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs! This process of discarding some of the color information is called Chroma Subsampling [^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally. Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information. Wait. That's it? Can we do something more? Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time. Motion compensation H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard. Motion compensation? What now? Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right? Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation? Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an I-frame (Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either P-frames (predicted) or B-frames (bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame. B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around. Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause? Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that? Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you. Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation. Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video. Looks pretty good to me. Now what? Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure. Entropy Coder The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video. An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in. And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks. Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now. The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get: 5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => 1.2 GB Compressed video => 175 KB If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get 0.4 lbs as the final weight. 6.5 ounces! Yeah. It's magic! Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive. Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use HackerNews or Reddit for voicing your opinion! Or hit me up on Twitter or LinkedIn if you want to chat.
