title: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
body_text: DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work | Surge AI DAYJOB: Tax A benchmark for AI tax agents Blog benchmarks Off-the-Shelf Training experts Products Enterprise Research Careers Contact Login Menu Close THE SURGE AI BLOG DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work October 27, 2026 October 27, 2026 No items found. TL;DR Real-world tax work is messy. Instructions are incomplete, records conflict, and the most important problems aren't always the ones explicitly assigned. DAYJOB: Tax evaluates whether AI agents can handle that reality, taking ownership of a tax professional's work from an initial client request to a finished deliverable. Across 50 environments and 1,789 files, agents must navigate complex tax records, uncover issues clients may not know to raise, and make consequential judgments with incomplete information. Success requires more than tax knowledge and accurate calculations. It demands the initiative and professional judgment to figure out what needs to be done, investigate what matters, and deliver work that meets professional standards. ‍ LEADERBOARD HUGGING FACE Table of contents Case Study Llama Analysis of Individual writings Appendix Anna was planning to sell her condo. She had moved out in August 2024 and wanted to know whether closing in October 2026 or January 2027 would be better for taxes. An AI agent reviewed both options and correctly concluded that either date would satisfy the residence requirement for a tax break worth up to $250,000 in excluded gains. But it left out an important deadline. Under the usual rules, homeowners must have lived in a property for at least two of the five years before selling it to qualify for the exclusion. Because Anna moved out in August 2024, she would stop satisfying that requirement around the end of August 2027. If her sale was delayed beyond August 2027, she could lose eligibility. Across five attempts, Astra never identified the deadline. Opus identified it in all five attempts. The agent evaluated the proposed dates correctly, but its advice left Anna unaware of a deadline that could affect a major financial decision. A tax adviser should recognize consequential issues even when the client doesn't know to ask about them. This is the kind of professional judgment we're testing with DAYJOB: Tax , the latest addition to Surge AI's DAYJOB benchmark family . Introducing DAYJOB: Tax DAYJOB evaluates AI agents on professional tax assignments requiring specialized expertise, complex materials, and decisions that aren't fully specified in the initial instructions. Our earlier releases covered Healthcare and Finance. DAYJOB: Tax extends that work into tax preparation, compliance, and advisory services. The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice. Agents receive client requests and supporting records, then produce tax returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or client advice. These assignments test professional judgment alongside tax knowledge, calculations, retrieval, and instruction following. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and carry those decisions into their final work. Results: Leaderboard and Pareto Frontiers Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads with a 10.8% pass rate on the DAYJOB: Tax leaderboard , followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%. We report pass@1 at a 95% rubric threshold. An attempt passes when it satisfies at least 95% of the task's criteria, which assess calculations, supporting evidence, consequential issues, and the completed deliverable. Performance versus cost We also compared model performance against average cost per trial. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 occupy the high-performance end of the measured Pareto frontier. The breadth of professional tax work DAYJOB: Tax covers eight areas, each requiring different rules, records, and expertise: Individual and family tax Small-business tax Partnerships Property and investments Estates, gifts, and trusts International tax Corporate transactions Tax review and disputes Some assignments require complete filing packages with supporting workpapers. Others ask agents to investigate transactions, review previous filings, or prepare advice about decisions clients haven't yet made. What's inside the assignments? The benchmark contains 1,789 workspace files , with a median of 30 per assignment and as many as 123. These include 1,487 PDFs, 117 Excel workbooks, 38 Word documents, and additional emails, images, CSVs, JSON records, and text files. The workspaces include filed and draft tax returns, K-1s, W-2s, IRS notices, general ledgers, payroll records, contracts, and correspondence. They also contain the less standardized evidence that tax professionals routinely work with. One assignment includes a photograph of a handwritten receipt for merchandise purchased for resale . The agent must read the item descriptions and amounts, reconcile them with spending records, and determine how the purchases affect inventory and cost of goods sold. Another assignment involves an industrial silo-services company whose client assumes it operates only in Alabama. But its field dispatch log shows crews working across five states . The job locations, crew sizes, and days on site provide evidence relevant to the company's multistate tax obligations. Other environments are similarly varied. One involves a cross-border household whose Polish employment and property records must be reconciled with cryptocurrency exchange exports, wallet histories, and historical purchase lots. Created and reviewed by tax experts DAYJOB tasks begin with real-world professional workflows. Tax experts turn these situations into realistic assignments, developing the supporting records, expected outcomes, and grading criteria. Each task undergoes a three-layer expert review for correctness, completeness, and solvability. Tax experts bring experience across corporate taxation, partnerships, individual returns, trusts, and multistate compliance. Their backgrounds include: Corporate and private-equity taxation: A tax attorney with over 10 years of experience at PwC, Deloitte, and Exxon, covering tax planning, compliance, audits, and controversy. Partnership and corporate taxation: A Baker Tilly Tax Director with experience at PwC, Moss Adams, and Windes, specializing in complex partnership allocations, consolidated corporate returns, REITs, and high-net-worth clients. Real estate and individual taxation: A tax professional with experience at Deloitte and EY, specializing in real-estate partnerships, individual taxation, and trusts. A retirement plan built on an unverified assumption A separating couple asked an AI agent how to divide their Roth IRA and 401(k). Opus 5.5 told them they weren't legally married and recommended keeping their accounts separate, with a cash payment to even out the balances. It opened one response: You aren't legally married, so neither account can be split without triggering taxes and penalties. But the couple's own records raised doubts about that conclusion. Although they now lived in Florida, where new common-law marriages generally aren't recognized, they had previously lived together in Texas and held a ceremony in Colorado. Texas recognizes informal marriages under certain conditions, and a valid marriage established elsewhere may remain valid in Florida. That distinction could change the tax consequences of dividing their retirement accounts. Across all five attempts, Opus based its recommendations around the assumption that the couple was unmarried , even when it acknowledged uncertainty. Astra recognized the need to verify their marital status in four of five attempts. One response advised: We first need to confirm your legal marital status. The client asked how to divide the accounts. The agent needed to establish whether they were married before recommending a course of action. The evidence that should have prompted that investigation was already in the files. Where DAYJOB: Tax fits Most existing tax benchmarks begin with a defined problem: a legal question to answer, a return to calculate, or missing taxpayer information to collect. These evaluations measure important capabilities, but much of a tax professional's work involves figuring out what the problem actually is. Clients provide incomplete instructions, records contain conflicting evidence, and consequential issues may never appear in the original request. DAYJOB tests whether agents can handle that end-to-end responsibility , including identifying issues the client overlooked, evaluating conflicting evidence, and deciding what needs to be done in the first place. TaxBench Can the model answer a difficult tax question? TaxBench evaluates 114 tax questions across multiple specialties, each with a defined problem and grading rubric. DAYJOB also asks whether the client asked the right question. Anna wants to compare two dates for selling her condo. Both satisfy the residence requirement for a tax exclusion, but does the agent warn her when that eligibility could expire? TaxCalcBench Can the model calculate an accurate return? TaxCalcBench evaluates tax-return accuracy against expected filing values, using realistic tax documents and taxpayer scenarios. DAYJOB also asks whether the underlying records actually support the tax treatment. A studio's ledger references an attached receipt, but the receipt is missing. Does the agent flag the missing evidence or incorrectly treat the reimbursement as verified? TaxLab Can the agent gather missing information and file correctly? TaxLab tests whether agents can question a simulated taxpayer, obtain missing information, and complete a federal individual tax return. DAYJOB extends that responsibility across the wider tax profession. The deliverable might be a partnership loss analysis, an estate return, a review of a disputed tax position, or a strategy letter. The central distinction is how much responsibility remains with the agent. DAYJOB evaluates whether agents can discover consequential issues, exercise professional judgment, and carry their findings through to a completed filing, review, or recommendation. What DAYJOB: Tax measures DAYJOB tests whether AI agents can take ownership of a professional assignment from start to finish. That means navigating messy records, identifying issues the client never raised, making sound judgments with incomplete information, and delivering work that meets professional standards. The results show how difficult that remains for frontier models. Even when agents can perform the individual steps, exercising professional judgment and reliably carrying out real-world tax workflows remain out of reach. Agents haven’t yet passed the audit. The full leaderboard, with every model we evaluated, is on the DAYJOB: Tax benchmark page . To learn more or request access to the full benchmark, contact benchmarks@surgehq.ai . title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart
body_text: DoorDash to Acquire Instacart to Help Local Stores Win | DoorDash DoorDash DoorDash Products Company Impact Advertise News Blog Help English (US) Español (US) English (CA) Français (CA) English (AU) English (NZ) US Get Started News Announcements Culture Policy Trends & Insights Archives Categories Announcements Culture Policy Trends & Insights Archives Announcements DoorDash to Acquire Instacart to Help Local Stores Win Together, DoorDash and Instacart would help stores of every size reach more customers with the kinds of innovative technology that the biggest online retailers and grocers build for themselves. Oct 29, 2026 Transaction values Instacart at $65.00 per share, representing a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026 Together, DoorDash and Instacart would help stores of every size reach more customers with the kinds of innovative technology that the biggest online retailers and grocers build for themselves Consumers to benefit from more choice and access to affordable delivery and savings Dashers and Shoppers to have more earnings opportunities and more choice over when and how they earn DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ: DASH) and Maplebear Inc. (d.b.a. Instacart, NASDAQ: CART) today announced a definitive agreement under which DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a total value of $65.00 for each Instacart share, or an equity value of approximately $17 billion. The aggregate transaction consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both, subject to proration so that DoorDash stock does not exceed 25% of the aggregate consideration. Instacart's board of directors has unanimously approved the agreement. DoorDash and Instacart share a mission to help local businesses succeed. Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour. The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash's delivery network and Instacart's grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores' own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built. On either app, customers pick a store in their own community, and the store makes the sale. Consumers will have more stores to choose from, more savings opportunities when they choose to shop with a local business, and faster delivery options, while Dashers and Shoppers will have more ways to earn. Most grocery shopping still happens in stores, but more people are buying groceries and everyday goods online. They expect fast, affordable delivery and an easy way to order. The biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs, and AI shopping assistants. A grocer or retailer running on thin margins cannot build all of that alone, and with AI, the playing field risks being tilted even further away from local commerce. DoorDash and Instacart believe that communities benefit when Main Street competes, and they build the tools that empower local businesses. Together, they could help local stores grow online. More grocers could deploy Instacart's technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, bringing them more sales and advertising revenue. Brands would gain a scaled alternative for reaching customers online. Grocers could add capacity for online orders through DoorDash's DashMart Fulfillment Services and offer faster, more accurate, and more affordable delivery. “Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” said Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash. “Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery. It’s still early innings, but we know that when more people shop local, more dollars stay local.” “Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. “When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers, and deliver compelling value for our shareholders. Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve.” Benefits and commitments DoorDash expects many benefits will flow from the transaction, including: More Choice for Consumers : Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today. Two Memberships for the Price of One : DashPass and Instacart+ members would pay one membership fee instead of two, which would save them an estimated $100 million per year on membership fees alone. More Ways to Earn for Dashers and Shoppers : More orders for local businesses can create more earning opportunities, with more choice over when and how they earn, whether that’s grocery orders on a quiet day, restaurant orders at peak times, or both. DoorDash is proud to share a few of the post-close commitments it is making today that demonstrate how this deal benefits local communities: Open Platform, No Grocery Exclusivity : Local grocers can work with any delivery platform they choose to help them grow. Shoppers Keep What They Love : Instacart Shoppers can keep the features they love, including the flexibility to choose how much they work and the information they need to decide which batches to accept, and choose whether to take on DoorDash orders or keep shopping only on Instacart. Following closing, DoorDash is expected to keep Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. Transaction details The value of $65.00 per Instacart share represents a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026, the last trading day before media reports about a possible transaction. Instacart stockholders will have the right to elect to receive, for each Instacart share: (i) $65.00 in cash, (ii) 0.3372 shares of DoorDash common stock, or (iii) a mix of $48.75 in cash and 0.0843 shares of DoorDash common stock, in each case, subject to a cap on the total stock consideration issuable by DoorDash equal to 25% of the aggregate consideration and certain proration mechanics. If stock consideration is oversubscribed, applicable Instacart stockholders will receive stock consideration on a prorated basis. DoorDash expects to fund the cash portion of the consideration with cash on hand and proceeds from debt financing. DoorDash has entered into a financing commitment letter with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. providing for a 364-day senior unsecured bridge loan facility in support of the debt component of the transaction, subject to satisfaction or waiver of certain customary conditions. The transaction is not subject to a financing condition. DoorDash is targeting a capital structure that will maintain investment-grade ratings. The transaction is expected to close in the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to approval by Instacart stockholders, the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, other regulatory approvals, including in Canada and Israel, and other customary closing conditions. title: Chained PHP2Shell exploit roots 25 servers, including US Government servers
body_text: Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers | Dream Research A New Reality - Read the CEO's Post > About Careers Research & News Manifest Contact Us Contact Us October 26, 2026 Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers, including US Government Servers Dream Research Updated: October 29, 2026. Since this discovery, the Dream research team has been sharing updates and collaborating on an investigation with Palo Alto Networks, the vendor of the firewall in question. More information is available on the Palo Alto Networks website . Additional details are now included in the post itself. Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Firewalls in the Wild On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems. The affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS. The exploited surface is the PAN-OS management web server, which also fronts the GlobalProtect portal. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has independently verified the attacker’s tooling and results, and Palo Alto Networks is releasing fixed PAN-OS versions across the affected branches. After rooting the firewalls, the attacker launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration. The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible. The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product, Hero . Discovery Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts. This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment. The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain. AI Usage in Attack We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure: Claude Code had been installed An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across ~40 scripts suggest AI-assisted development. That said, this operation does not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack . The Exploit: Two Vulnerabilities Chained Into One Request The attacker developed two separate exploits and chained them together to achieve root access on any internet-facing PAN-OS firewall running a vulnerable build in a single HTTP request without any credentials. PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) — Remote Code Execution The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell. It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for PAN-OS. The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server (appweb). PAN-OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack. The attack works in four orchestrated stages: A1 — Memory Exhaustion (~383MB): The attacker floods the server with crafted multipart POST requests, each containing massive filenames and session progress data. This pushes PHP's memory allocator to its limits, forcing the system into a predictable memory layout. B1 — Information Leak: A second request forges the stale session ID length from A1, forcing an out-of-bounds read. The server's Set-Cookie response header carries the leaked pointer value — giving the attacker the base address of libphp.so in the running process. A2 — Stale Reference Setup (~500MB): Another round of memory pressure initializes a session, leaving http_session_vars as a live zend_reference , then triggers a second OOM that leaves mod_data=NULL — creating a stale reference the attacker can forge in B2. B2 — Code Execution: The final request forges a PHP HashTable entry in the freed memory region. The forged entry's pDestructor callback points to zif_system (PHP's system() function), and its data points to a shell command string. When PHP's cleanup handler walks the HashTable, it calls the forged destructor — executing arbitrary commands as the nobody user. Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) — Kernel Privilege Escalation Getting code execution as nobody isn't enough since SELinux confines httpd_t from modifying system files. In order to complete the root, the attacker chained in a second exploit: a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem. Fragnesia uses page-cache writes to overwrite /etc/pam.d/su — replacing its authentication rules with pam_permit.so (accept all). Because the PAM file is only 774 bytes, the exploit uses a per-byte splicing variant to write it precisely. After the overwrite, su root succeeds without a password. Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes. The Lab: Version Profiling at Scale The exploit is not a single fire-and-forget payload. It requires precise memory offsets that differ between PAN-OS versions — the address of zval_ptr_dtor , the address of zif_system , HashTable structure sizes, and memory geometry parameters that control the heap layout during each stage. Among the recovered artifacts, we found 11 JSON version profile files — one for each PAN-OS version that had been tested: PAN-OS branch PHP Profiles Notes 11.1 7.4.33 2 provisional PHP 7.4 — RCE as nobody verified in lab, but full chain not calibrated (base build plus one hotfix variant) 12.1, 12.2 8.0.30 1 calibrated, 8 provisional One base profile fully lab-tested; the others inherit its geometry or share offsets with neighboring builds Each profile contains the exact offsets extracted from the libphp.so binary of that version — with SHA256 hashes of each library, ELF build IDs, and precise memory geometry parameters (chunk sizes, fill counts, drain counts, spray offsets) tuned through lab testing. The difference between "calibrated" and "provisional" profiles is notable — calibrated means the attacker tested the exploit against a running VM of that version and confirmed the memory geometry works. Provisional means they calculated offsets from the binary but haven't verified on a live instance. The Campaign Funnel: From 19,000 Discovered to 25 Exploited Figure 1: Operational timeline of the campaign, from setup on October 8 through exploitation, the pivot into the internal network, and post-exploitation on October 24. With the exploit ready and profiles for 9 exploitable versions, the attacker launched a targeting campaign that followed a clear funnel: Stage 1: Global Discovery (19,000 targets) Using FOFA — a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan — the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. These were devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet, discoverable through certificate fingerprints and HTTP response signatures. Stage 2: Version Fingerprinting (5,000 alive) A custom version scanner ran with 200 concurrent threads against all 19,000 targets, identifying which devices were actually online and what PAN-OS version they were running. Approximately 5,000 responded with version information. Stage 3: Geographic and Version Filtering (240 targets) From the 5,000 alive devices, the attacker filtered to servers located in only United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. They then further filtered to versions matching their exploit profiles (the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30). This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls. Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts. Stage 4: Automated Exploitation (24 rooted) The 240 targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target. For each success, the batch: Ran the full PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain Planted a 103-byte PHP root webshell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall ( /unauth/php/change_password.php ) Verified root by executing id through the webshell Logged the target's hostname and IP to a success CSV Moved to the next target At this point, 24 firewalls had been successfully rooted. Stage 5: Triage (2 firewalls prioritized) For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker did nothing beyond planting the webshell. No persistence, no tunnels, no post-exploitation tools. The servers were effectively owned and parked , allowing the attacker to return through the webshell at any time. Two servers seemingly associated with one target progressed beyond this stage. Both appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment. Stage 6: The Pivot (Shifting from Firewall to Domain) Among the 24 rooted firewalls, two belonged to a US government-affiliated organization. The running configuration extracted from the first firewall revealed an environment with characteristics suggesting government affiliation: CAC (Common Access Card) authentication, a specific naming prefix, and standardized government-style asset naming. The configuration file contained the organization's complete internal network topology: domain controllers, a central firewall management server, a Keycloak SSO server, a GitLab instance, GlobalProtect VPN gateways, and the Active Directory domain. The first firewall was rooted on Oct 23 at 18:14 UTC during the automated batch. But it crashed shortly after — likely from the ~900MB of exploit traffic — and never came back online. The attacker monitored it with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn't. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch. Recognizing the organization's value from the first firewall's configuration, the attacker created a separate, dedicated campaign and successfully exploited it on Oct 24 at 10:09 UTC. Within hours, the attacker: Built a persistent tunnel into the internal network. An 8-port reverse SSH tunnel connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure, forwarding access to: Domain controllers (LDAP, LDAPS, RDP) The internal firewall management server GlobalProtect VPN infrastructure A SOCKS5 proxy for arbitrary internal network access The tunnel was wrapped in a systemd service and an rc.local boot hook, both launching scripts from /usr/local/lib/.panops/ — it survives reboots and automatically reconnects. Exploited the management server through the tunnel. At 11:35 UTC, less than 90 minutes after rooting the second firewall, the attacker used the newly gained server access and the same PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain against a third government server - the internal firewall management server that was only reachable through the tunnel. This server centrally manages all of the organization's firewalls. Compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials, and network settings. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25. Launched an AD attack campaign from the management server. Because the management server already had LDAP connectivity to Active Directory (it needs it to authenticate VPN users), the attacker used it as their launch platform for domain attacks: Decrypted the LDAP service account password — the device config stores it encrypted, but with root access the attacker has the master key. They extracted it in plaintext and hardcoded it into every subsequent script. Enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries. Sprayed passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords. The domain had lockoutThreshold=0 — meaning no account lockout, allowing unlimited spray attempts. Attempted to create backdoor AD accounts — both a user account (tried in every OU) and a machine account (exploiting the default MachineAccountQuota setting). Analyzed AD ACL chains for privilege escalation paths. Attempted SAML signing key extraction from the Keycloak IdP configuration. Probed Keycloak SSO for authentication bypass. The attack results — whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted — stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered. This means we cannot determine the full extent of the compromise. Figure 2: The attack path. PHP2Shell and Fragnesia root the perimeter firewall, a reverse SSH tunnel reaches the internal management server, and the decrypted LDAP service account opens Active Directory. Management Server → Active Directory Status Activity ✓ LDAP password decrypted from config ✓ Full user & group enumeration ? Password spray (all users, no lockout) ? Backdoor user + machine account creation ? SAML signing key extraction What the Attacker Has Now From the recovered artifacts, we can confirm the attacker possesses: Persistent remote access to the organization's internal network via a boot-surviving reverse tunnel and SOCKS proxy — likely still active Root webshells on two firewalls and the firewall management server — likely still active The full Active Directory user and group listing — a complete organizational blueprint Decrypted LDAP service account credentials — enabling direct AD queries at any time Private keys harvested from the PAN-OS firewall filesystem — HA replication keys, SSL/TLS certificate keys, and device authentication keys Complete network topology — every IP, hostname, subnet, server role, and VPN gateway SAML IdP configuration with weak security settings ( validate-idp-certificate: no ) 22 additional parked firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea — ready for exploitation at any time What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure. Attribution Indicators We do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 tracks this activity as CL-UNK-1280 and attributes it to a Chinese-speaking attacker in the UTC+8 time zone. However, multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation: Indicator Detail Target selection US, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea exclusively. These are the primary strategic intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned operations in the Pacific. FOFA The internet reconnaissance platform used to discover targets is a Chinese service. iox A Chinese-developed tunneling utility observed among the recovered tools. DeepSeek and Kimi The LLMs configured in the aiscan offensive security platform are Chinese language models. UTC+8 timestamps The infrastructure's clock ran on China Standard Time, confirmed by comparing log timestamps against HTTP Date: response headers from targets. Chinese-language prompts The aiscan session logs contain user messages in Chinese. Conclusion This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing. The exploitation itself was automated and efficient: 240 targets attempted in a single batch, with version-specific profiles selected automatically. There was a clear-cut focus on government targets. The attacker scanned 19,000 firewalls, rooted 24, and immediately identified the two that mattered. Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign — all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet. The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active webshells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions. Palo Alto Networks device telemetry shows continued exploitation attempts against exposed PAN-OS devices. See the Palo Alto Networks website for full guidance and indicators of compromise. Closing the Gap Between Discovery and Defense For governments and critical infrastructure, finding a vulnerability is only the beginning. Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise. Dream addresses that challenge through two complementary cyberdefense platforms: Sphere scales national cyber defense. It maps exposure, prioritizes risks, and detects and responds to attacks across government networks, tailored to each nation’s threats and infrastructure. Hero scales cyber research. Its autonomous research agents help experts investigate threats, discover and validate vulnerabilities—including in software without source code—and develop remediation guidance and patches. This is the tool that was used by Dream researchers to conduct the investigation detailed in this post. Together, they connect deeper investigation with defense across the national attack surface. Install Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin . Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app . For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications. Windows Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1 | iex Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. Find your work A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as: Working: still busy. Blocked: waiting for you. Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere. Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine. The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. Work on another machine Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. Make it yours Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format. Layouts and mods · Commands Updates and privacy Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves. Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod. For agents herdr-app --skill This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. herdr-app ls herdr-app status herdr-app commands The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments. Build from source For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing . Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI . Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git cd herdr-app just build just test just install Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages. To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: python scripts/bench.py --bin < app executable > --set spinners --seconds 20 The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py . title: GitLab Security Incident: Attempted Exploitation of CVE-2026-97229
body_text: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 | Alpine Linux About Downloads Releases Community Sponsors Donate docs wiki git issues packages mirrors security Small. Simple. Secure. Alpine Linux is a security-oriented, lightweight Linux distribution based on musl libc and busybox. 2026-10-28 GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 Update October 30: GitLab is open again. See GitLab is back: what you need to do for what to set up again and the new SSH host key fingerprints. On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with. GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites. If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org. What happened The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12 , but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23 , in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9. The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out. Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch. If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later. If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable. Incident Timeline Date Event Oct 29 GitLab reopened, upgraded to 19.3.7 Oct 28 GitLab rebuild complete; all passwords reset and GitLab's secret keys replaced Oct 27 GitLab closed to everyone except developers and build servers; rebuild started Oct 26 Found the instance still vulnerable after the upgrade Oct 25 to 26 Attacker returns and tries to get back in; attempts fail Oct 24 aports, packages and Oct 21 releases verified against outside records Oct 23 Attacker's account blocked; Ruby releases the fix Oct 22 Upgraded to GitLab 19.3.6 Oct 21 Main attack; GitLab crashes, 502 errors and failed CI jobs Oct 20 Attacker registers an account and starts probing Oct 13 CVE-2026-97229 published; we upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5 (which had the fix) by mistake Oct 12 GitLab releases the fix What we know and what we can’t rule out What we found Alpine releases and packages were not modified. The October 21 stable releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3), including their ISO images and the minirootfs tarballs the official alpine Docker images are built from, and all packages built from October 20 to 24 came from aports commits we verified against records outside GitLab. See the FAQ below for details. No signing keys were exposed. The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server. No evidence that the attacker’s code ran: timing probes showed no delays, and we found no unexpected files, keys, hooks or processes. No private data was returned to the attacker through any web or API request we can see. Why we can’t be sure A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs. Some logs from the attack day are gone (background job logs, the old container’s filesystem). We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either. What could have been exposed if the attack succeeded Email addresses, names and IP addresses of all users Password hashes 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials Personal access tokens (stored as hashes) Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests FAQ Why did we rebuild GitLab if we were able to mitigate the attack? Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind. While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal. Are Alpine packages and releases affected? We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases. Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer’s clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits. We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date. Is Alpine’s ruby package affected? The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21 ships Ruby 3.3.13; both include the fix. Run apk upgrade to get it. What are we changing in response to this event? Fixed Ruby: the rebuilt instance runs a Ruby with the fix (3.3.13 or later). Faster patching: apply critical GitLab security releases within a day, and check each release for Ruby or other component patches our own build must apply. Better logging: record outbound connections from the GitLab host and database connections, and keep logs longer than 14 days. Signed release tags , so releases can be verified independently of GitLab. © Copyright 2026 Alpine Linux Development Team all rights reserved | Privacy Policy

title: How Google determines the names for bodies of water in Google Earth (2008)
body_text: Google Public Policy Blog: How Google determines the names for bodies of water in Google Earth Public Policy Blog Updates on technology policy issues How Google determines the names for bodies of water in Google Earth Tuesday, April 8, 2008 Posted by Andrew McLaughlin, Director of Global Public Policy Hundreds of millions of users around the world use Google Earth . Many of them have strong -- and sometimes conflicting -- opinions about how places should be named and where borders should be drawn. Disputes over place names and territorial borders exist in nearly every region, and constitute some of the most emotionally charged geopolitical issues in the world today. Since we launched Google Earth in 2004, we have done our best to anticipate these controversies and to address them in a principled, rigorous, and consistent way. We want Google Earth to merit users' trust as an authoritative reference for geographic information; to do that we're aiming to be transparent about the policies we follow when we encounter sensitive geopolitical disputes. In this blog post, I present our approach to naming bodies of water. In future blog posts, I'll discuss our policies on issues like place names, border locations, the content of placemarks generated by the Google Earth community, and the reasons for the blurred imagery that appears in a number of locations. Like any cartographic publisher, our policies have come under scrutiny from many groups, particularly when multiple countries disagree about the correct name for a shared body of water. While most bodies of water have a common name (think "Pacific Ocean"), others are called different names by different countries and cultures. Some variations in placenames are attributable to language-based variations (think "Germany" in English, "l'Allemagne" in French, "Deutschland" in German, etc.). Other differences, however, reflect broader political, historical, or cultural disputes. For example, the body of water between the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula is known as the "Sea of Japan" in Japan, but as the "East Sea" in South Korea. As the publishers of a geographic reference tool, we believe that Google should not choose sides in international geopolitical disputes. For this reason, we've chosen to implement a uniform policy of Primary Local Usage . Under this policy, the English Google Earth client displays the primary, common, local name(s) given to a body of water by the sovereign nations that border it. If all bordering countries agree on the name, then the common single name is displayed (e.g. "Caribbean Sea" in English, "Mar Caribe" in Spanish, etc.). But if different countries dispute the proper name for a body of water, our policy is to display both names, with each label placed closer to the country or countries that use it. One of the great features of Google Earth is that it enables us to provide significantly greater amounts of information than flat paper maps. So in addition to showing both disputed names, we also provide a clickable text box that provides some more detailed explanatory text. For example, if you click on the "Yellow Sea" or "West Sea" placemarks, you will get: "The Yellow Sea is the common English name associated with this maritime feature, known in China as Huáng Hǎi or 黄海 (Mandarin). In Korea, this feature is commonly referred to as the West Sea; in Korean Sŏ Hae or 서해 (Hangul)". For language clients other than English, we display only the preferred name in the relevant language. For example, the Japanese client of Google Earth shows "Sea of Japan" in Japanese (日本海), while the Korean version shows "East Sea" in Korean (동해). In these cases, we still include both labels in the click-box political annotation. We believe this solution makes our product more helpful to users in each language by presenting the name they expect to see, but without sidestepping the existence of a disputed alternative name. In that way, we provide more, rather than less, information while maintaining a good user interface and experience. When our policy says that we display the "primary, common, local" names for a body of water, each of those three adjectives has an important and distinct meaning. By saying "primary", we aim to include names of dominant use, rather than having to add every conceivable local nickname or variation. By saying "common", we mean to include names which are in widespread daily use, rather than giving immediate recognition to any arbitrary governmental re-naming. In other words, if a ruler announced that henceforth the Pacific Ocean would be named after her mother, we would not add that placemark unless and until the name came into common usage. Finally, by saying "local", we aim to reflect the primary and common names used by countries that actually border the body of water, as they are the countries recognized under international law as having a special sovereign stake in it. In our view, the Primary Local Usage rule generates the optimal combination of neutrality, objectivity, and legitimacy. We also hope that it meets the expectations of the vast majority of our users and demonstrates the proper sensitivity to these important geopolitical disputes. Alternative Policies We Considered As we worked our way through the current set of disputed names for bodies of water, we considered and ultimately decided against several alternative policy approaches, including: Authoritative International Institutions. We considered attempting to extricate Google entirely from the problem of deciding placenames by simply deferring to the determinations of an existing, authoritative, multilateral or multistakeholder institution. Under this policy, we would simply adopt in toto the naming choices set by that body, without exercising any independent judgment of our own. In particular, we considered using the publications and documents of the United Nations Cartographic Section as the authoritative references for naming bodies of water. Under scrutiny, though, the U.N. Cartographic Section's publications do not provide the level of coverage and detail that we hope to achieve for Google Earth. Moreover, quite understandably, the United Nations as an institution does not take official positions on geographical names (which would occasionally require it to take sides among the competing claims of two or more member states), but instead the Cartographic Section only issues guidance in the form of "informational practices" for use in U.N. documents and publications. Moreover, the U.N. is viewed by some as a politicized organization, favoring the claims of some countries and regions over others. Also within the U.N. system, we looked at the reports of the U.N. Conference on the Standardization of Geographical Names, which convenes every five years. That Conference, however, does not take positions on geopolitical disputes between countries, and so reliance on its reports is not a realistic option. We also considered adopting the names used by the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), an international group that works, among other things, to standardize nautical charts and documents. But the IHO's naming work in recent decades has focused on (a) the naming of undersea features, and (b) setting the boundaries and limits of oceans and seas. It has not undertaken to resolve current geopolitical disputes. Moreover, the organization's membership includes the national hydrographic offices of fewer than half of all countries. Geographic Organizations. We considered adopting the naming conventions of one or more widely-respected national-level geographic organizations like the US National Geographic Society and the UK Royal Geographical Society. But these organizations exist only in a handful of large, rich economies, and many believe they do not represent the views and values of other parts of the world. They also occasionally reach differing conclusions on names and naming conventions, and it would be difficult to set a neutral, objective rule for deciding which organization to follow. Academics. Finally, we also considered conducting a survey of credentialed geography academics to assess their views as to the proper name(s) to be displayed. But this option too is fraught with likely bias -- the mere process of choosing which academics to survey would be highly subjective. And we reasoned that if our chosen experts were evenly split or undecided, we'd still be no closer to delegating the responsibility to outside authorities. All things considered, we believe that the Primary Local Usage rule, if rigorously and evenhandedly applied, is a better choice than any of these three alternatives. Of course, we recognize that this policy will leave some people unhappy about a resulting name that is displayed for each disputed body of water. But we hope they will accept that showing all the names of primary and common use by all the countries bordering a body of water is fair and diplomatic. Perhaps most importantly, we also recognize that we have no monopoly on geographic truth. Debate about the right policies and practices for Google Earth is valuable. Happily enough, one of the great features of Google Earth is its ability to support the creation and display of data layers by an interested person. It is our fervent hope that different communities will use Google Earth as an open platform to create content that accurately reflects their views. We welcome additions to our community and web layers so that users can access all points of view. title: LLM Voice
body_text: LLM Voice Refactoring Agile Architecture About Thoughtworks Topics Architecture Refactoring Agile Delivery Microservices Data Testing DSL about me About Books FAQ content Videos Content Index Fragments Board Games Photography Thoughtworks Home Insights Careers Radar Engineering follow RSS Mastodon LinkedIn Bluesky X BGG LLM Voice 29 October 2026 Martin Fowler Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about âadopting a new sales motion ,â or âa sharp round-up of newsâ. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves. 1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up. 2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source). Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress. In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease . I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom. A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM. There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3 . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose. 3: Michael Nygard commented: âThere you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.â Notes 1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up. 2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source). 3: Michael Nygard commented: âThere you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.â Acknowledgements Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post. I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post. The Founders Edition is a limited run of the Form Studio 1, available at launch while supplies last. It comes in signature Graphite or limited-edition Aqua, Violet, or Teal, and each printer displays a Founders Edition tag in its interface. Founders Edition perks include your first bottle of Alpha Resin for $29, a limited-edition Form Studio 1 plushie, and 25% off Form Now orders, up to $100 (US only). What is the Form Studio 1 used for? The Form Studio 1 is a desktop resin 3D printer for creators, designers, hobbyists, and studios who want professional-quality prints. Popular uses include tabletop miniatures and figurines, cosplay props, product design prototypes, art and sculpture, custom gifts, and small-batch parts for side businesses. What technology powers the Form Studio 1’s speed? The Form Studio 1 is an MSLA printer built on Low Force Display (LFD) technology. Its backlight unit uses 28 high-powered LEDs and collimating lenses to cure resin quickly and evenly across the entire build platform. How fast is the Form Studio 1? Most prints finish in under 2 hours (based on the 80th percentile print height of 53 mm at 100 µm layer height), and print time stays the same whether you print one part or a full build platform. With Alpha Fast Resin, the Form Studio 1 prints at up to 130 mm/hour. How accurate are parts printed on the Form Studio 1? XY dimensional tolerances are ±0.5% for 1–30 mm features, ±0.2% for 31–80 mm features, and ±0.03% for 81–150 mm features, with a lower limit of ±0.08 mm. A 35 µm pixel size and pre-tuned anti-aliasing deliver sharp detail, smooth surfaces, and parts that fit together as designed. How reliable is the Form Studio 1? In internal testing, the Form Studio 1 has shown print success comparable to Form 4, which achieved a 98.7% print success rate in independent testing . Full reliability testing for the Form Studio 1 is underway. How long does it take to learn to use the Form Studio 1? The system is designed to be highly intuitive. Most users can learn the full printing workflow in about 10 minutes. What software do I use to prepare prints for the Form Studio 1? PreForm , Formlabs’ free print preparation software, automatically orients models, generates supports, and slices your files, so you can optimize your layout and send jobs straight to the printer. Form Studio 1 is not compatible with third-party slicers or print preparation software. What materials can I use with the Form Studio 1? The Form Studio 1 supports six Alpha Resins developed specifically for it: Alpha Grey , Alpha White , Alpha Black , Alpha Clear , Alpha Fast , and Alpha Model . It also supports Tough 1500 Resin , Flexible 80A Resin , and True Cast Resin . Every supported material comes with validated print settings tested on the Form Studio 1, so you get reliable results without calibration or trial and error. Most other Formlabs resins are also compatible. These dispense automatically from the cartridge, but you'll need to tune your own settings and use the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank Pro . Print performance may be lower, and mechanical properties may differ from published values. You can also print third-party 405 nm resins using Open Material Mode. Automatic dispensing is disabled in this mode, so you'll pour resin manually and tune your own settings. What’s the difference between the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank and the Resin Tank Pro? The Form Studio 1 Resin Tank uses a film engineered for Alpha Resins, which gives faster prints and a better finish on supported surfaces. Some materials, including Tough 1500 Resin V2 and most third-party resins, contain ingredients that damage this film, so they require the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank Pro . Never print these materials in the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank. The film can degrade quickly and leak resin, which can damage your printer and leave a mess to clean up. How long do resin tanks last? Can I replace the tank film? Resin tanks are consumables, and their lifespan depends mainly on the number of layers printed and accumulated wear. With proper maintenance and Formlabs materials, Form Studio 1 resin tanks are designed to last more than 75,000 layers. The tank film can’t be replaced on either the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank or the Resin Tank Pro . What post-processing does the Form Studio 1 require? After printing, wash parts in IPA or Formlabs Resin Washing Solution to remove uncured resin, then UV-cure them to reach final mechanical properties. Form Studio Wash+Cure , or Form Wash and Form Cure , automate both steps. Can I monitor my prints remotely? Yes. A built-in camera lets you watch active prints, view time-lapses, and review your print history from the Form Mobile app or Formlabs Dashboard . Can the camera be disabled? Yes, in three ways: cover it with the included camera cap (in the accessories box or print your own from the preloaded print jobs), turn it off in the printer settings (also shown during onboarding), or unplug the camera cable to disconnect it completely. The camera and time-lapse are separate settings, so you can turn off time-lapse while keeping the camera on.
